Another riddle describes a pillar that stands and supports a house; the riddler uses the word \"man\" to entangle the guessers’ thoughts until revealing that the pillar is like a man upholding a great house. A further explanation discusses the ear of a man, noting that wind moves trees, grass, and houses, but not the ear; the man moves or is carried away while the ear remains erect. {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l27839-l28008","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"UNTHLANGUNTHLANGU.24 / IZINGANEKWANE. / IZINGANEKWANE. / UXTIILANGUNTHLANGU.; lines 27839-28008","start":"27839","end":"28008","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this portion of the tale, the woman who had given birth to a snake-child is housed near the village gateway and quarrels with the other women. They mock her for exalting herself despite having borne a beast instead of the long-expected royal child, call her a dog, boast that they have "given birth" to the village, and tell her to return to the pool where her snake-child lives. She is ashamed and falls silent. The king intervenes, telling them to leave her alone, saying he had thought she would bear him a king but instead bore a monster, and he urges them not to laugh at her. The other women complain that she tries to make herself chief because she gave birth to a snake, and she replies that she now understands they took her into their village only because she bore an animal.

The narrative then shifts to the pool, where the snake lives in the water. The foremost child turns back the snake’s skin and emerges as a human boy, removing the snake-skin entirely. Many human children follow in order; they are all the children of their mother. The boy, Unthlatu-ye-siziba, tells a girl called Ntombi-ntombi that they are brother and sister. The children remain for a time in the pool, then Unthlatu-ye-siziba urges them to go out, ascend to the land, and travel toward their home. There are ten children in all, five boys and five girls.

On their journey they reach a thicket, decide to look for ox-bones, find the bones of ten oxen, and set them in order. By doing so they restore the oxen to life. They mount the revived cattle to ride on; Unthlatu-ye-siziba’s ox is named Umpengempe.

An editorial footnote comments that the motif of women giving birth to animals is common in Zulu tales and suggests a connection with the West African custom called "roondah," a system of food prohibitions likened to Polynesian taboo. Citing Du Chaillu, it describes families for whom the meat of a particular animal (such as Bos brachyceros or crocodile) is forbidden because an ancestress once gave birth to such a creature. These families are said to avoid the tabooed meat even at risk of starvation, fearing that eating it would cause miscarriages, monstrous animal-shaped births, or terrible content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l25514-l25717","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / UMDHLUBU  NESELESELE. / IZINGANEKWANE. / IZIN  G AN  EK  WANE.; lines 25514-25717","start":"25514","end":"25717","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In the conclusion of the Uselesele (frog-man) episode, people take oxen and dance for someone in the bush at a father's command, bring him home, and the king feeds him and asks what reward he wants. Uselesele, identified in a footnote as \"The-frog-man,\" builds a great town, becomes a great chief, continually slaughters cattle so men come to ask for meat, and gains followers who leave their former chiefs because of the abundant food. People explain that he received cattle and men as a reward for bringing their princess to the king, warn others not to speak ill of him, and he ultimately reigns as a king. The narrative then shifts to another story: Unkosi-yasenthla (King of the Uplands) hears that Unkosi-yasenzansi (King of the Lowlands) has a very beautiful daughter named Umdhlubu. He sends his people to see her and select a beautiful damsel from among Unkosi-yasenzansi’s children. The daughters are summoned; the envoys, described as the king’s eyes, carefully inspect them and see that Umdhlubu surpasses the others in beauty, so they choose her as the only one fit to be the king’s queen. Questioned by the people and by messengers from the king, they explain that a snake had been put into the pool, that the snake’s father is Unthlangunthlangu, and that their mother is the daughter of an unnamed man. A man explains that this is the Isitshakamana, an animal that knows the names of all the old people. The youth describes the beast as having its eyes, nostrils, ears, and mouth all in one place and says it is destroying him with fear, especially when it calls him by the names of his father, grandfather, and earlier ancestors, including generations unknown even to his father and grandfather. In the evening many young men enter the house so the damsels can point out their favourites, and Umamba, another child of the king who appears as a snake, also comes in. The damsels flee screaming to the upper end of the house until the king and the people tell them not to fear, since Umamba is the king’s child. Umamba sits on his mat. The damsels ask how he became a snake, and are told that his mother had previously lost her children by death, and finally bore him; they marvel greatly. Later, when the damsels are choosing favourites among the young men, the bride’s sister points out Umamba. After they rest, Unanana-bosele rises in the morning, grinds much maize, puts it into a large pot with amasi (soured milk), and sets out carrying a knife. She comes to an antelope and asks it to point out the elephant that has eaten her children, noting that the elephant has one tusk. The antelope directs her toward a place where the trees are very high and the stones are white. She then asks a leopard the same question and receives the same directions. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l36397-l36497","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / UTIKOLOSHE. / THE  ABATWA. / THE  ABATWA.; lines 36397-36497","start":"36397","end":"36497","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes the Abatwa, a people who dwell among rocks and have no fixed village; wherever they kill game and consume it serves temporarily as their village before they move on. When a traveler unexpectedly meets an individual Umutwa, the Umutwa asks where he was seen. Initially, travelers answered truthfully that they saw him in that very place, which caused the Umutwa to feel despised for his littleness and to shoot and kill the man with his bow. People then realized that the Abatwa like to be magnified and hate reminders of their smallness, so they adopted a new greeting: when asked where they saw the Umutwa, they reply that they saw him from far away, on a distant mountain, which makes him rejoice that he has become great; this became the regular salutation. It is also said that when game is exhausted where they have been living, the Abatwa travel by mounting a single horse, sitting in a line from its neck to its tail, and if they fail to find new game they eat the horse. It explains how cattle given in marriage and their offspring become the property of particular wives' houses, creating separate household units. A wife whose cow's remaining offspring form a new house is called a 'hill' (intaba), and her son, the iponsakubusa ('almost-a-chief'), leads that house. The text further describes the rights of the chief wife of the great house, the formation and separate inheritance of a secondary great house established with the husband's private property, and the seating and authority hierarchy between the eldest son of the great house and the iponsakubusa.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"When a cow has been used to pay a wife's dowry, the offspring not required for further dowries remain as the property of that wife's house, and she is called a 'hill' (intaba).","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The son of the wife who is called a 'hill' is called iponsakubusa ('almost-a-chief'); he is not chief over with.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"When cattle remain after paying a dowry, the father may give his chief wife a cow so that it becomes the property of her house, instead of letting the remaining cattle belong to the house of the wife who is a 'hill'.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The chief wife can make a strong claim on cattle if her husband marries another wife and does not place the new wife under her authority, saying, \"Why is my village devoured?\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the dispute over a new wife, the husband replies that the wife he is about to take does not belong to the chief wife's house, but is his own wife, a secondary wife.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The dispute between the chief wife and the husband over the secondary wife is settled by the rule that the first-born female child of the secondary wife becomes the property of the chief house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"\"Indhlu yakwabo\" is the term for the house of a secondary or tertiary wife.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The husband has private or personal property with which he can do as he pleases, and if any of this property remains unappropriated at his death, it is the heritage of his eldest son.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The secondary great house (indhlu yakwabo-ponsakubusa) is constituted when the husband takes a secondary chief wife using his own private property.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The secondary great house has no right to inherit the property of the great house except if death removes all the heirs of the great house, and the heir of the great house cannot claim the heritage of the secondary great house so long as any male child of that house survives.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"An intaba ('hill') is defined as a single hill standing out alone, used as a name for a wife who stands alone as the beginning of a new house owing nothing to the husband's ancestral great house nor to the house of the chief wife.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The eldest son of the chief wife is chief and heir of his father's great house.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The iponsakubusa is chief and heir in the secondary great house but is not chief with respect to his father's great house.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In a kraal or hut, the chief's place doorway.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"If neither the father nor the eldest son of the great house is present, the iponsakubusa sits in the chief place above content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l9413-l9511","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    VI.  73 / FARGARD    VII.  75 / FARGARD    VII.  77 / FARGARD    VII.  79; lines 9413-9511","start":"9413","end":"9511","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"He shall go away into the world of the fiends, into that dark world, made of darkness, the offspring of darkness.\"","summary":"Ahura Mazda, in dialogue with Zarathustra, lays down rules about ritual impurity and the treatment of clothes and corpses. Clothes rendered impure can never again be used by priests or laymen but may be reused as coverings for the sick, reflecting a prohibition against wasting even small amounts of valuable material. Throwing clothing on a corpse marks a person as impious and deprives them of a place in the happy realm after death, consigning them instead to a dark world of fiends reached by their own deeds. Zarathustra asks whether those who eat the carcass of a dog or a man, or who bring a corpse with filth into water or fire, can ever become clean again. Ahura Mazda replies that they cannot: such sinners become associated with the demonic corpse-pollution Nasu, suffer severe punitive measures, remain unclean forever, and are linked to the proliferation of gnats, locusts, drought, and a harsh, fiend-produced winter. Translator’s notes elaborate that a carcass-eater becomes a Nasu, must be destroyed, and that his soul abides in hell until the resurrection, and that outbreaks of insects are attributed to corpses being brought to water and fire.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ahura Mazda declares that certain clothes can never be used by a Zaotar, Havanan, Atare-vakhsha, Frabaretar, Aberet, Asnatar, Rathwiskar, Sraosha-varez, or by any priest, warrior, or husbandman, even when washed and cleansed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The same clothes may be used in a Mazdean house as coverings or sheets for a woman in her sickness or a man unfit for work who must sit in the place of infirmity, until they can withdraw and move their hands.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The text states that Ahura Mazda does not allow wasting anything of value, not even as little as an Asperena’s weight of thread or the amount of thread a maid lets fall while spinning.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Whoever throws any clothing on a dead body, even as much as a maid lets fall in spinning, is described as not a pious person while alive and will not have a place in the happy realm after death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Such a person is said to go away into the world of the fiends, a dark, dismal world made of darkness and called the offspring of darkness.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage explains that sinners are delivered to the dark world of the fiends by their own doings and their own souls.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda whether someone who has eaten the carcass of a dog or of a man can become clean again.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A translator’s note explains that the carcass-eater lodges the Nasu in himself, becomes a Nasu, and therefore must be destroyed.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that the carcass-eater cannot become clean: his burrow shall be dug out, his life torn out, his bright eyes put out, and the Druj Nasu falls upon him and takes hold of him even to the end of the nails, leaving him unclean forever.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A further note states that if a man eats of a carcass with sinful intent, his house and family shall be destroyed, his heart torn out, his eyes put out, and his soul shall abide in hell until the resurrection; ritual washings are of no avail for him, though without sinful intent a person may be washed and purified.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Zarathustra asks whether one who has brought a corpse with filth into the waters or unto the fire, and made either unclean, can be clean again.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Ahura Mazda replies that such a person cannot become clean and calls them wicked ones, men turned to Nasus, who most increase gnats and locusts and the grass-destroying drought.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The same wicked, Nasu-turned men are said to increase the power of the winter produced by the fiends, described as cattle-killing, thick-snowing, overflowing, and piercing.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A note glosses the phrase “men turned to Nasus” as possibly meaning “those Nasu-makers.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Another note reports a tradition that when there are many gnats and locusts it is due to corpses having been brought to water and to fire.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura Mazda","description":"Supreme deity who answers Zarathustra’s questions, sets rules about purity, waste, and the treatment of corpses, and pronounces punishments for transgressors.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:6","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Zarathustra (Zarathuitra / Zarathiutra)","description":"Prophetic figure who addresses Ahura Mazda as Maker of the material world and asks whether various offenders can become clean again.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Corpse-related sinner / Nasu-bearer","description":"Generic figure representing humans who mishandle corpses—throwing clothing on a dead body, eating the carcass of a dog or a man, or bringing a corpse with filth into water or fire—and are described as wicked, turned to Nasus, impious, and irreversibly unclean.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Sick woman or infirm man in a Mazdean house","description":"Ill or incapacitated household member who may use impure clothes as coverings or sheets in the place of infirmity until recovery of strength.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Druj Nasu","description":"Demonic or personified force of corpse-pollution that falls upon the carcass-eater, cakes offered in honour of angels or deceased persons and shared among participants.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ahura Mazda is content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l1024-l1125","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / UHLAKANYANA. / PREFACE  TO  THE  TALE  OF  UTHLAKANYANA. / IZINGANEKWANE.; lines 1024-1125","start":"1024","end":"1125","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes the weasel (ikcakide). It harasses men by leaving the path only slightly and growling so that they fear a dangerous animal and go around, later realizing it was only a weasel and feeling ashamed. The weasel is said to be fiercely hostile to snakes, especially the imamba: it watches the snake’s hole, enters while the snake is out feeding, then seizes the snake’s head as it re-enters, kills it, plays with the dead snake, and finally jumps back and forth over it before eating it. The weasel is also regarded as causing very bad luck: if trappers catch a weasel in their traps, they believe it will prevent them from catching other animals, as the weasel mystically “stands in the way,” and what follows after its entry into the trap is misfortune.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The weasel, if it does not choose to get out of the way, quits the path only a little, growls, and frightens a man who then goes around, thinking a wild animal obstructs the path.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After going some distance and looking back, the man sees the weasel depart and run away, feels ashamed that he quit the path because of such a small creature, and returns to the path.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The weasel is described as being at great enmity with snakes and Citing Dr. Bleek, he summarizes a prevailing theory that clicks in Kafir dialects are a relatively modern intrusion linked to contact with Hottentots, while some related dialects and languages lack clicks entirely. Historical observations by Kolben about non-clicking natives of \"Terra du Natal\" are mentioned, and the narrator suggests comparative philological research may clarify whether clicking developed later or non-clicking peoples were displaced. The text then offers technical distinctions between Hottentot and Kafir clicks, the narrator's disagreement with Bleek, his description of how clicks in Zulu always accompany consonants, the orthographic use of letters c, q, and x to represent click-consonant clusters, the specific consonant combinations involved, and scholarly disagreement (Lepsius and Bleek versus Grout and Dohne) over whether clicks precede or follow consonants in pronunciation. Ahura Mazda orders that the man burning the corpse must be killed and the cauldron and tripod removed. The polluted fire is then to be extinguished by kindling wood from it and laying out nine bundles of wood, each a Vitasti away from the fire, separating and dispersing them so the fire dies out quickly. Later, Ahura Mazda tells Spitama Zarathustra that if a man devoutly brings specific sweet-smelling woods or other fragrant wood to the fire, then wherever the wind carries the perfume of the fire, Fire, the son of Ahura Mazda, will go and kill thousands of unseen Daevas, fiends (brood of darkness), and pairs of Yatus and Pairikas.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Mazda-worshippers are described as walking, running, riding, or driving when they may come He reviews Lewis Grout’s adoption of Lepsius’ special characters for clicks and explains why he finds them impractical. After consulting Max Müller, who suggested using the letters k, t, and l with dots or italics as click signs, the author rejects this proposal because those letters already have established phonetic values in Zulu. Provisionally he decides to continue using the letters c, q, and x (written in italics as diacritic marks without inherent consonantal value) to denote clicks, and notes a personal preference for diacritics based on g, k, and n. He then describes Zulu aspirate sounds, identifying four types (h, a lateral fricative, and two guttural fricatives), and criticizes the practice of using the letter r to represent a guttural I  45 / I46  VENDIDAD. / FARGARD    XII.  147 / FARGARD    XII.  149; lines 12878-12967","start":"12878","end":"12967","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In a dialogue between Ahura Mazda and Spitama Zarathustra, Zarathustra repeatedly asks how to cleanse a house. Ahura Mazda prescribes a ritual: washing bodies and clothes three times, chanting the Gathas three times, offering sacrifice to his Fire with bundles of baresma, and bringing libations to the good waters. After this, the house is called clean, and the waters, the fire, and the Amesha Spentas are allowed to enter. The text also lays down different periods during which \"they shall stay\" after the death of various kin: for a male or female cousin, fifteen days for the righteous and thirty for sinners; for a cousin’s son or daughter, ten and twenty days; for a cousin’s grandson or granddaughter, five and ten days. earlier.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaker addresses Ahura Mazda as \"Holy One\" and \"Maker of the material world\" and asks First, a case involving a woman who drinks \"strength-giving\" water (elsewhere described as defiled) leads to instructions that worshippers of Mazda consult priestly judges (the Ratu and Sraosha-varez) to fix a penalty; Ahura Mazda identifies the deed as that of a Peshotanu and prescribes a severe whipping. A commentary note adds that in later practice the husband performs a penitential rite for his wife's fault before the Dastur. Next, Zarathustra asks whether eating vessels touched by a dog's carcass or a human corpse can be purified; Ahura Mazda replies that metal and stone vessels can be cleansed by repeated washings with gomez, earth, and water in set numbers, while earth, wood, and clay vessels remain permanently unclean. Zarathustra then asks about a cow that has eaten a dog's carcass or a human corpse; Ahura Mazda says she can be made clean, but for one year the priest must not take her milk, cheese, or meat for use with the baresma and libation, after which the faithful may eat of her again. Notes explain that the libation waters are accompanied by offerings of milk, cheese, and meat consumed by the priest holding the baresma, and that products and offspring of the defiled cow have differing purity depending on how they are obtained and when they were conceived. The section ends with the beginning of a new, incomplete question to Ahura Mazda.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The text mentions a that the penalty is two hundred stripes with the Aspahe-astra and two hundred stripes with the Sraosho-karana.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A later note says of death or serious illness.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Zarathustra addresses Ahura Mazda as Maker of the material world and Holy One, asking whether eating vessels that have been touched by the carcass of a dog or the corpse of a man can be made clean.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that such vessels can be made clean if they are of certain materials.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"For gold vessels, the prescribed procedure is to wash once with gomez, rub once with earth, and wash once with water, after which they are considered clean.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"For silver vessels, the same sequence with faithful may eat of her as before.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A note explains that the libation waters (Zaothra) are accompanied by offerings of milk, cheese, and meat, which the priest eats while holding the baresma in his hand.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Another note states that whatever comes from the His own people constantly despise him, believing that only full-grown men can deceive them, and misunderstanding his smallness as contemptible dwarfhood rather than a result of his great cunning and wisdom. He nevertheless deceives them because they do not recognize him as the deceiver. The text gives him additional names and explains that Ukcaijana also denotes a little red animal with a black-tipped tail, portrayed as cleverer than all other animals by stealing and eating the mouse bait from traps set for wild cats before the intended prey arrives. A footnote explains that the mouse used as bait is given special respectful names (umjonjo, injova, umvuzane) and should not be called by its ordinary name impuku, or traps will fail, and mentions beliefs about a captured weasel hindering further success. The tales involve contests between good and malicious genii and notably omit the powerful medicines common in contemporary native beliefs, suggesting antiquity. Two tales feature a Magical Tree and a Rock of Two-holes that opens to those who know a secret phrase, reminiscent of “Open Sesame” in the Forty Thieves. Huge fabulous monsters appear, including Isikgukgumadevu as big as a mountain, Isitwalangcengce (Isidawane) who carries people on its head and eats their brains and serves as a nursery bogey, a giant River Tortoise mistaken for an island, and an enormous Fiery Serpent described as a “Myth of Observation.” The editor notes he has combined Nursery Tales with some fables and other narratives.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Uthlakanyana is described as a cunning, malicious dwarf who possesses magical powers.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Uthlakanyana’s cunning is not exerted on giants alone; the editor comments that “All is fish that comes to Uthlakanyana’s net.”","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The tales include gigantic cannibals, such as the Guzzler in the story of Uthlakanyana, who can carry a man in Hottentots.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Various animals—the leopard, hare, iguana, doves, swallows, pigeons, and mice—appear talking freely and naturally and holding intercourse with humans.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Some animal figures appear in their own characters, while others act as forms assumed by I  35 / I  26  VENDIDAD. / I38  VENDIDAD. / I4O  VENDIDAD.; lines 12426-12475","start":"12426","end":"12475","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"If thou wantest to cleanse the water, say these words aloud: 'Waters we worship, the waters in the tree, the waters in the stream, the waters in the rain.' ... If thou wantest to cleanse the earth, say these words aloud: 'This earth we worship, this earth with the women, this earth which bears us and those women who are thine, O Ahura.' ... If thou wantest to cleanse the cow ... If thou wantest to cleanse the trees ... If thou wantest to cleanse the faithful man or the faithful woman, say these words aloud: 'May the beloved Airyaman come hither ... with the desirable reward that is won by means of the law, and with that boon for holiness that is vouchsafed by Ahura.'\"","summary":"The passage prescribes specific spoken formulas for ritually cleansing water, earth, cattle, trees, and faithful men and women. Waters in trees, streams, and rain are worshipped; the earth is worshipped along with its \"women,\" glossed as heavenly rivers who are wives of the heaven-god and spouses of Ahura. The cow is cleansed by ordering excellent deeds on her behalf, such as providing stables, water, and fodder. Trees are cleansed by recalling that Mazda, through his holiness, made plants grow from a primordial \"him,\" identified in a note as the first-born bull whose corpse produced all plants. Faithful people are cleansed by invoking the beloved Airyaman to come and bring rejoicing, a lawful reward, and a boon of holiness from Ahura. A note adds that no similar spell exists for cleansing the sun, moon, and stars.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"To cleanse the water, the rain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The waters are explicitly described as being present \"in the tree,\" \"in the stream,\" and \"in the rain\" within the worship formula.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"To cleanse the earth, the officiant must say aloud a formula worshipping \"this earth,\" \"this earth with the women to be the Faroers of godly men.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"To cleanse the cow, a formula is given ordering a divine addressee to perform \"most content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l9811-l9957","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    VII.  85 / S6  VENDIDAD / VIII. / FARGARD   VII.  87; lines 9811-9957","start":"9811","end":"9957","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ahura Mazda tells Zarathustra that the ground of a Dakhma remains affected until the corpse’s dust mingles with the earth, and commands him to urge people to pull down Dakhmas; anyone who does so has sins remitted and is spared the post-mortem struggle between two spirits, entering a blissful, undecaying world greeted by the heavenly bodies and Ahura Mazda. An explanatory note describes how, at death, demonic and beneficent beings contend for the soul over three days, with prayers and sacrifices aiding the good powers to lead righteous souls to paradise while others are dragged to hell. Zarathustra then asks where fiends and their worshippers gather, and Ahura Mazda answers that earth-built Dakhmas bearing corpses are the place where fiends congregate, feed on corpses, excrete, revel, and generate stench and diseases, with death having greatest power after sunset; for people of evil spirit, disease-bringing beings intensify these afflictions. Finally, Zarathustra inquires how Mazda-worshippers should deal with a stillborn child in their house, and Ahura Mazda instructs that it be placed on the cleanest, driest, least-traveled ground, at fixed distances from fire, water, consecrated baresma, and the faithful, to keep sacred elements and persons separate from corpse impurity.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ahura Mazda states that the ground on which a Dakhma stands is not restored until the dust of the corpse laid there has mingled with the dust of the earth, and he commands Zarathustra to urge everyone in the material world to pull down Dakhmas.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Whoever pulls down Dakhmas, even as much as the size of his own body, has his sins in thought, word, and deed remitted and atoned for, as by a Patet, including a serious \"tanafuhr\" sin according to the commentary.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"For the man who pulls down Dakhmas, the two spirits will not wage war for his soul, and when he enters the blissful world the stars, moon, and sun rejoice in him, and Ahura Mazda greets him as one who has passed from the decaying world into the undecaying one.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"An explanatory note says that when a man dies, hell and paradise, fiends and gods struggle for possession of his soul for three days and nights; Astovidhotu, Vizaresha, and the bad Vayu drag the souls of the wicked to hell, while Mithra, Sraosha, Rashnu, and the good Vayu take the souls of the good to paradise, helped by the relatives’ prayers and sacrifices to these powers.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda where the fiends and their worshippers are, and where the troops of fiends rush together and come rushing along to kill fifties, hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and myriads of myriads of victims.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that Dakhmas built upon the face of the earth, on which corpses of dead men are laid, are the places where the fiends are and where their troops rush together and come rushing along to kill multitudes.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"On those Dakhmas, fiends take food by eating corpses and void filth, in a way compared to humans eating cooked meal and meat, and humans perceive the smell of this feeding.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Fiends revel on the Dakhmas until the stench is rooted in them; from the Dakhmas arise the infection of diseases such as itch, hot fever, humours, cold fever, rickets, and premature white hair, and death has most power on man there from the time the sun is down.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"If people of evil spirit do not seek a better spirit, the Gaini make those diseases grow stronger by a third on their thighs, hands, and plaited hair; the commentary adds that Dakhmas are seats of infection whose harmful action becomes worse when people live in impiety and vice.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Zarathustra asks what worshippers of Mazda should do if, in the house of a worshipper of Mazda, a woman with child at any month of pregnancy brings forth a stillborn child.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Ahura Mazda replies that the place in that Mazdean house where the stillborn is dealt with should be the ground that is cleanest and driest and least passed through by flocks and herds, by Fire the son of Ahura Mazda, by the consecrated bundles of baresma, and by the faithful.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Zarathustra further asks how far from the fire, the water, the consecrated bundles of baresma, and the faithful this place should be.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that the place should be thirty paces from the fire, thirty paces from the water, thirty paces from the consecrated bundles of baresma, and three paces from the faithful.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura Mazda","description":"Supreme deity who answers Zarathustra’s questions, commands the pulling down of Dakhmas, remits sins, rejoices over the righteous soul, and gives detailed ritual instructions.","role_refs":["role:1","role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4","ev:7","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Spitama Zarathustra","description":"Prophet who addresses Ahura Mazda, The boy pleads with the cannibal not to kill or beat him, asking to be taken out, cleaned of the birdlime, and taken home to the cannibal’s mother, insisting that if he is beaten he will be \"bitter\" and \"not nice.\" An appended discussion then turns to European materials: it notes that people devise various plans to get rid of certain troublesome beings and cites a Danish tradition in which a shrewd woman drives a fiend from a house by killing a pig and making a grotesque pudding including skin, hair, eyes, and bones, which causes the fiend to leave. The cannibal recognizes his cunning, refuses kinship and refuses to lend the calabash, so Uthlakanyana leaves. The narrator notes that Uthlakanyana will use this distrustful cannibal to frighten another cannibal. Uthlakanyana then enters the house of a second cannibal, again claiming him as an uncle. This cannibal, calling Uthlakanyana \"child of my sister,\" invites him to help bray his skin. As they pound the skin, the calabash carried by the first cannibal emits loud \"Boo\" sounds that seem to come from outside and approach with \"loud blowings.\" Uthlakanyana prompts the second cannibal to listen; the noise grows nearer until both flee in fear. The owner of the calabash appears, while the frightened cannibal and Uthlakanyana stand on separate hills; they ask who is alarming them. The calabash carrier identifies himself as \"Mr. Guzzler,\" boasting that he gulps wild spinach and bolts men whole without chewing, which sends the other cannibal running away. An editorial footnote compares this to Gargantua swallowing pilgrims in Rabelais. Uthlakanyana later returns to the calabash owner, who has taken possession of the abandoned house. He again claims him as \"uncle\" and asks to live with him as his child, saying he has lived as a child in other places. The cannibal agrees because Uthlakanyana is smaller, and they live together. The old women suckle the child and leave him with his maternal uncle. When the boy grows into a young man he enjoys herding his uncle's cattle and is respected by the other boys. While they are herding he orders the boys to gather large stones and heat them, then to choose a fine calf from the herd, kill it, skin it, and roast its meat on the heated stones, despite their questions about his motive. On another day, as they herd, officers of the king (who is actually the young man's father) pass by on a journey. They ask the youth who he is, but he does not tell them. Noting that he resembles their king, they take him and bring him to his father. An editorial footnote comments that baking meat with heated stones is not a current custom among the local natives but is common among other peoples, such as Polynesians, suggesting the legend may Usikulumi sews the shin and places it in his sticks. At Uzembeni's place the shin speaks, announcing Uzembeni's arrival. That night, while Usikulumi sleeps alongside the girl in Uzembeni's house, Uzembeni rises, creeps in to seize him, but the shin wakes Usikulumi and tells him to get up because Uzembeni has come; Uzembeni then withdraws, preferring to catch him asleep. At dawn the shin again speaks, telling Usikulumi to depart because Uzembeni has gone. It then introduces Fargard IX, describing the Barashnum nu shaba, the nine nights' Barashnum, as a great purification that lasts nine nights, cleanses a defiled man, and opens the heavens to him. Editorial notes explain that the ceremony, originally meant only for those defiled by contact with the dead, later became a general Parsi pious practice and was required at the Nu zudi coming-of-age ceremony at age fifteen to wash away natural uncleanness contracted in the maternal womb. The section \"I a\" begins a dialogue: Zarathustra addresses Ahura Mazda, asking how people on earth should cleanse a body defiled by the dead. Ahura Mazda responds that a godly man or priest, who speaks truth, learns the Holy Word, and knows the cleansing rites, must fell the trees over a square area of nine Vibazus to prepare the Barashnum-gah. The site must be the driest and cleanest ground with little water or trees and minimal passage by animals, Fire (the son of Ahura Mazda), consecrated baresma bundles, and the faithful. The text specifies that the place should be thirty paces from fire, water, and baresma, and three paces from the faithful. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l15109-l15205","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    XVII.  I  87 / FARGARD    XVIII.  1 89 / FARGARD    XVIII.  I9I / FARGARD    XVIII.  193; lines 15109-15205","start":"15109","end":"15205","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ahura Mazda explains to Zarathustra that a bird named Parodany (the cock), also called Kahrkatas, cries out at dawn, urging men to arise and recite a powerful Ashem prayer that smites the Daevas and warning them about the demon Bushyasta, who lulls the world back to sleep. The text exhorts people to be diligent in good thoughts, words, and deeds, and negligent in their evil counterparts. It then portrays Fire, the son of Ahura Mazda, speaking during each of the three parts of the night: first to the master of the house, then to a husbandman, and finally to the holy Sraosha, asking them to rise, purify themselves, bring clean wood, and protect the fire from Azi, a being made by the Daevas who seeks to extinguish it. Sraosha brings wood, wakes the cock, and the bird repeats the dawn call and warning. Translator’s notes identify the bird as the cock, describe it as the 'drum of the world' created to fight fiends and wizards and allied with Srosh and the dog against demons, and add that demons cannot enter a house with a cock. Another note describes Parsi practice of rising, putting on the sacred girdle, washing hands, and adding wood to the fire, and glosses Bushyasta’s claim that 'the time is not yet come' as a delay of religious duties.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ahura Mazda tells Zarathustra that the bird named Parodany, which ill-speaking people call Kahrkatas, is the bird that lifts up its voice against the mighty dawn.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The bird addresses men at dawn, telling them to arise and recite the Ashem prayer that smites down the Daevas.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The bird warns that Bushyasta, described as 'the long-handed', is coming upon men.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Bushyasta lulls the whole living world to sleep again as soon as it has awoken, saying 'Sleep! sleep on, O man! the time is not yet come.'","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The text exhorts people never to be slack in three excellent things—good thoughts, good words, and good deeds—and always to be slack in three abominable things—bad thoughts, bad words, and bad deeds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In the first part of the night, Fire, called the son of Ahura Mazda, calls the master of the house for help.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Fire instructs the master of the house to put on his girdle and clothes, wash his hands, take wood, bring it to the fire, and let the fire burn bright with clean wood carried by well-washed hands.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Fire warns that Azi, made by the Daevas, is coming to strive against him and wants to put out his life.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In the second part of the night, Fire similarly calls the husbandman to arise, purify himself, bring clean wood, and warns again of Azi’s attempt to extinguish him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the third part of the night, Fire calls the holy, tall-formed Sraosha for help, clean wood with his well-washed hands to Fire.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Sraosha wakes the bird named Parodar, which ill-speaking people call Kahrkatas, and Bushyasta.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A commentator explains that the name of the bird means 'he who foresees the coming dawn' and identifies it as the cock.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Commentary states that the cock is called 'the drum of the world' and that, by crowing in the dawn that dazzles away the no demon can enter a house in which there is a cock, and that if the cock comes to the residence of a demon and chants praises of the Creator, the evil spirit immediately takes flight.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Commentary notes that as soon as a Parsi has risen, he must put on the Kostr (sacred girdle), wash his hands, and put wood content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l15615-l15719","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    XVIII.  1 97 / FARGARD    XVIII.  I  99 / FARGARD    XVIII.  201 / FARGARD    XIX.  203; lines 15615-15719","start":"15615","end":"15719","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"If he shall pay it, he shall enter the world of the holy ones; if he shall not pay it, he shall fall down into the world of the wicked, into that dark world, made of darkness, the offspring of darkness.\"","summary":"The passage prescribes a severe atonement involving killing noxious creatures, building bridges, and enduring stripes; fulfilling this penalty allows a sinner to enter the world of the holy ones, while refusing it leads to a dark world of the wicked. An editorial outline then presents Fargard XIX as a revelation in which Angra Mainyu repeatedly attacks Zarathustra, who withstands him and receives divine law from Ahura Mazda, and Angra Mainyu ultimately flees to hell with his host. The narrative proper shows Angra Mainyu sending the death-demon Drug/Buiti against Zarathustra, who repels the attack by chanting the Ahuna-Vairya prayer and urging prayer to the good waters of the Daitya river and profession of Mazda’s law, causing the demon to flee.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A prescribed atonement requires a man to kill large numbers of creatures that go upon the belly, land and water frogs, and corn-carrying ants and others.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The same atonement instructs him to throw thirty bridges over canals and to undergo a thousand stripes with the Aspahe-astra and a thousand stripes with the Sraosho-Z'arana scourges.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The text explicitly calls this set of actions \"the atonement\" and \"the penalty\" that he shall pay to atone for the deed he has done.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"If the man pays the atonement, he will enter the world of the holy ones; if he does not, he will fall into the world of the wicked, a dark world made of darkness and called the offspring of darkness.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"An editorial summary states that Angra Mainyu attempts to kill Zarathustra and, failing that, tries to tempt him, but Zarathustra withstands both assaults with material and spiritual weapons.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The summary adds that Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda for a revelation of the law and is taught how to repel the fiend, worship Mazda’s creation, wash away uncleanness, and what becomes of the soul after death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The summary concludes that Angra Mainyu and his host, feeling powerless and in despair, flee down into hell.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The chapter is described as \"The Revelation\" and as the framework of the Vendidad, whose first part shows the fiend’s struggles to prevent the revelation, the second part summarizes the law, and the third shows its effects.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"From the regions of the north Angra Mainyu, called \"the deadly\" and \"the Daeva of the Daevas,\" rushes forth and commands: \"Drug, rush down upon him! destroy the holy Zarathustra!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In response to Angra Mainyu’s command, the Drug, identified as the demon Buiti, \"the unseen death, the hell-born,\" comes rushing along.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A note explains that Angra Mainyu is \"the fiend of fiends,\" the arch-fiend, and that he comes from hell.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A note explains that the Drug known as But enters the body and soul of man as a forerunner of death, producing such excessive heat that the person falls ill when the end is near.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Zarathustra chants aloud the Ahuna-Vairya formula, declaring that the will of the Lord is the law of holiness and that the riches of Vohu-mano will be given to the one who works in this world for Mazda and uses the power given by Ahura to relieve the poor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Zarathustra further instructs listeners to offer up prayers to the good waters of the good Daitya and to profess the law of the worshippers of Mazda.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After Zarathustra’s prayer and exhortations, the Drug Buiti becomes dismayed and rushes away.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"A note identifies the Daitya as a river in Airyana Vaego and calls its waters \"good.\"","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The atonement includes both destructive acts against animals deemed harmful and constructive acts such as building bridges over canals.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Angra Mainyu","description":"Primary evil being described as \"the deadly\", \"the Daeva of the Daevas\", the \"fiend of fiends\" and arch-fiend, who rushes from the north, commands the Drug to attack Zarathustra, and is later said to flee into hell with his host.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Zarathustra","description":"Holy man and protagonist whom Angra Mainyu tries to kill and tempt; he withstands assaults with material and spiritual weapons, chants the Ahuna-Vairya prayer, instructs others to pray to the Daitya, and seeks a revelation of the law from Ahura Mazda.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8","ev:11","ev:12","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Drug / Druj / demon Buiti (But)","description":"A demon sent by Angra Mainyu, called the Drug and Buiti or But, described as \"the unseen death\" and \"hell-born\"; she rushes toward Zarathustra and later flees dismayed; commentary portrays her as a spirit entering the body as a forerunner of death and causing excessive heat and illness.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:12","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Ahura Mazda (Lord / Mazda / Ahura)","description":"Supreme deity whose will is called the law of holiness, who gives power to relieve the poor, and who reveals the law to Zarathustra concerning repelling the fiend, proper worship, purification, and the soul’s fate after death.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Vohu-mano","description":"Divine figure whose poor.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"River Daitya / good waters of the Daitya","description":"A river in Airyana Vaego whose waters are called \"good\"; Zarathustra instructs people to offer up prayers to its good waters.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11","ev:12","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Unnamed transgressor / penitent","description":"An unspecified man referred to as \"he\" who must perform the specified atonement of killing harmful creatures, building bridges over canals, and receiving stripes; whether he content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l15009-l15106","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    XVII.  1 85 / FARGARD    XVII.  I  87 / FARGARD    XVIII.  1 89 / FARGARD    XVIII.  I9I; lines 15009-15106","start":"15009","end":"15106","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"'What is it that makes the unseen power of Death increase?'","summary":"Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda what increases the unseen power of Death. Ahura Mazda replies that it is a man who teaches a wrong law and who for years neglects key religious duties such as wearing the sacred girdle, chanting the Gathas, and worshipping the good waters. A commentator explains that this man is the heretic Ashemaogha and describes the sacred girdle (Kosti) in detail as the badge of the faithful, symbolically linked with Ormazd, the community, liturgical units, good thought, speech and work, and the four elements (fire, air, water, earth), and notes a similar sacred girdle in the Brahmanical tradition (Mekhala). Freeing such a heretic from prison is said to be no better a deed than flaying a man alive and cutting off his head. Blessings pronounced over one or more wicked Ashemaoghas become ineffective and ultimately turn into a curse against the one who blesses. Giving Haoma juice or consecrated Myazda to a wicked Ashemaogha is equated with leading a large cavalry force against the cities of Mazda-worshippers, slaughtering the men, and driving off their cattle. Ahura Mazda then invites Zarathustra, called upright, to ask questions of him, describing himself as the Maker, the best and most knowing of beings, and promising that such questioning will make Zarathustra better and happier. Zarathustra asks who is the Sraosha-varez of Sraosha, and Sraosha is described as a holy, strong, mighty-speared and lordly god, the incarnate Word. A commentator glosses Sraosha-varez as the one who sets the world in motion.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Zarathustra addresses Ahura Mazda as Maker of the material world and asks what makes the unseen power of Death increase.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Ahura Mazda replies that the increase of the unseen power of Death is caused by a man who teaches a wrong law and who goes for three years without wearing the sacred girdle, chanting the Gathas, or worshipping the good waters.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A commentator identifies the man who teaches a wrong law as the deceiver Ashemaogha, described as a heretic.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A note explains that the sacred girdle, the Kosti, must be worn by every Parsi from the age of fifteen, is the badge of the faithful, and is the girdle by which the wearer is united with Ormazd and fellow believers; one who does not wear it is to be refused water and bread, while the wearer shares in the merit of good deeds performed throughout the Zarathustrian world.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Kosti is described as consisting of seventy-two interwoven filaments that encircle the waist three times, with symbolic equivalences between its threads and liturgical units, between its three circumvolutions and good thought, good speech, and good work, and between its four knots and pleasure conferred on the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The same note observes that in the Brahmanical system the faithful are also bound to their god by a sacred girdle called the Mekhala.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Another item of clothing prescribed for every Parsi is the Sadarah, a sacred muslin shirt with short sleeves, ending above the hips and having a small pocket at the opening in front.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The text states that whoever sets the heretical man at liberty when he is bound in prison does no better deed than if he flayed a man alive and cut off his head.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A commentary suggests that the same sentence can be understood as saying that freeing the man from hell would be no less a feat than cutting off a man\u0019s head and then making him alive again.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The text asserts that a blessing uttered on a wicked, ungodly Ashemaogha does not go beyond the blesser\u0019s mouth; the blessing for two Ashemaoghas does not go beyond his tongue; the blessing for three is no word at all; and the blessing for four turns into a curse against himself.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The text states that whoever gives Haoma juice or Myazda consecrated with blessings to a wicked, ungodly Ashemaogha does no better deed than leading a thousand horse against the cities of the worshippers of Mazda, slaughtering the men there, and driving off the cattle as plunder.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Ahura Mazda invites Zarathustra, addressed as an upright one, to demand answers from him as the Maker, the I  79; lines 14398-14496","start":"14398","end":"14496","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In a question-and-answer dialogue, an unnamed human interlocutor addresses Ahura Mazda as \"Maker of the material world, Holy One\" and asks which worshipper of Mazda is responsible for supporting a pregnant bitch (female dog) near her time if she lies in a moat or a pasture-field. Failure to support her so that the whelps perish is treated as wilful murder. Ahura Mazda defines canine self-sufficiency as the ability to run around a circuit of twice seven houses; young dogs should be supported for six months and human children for seven years. He adds that Atar, the Fire and son of Ahura Mazda, watches over a pregnant bitch just as he watches over a woman. \n\nIn a further exchange, the interlocutor asks what worshippers of Mazda should do if they want a bitch to be covered so that her offspring will be of strong nature. Ahura Mazda instructs them to dig a hole of specified depth in the middle of the fold, tie the bitch there far from children and from the Fire, and watch until a dog comes. Then they are to bring a second and then a third dog to her in turn, keeping the males apart so they do not fight. Covered thus by three dogs, the bitch becomes pregnant, her milk comes in, and she bears a young one \"born from (three) dogs.\" A final question asks the penalty for smiting such a specially covered, milk-bearing, pregnant bitch. He notes pronunciation difficulties faced by colonists and offers guidance for English readers on approximating these sounds using analogies with English and Welsh consonants.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The author, following a suggestion from Max Muller, prefers to represent a Zulu guttural Lepsius, Bleek, Grout, and Colenso, have used different symbols—Greek x, italic x, or Greek x with a diacritic—to represent a second, rare guttural fricative in Zulu-Kafir.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"This second guttural fricative is described as a rare and extremely difficult sound, somewhat resembling an imperfect faucal click but not actually a click, and as a hard, rough guttural produced by contracting the throat and expelling the breath forcibly with a tremulous motion of the epiglottis.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The author proposes to call the second sound the 'lateri-guttural fricative' and reports that natives who can pronounce it share a view of how it is produced.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"According to the author, in producing the lateri-guttural fricative the front of the tongue lies flat and relaxed, the base of the tongue curves upward to close the center of the faucal region, and the breath is expelled forcibly on each side; the sound generally has a k quality and can alternate with the other guttural fricative, so he chooses to represent it with italic 'hh', often preceded by 'k'.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The author states that Zulu aspirated lingual 'l' occurs in at least two forms, usually spelled 'hl' and 'dhl', and that the aspirate involved is not the common aspirate 'h'.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Dr. Bleek is quoted as saying that the aspirated lingual 'hl' in Kafir sounds as if a guttural fricative (like German 'ch' in comparing 'dhl' to the Welsh 'll'.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The aspirated 'l' sounds are said to be difficult for colonists, who tend to produce substitutions such as 'shla' or 'thla' with the 't' pronounced too strongly.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The author suggests that aspirated 'l' probably occurs in three forms—simply aspirated, and preceded by 'th' and by 'dhl'—with the aspirate being a lateral fricative rather than ordinary 'h'.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"To help English readers, the author advises approximating 'hl' as if 'l' were preceded by voiceless 'th' (as in 'thigh' or 'breath') and 'dhl' as if 'l' were preceded by voiced 'th' (as in 'thy' or 'breathe'), and notes that the contrasts between these English pairs correspond closely to the difference between 'hl' and 'dhl'.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The author proposes that Zulu aspirated 'l' might be better spelled 'thl' and 'dhl' in Roman orthography, and mentions that Ahura Mazda prescribes extremely severe corporal punishments for killing specially valued dogs and for killing a shepherd's dog. He identifies the daeva Zairimyangura (Zairimyaka), described in commentary as a tortoise, as the evil creature of the evil spirit that kills many creatures of the good spirit at night, and says that killing this daeva fully atones a person's sins like a confessional. Further laws describe how injuring working dogs brings civil liability for resulting theft or loss, and how smiting certain dogs brings afterlife punishment: the offender's soul is pursued with howls (of Divs), receives no help from other souls, and is refused aid by the dogs that guard the Kinvad (Chinvat) bridge to the other world.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A scenario is posed in which a man kills a dog with a prickly back and a long thin muzzle, called Vanghapara and also Dusaka by evil-speaking people.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The prescribed penalty for killing the Vanghapara dog is a thousand stripes with the Aspahe-aitra and a thousand stripes with the Sraosho-charana.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Vanghapara dog is described physically as having a prickly back and a long and thin muzzle and is given alternative names.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The daeva Zairimyangura, also called Zairimyaka, is identified as the evil creature among the creatures of the evil spirit.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"From midnight until sunrise, the daeva Zairimyangura kills thousands of the creatures of the good spirit.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Whoever kills the daeva Zairimyangura/Zairimyaka has all sins in thought, content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l411-l482","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"PREFACE  TO  THE  FIRST  VOLUME. / HENRY  CALLAWAY. / PREFACE / PREFACE.; lines 411-482","start":"411","end":"482","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"...endeavouring to trace out their connection with other nations by the similarity which might exist in their traditions and myths, their nursery tales and proverbs.","summary":"In this part of his preface, Henry Callaway explains that his initial Zulu language exercises became a means to learn about Zulu customs, histories, religion, and modes of thought, and to investigate how similarities between Zulu traditions, myths, nursery tales, and proverbs and those of other nations might reveal historical connections. He notes that his findings exceeded expectations and may help illuminate Zulu history and its relation to other peoples. He justifies publishing the materials, decides to print Zulu and English side by side for both English and Kafir scholars, and describes his translation strategy as idiom-for-idiom rather than strictly literal, preserving the original’s peculiarities even if the result sounds ‘un-English.’ He remarks on the greater frankness about sexual matters among the natives and softens some expressions, while warning against equating outspokenness with impurity or reserve with purity. Finally, he outlines two competing systems for writing Zulu—one that runs small words together and another that divides them more—and criticizes the run-together method as confusing and ambiguous for readers.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The author states that his early Zulu language lessons became a way to learn Zulu customs, histories, religion, and the character of Zulu thought, and to explore connections with other nations through similarities in traditions, myths, nursery tales, and proverbs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"He says the results of his investigation surpassed his expectations and may help clarify the past history of the Zulus to the other.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"He explains that his translation aims to be a true representation of the original by giving idiom for idiom rather content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l16937-l16984","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VII,  59)- / FARGARD    XXI.  2  25 / FARGARD    XXI.  22  7 / Q    2; lines 16937-16984","start":"16937","end":"16984","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"'A woman rich in seed, in milk, in fat, in marrow, and in offspring. I shall make for thee a thousand springs flow and run towards the pastures that will give food to the child.'","summary":"A ritual speaker declares a woman's body and strength pure and promises to make her rich in offspring and milk. He describes her as rich in seed, milk, fat, marrow, and offspring, and promises that a thousand springs will flow toward pastures to feed her child. The sea Vouru-kasha is named as the gathering place of waters, and the waters are commanded to rise, gather, and move along the aerial way and the earth. As the command 'Up! rise up!' is given, malevolent beings (Ka/wu^i, Ayehi, and Gahl, who is addicted to the Yatu) are said to fly away crying. The speaker then recites a long exorcistic formula, driving away a series of named beings and afflictions, as well as sickness, death, pain, fever, and all kinds of diseases and deaths. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l6175-l6275","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / UNTOMBINDE. / UNTOMBINDE.55 / I ZING  AN  E E WANE.; lines 6175-6275","start":"6175","end":"6275","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two wedding companies travelling together ask some merchants to say which girl is the prettiest. Offended, Utintakabazana’s marriage company kills the merchants. Later, the two wedding companies arrive at the river Uulange and its pool, remove their bracelets, breast ornaments, collars, and beaded petticoats, place them on the bank, and bathe together in the water. Untombinde asks what they can do, one girl suggests petitioning, and another directly addresses the monster, asking it to return her things and saying she has been brought into this trouble by Untombinde’s suggestion to bathe. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l38030-l38129","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"RIDDLES. / IZINCANEKWAUE. / KEY  TO  THE  KIDDLES. / KEY  TO  THE  RIDDLES.; lines 38030-38129","start":"38030","end":"38129","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“We mean a house by the cow which gives much milk; the milk is the joy a house affords those who live beneath it… We say ‘cow’ that a man may not think of a house… A village and the paths which pass from it are the branches which bear fruit… The pumpkins are villages from which the paths go out… A louse… he cannot kill it with one thumb; but only by bringing the two thumbs together… We say ‘ox,’…”","summary":"The passage explains the answers to several Zulu riddles. The riddle deliberately uses the word “cow” to misdirect the solver away from thinking of a house. The first explains an image of a supernumerary finger: an extra finger prevents the hand from pairing and counting properly, and if removal were painless it would be dismissed with the words, \"Away with you; you are not fit for this place.\" This figure is linked to the idea of being slow in settling a dispute. The second key explains a riddle in which fire is called \"a man\" so that the answer is not immediately evident. People compete to solve such riddles, which are considered better when not quickly understood. The explanation then describes how fire in a house can throw sparks onto clothes so that the owner cries over the damage, how a strong fire can burn the cooking pot and spoil the food, and how a spark in the thatch can burn down an entire hut with all its contents. In such a conflagration goats, calves, and children are burned; cows bellow for their dead calves; men cry for their goats; and husband and wife lament the loss of their house and possessions. Fire, called \"the man,\" is thus portrayed as laughing while people weep.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage describes a bad.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The extra finger is linked to the expression that they are slow in settling the dispute, and it is said that if removal could place.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Fire is called \"a man\" in the riddle so that what is meant will not be at once evident, the answer being concealed by the word \"man.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Men say many things in rivalry when trying to solve riddles, often missing the mark, and a riddle is said to be Later, boys playing on the banks of the river Umtshezi see a beautiful rock and decide to build cattle pens on it with cow dung, but the narrator states it is actually a tortoise. One little boy notices that the rock has eyes, pokes the tortoise’s eye with his stick, and tells his skeptical father at home that there is a rock with eyes. On another day the tortoise turns over with the boys; one little boy crosses the river at a distance, escapes, and goes home crying, saying that the rock has turned over with the other boys and gone with them, the sentence breaking off before stating where.","language":"English (with Zulu segments)","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"All the people of the Umtshezi.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"On arriving, the boys see what they call a beautiful rock and propose to make their cattle-pens on it with cow dung, but
