They lay in wait for it; when it was coming out of the pool, they cut off its head... the pool dried up, and the water ceased to flow from the pool.\"","summary":"An editor introduces a Zulu story linked to an earlier tale of a monstrous serpent and describes it as a recent \"myth of observation\" arising around the arrival of the Dutch in Natal, noting that the original storyteller associated the snake with the rainbow, imagined by some as a great serpent living in the river. The first-person narrator recalls that as a boy he heard men say that, at the time of the Dutch arrival, there was a fiery serpent that came out of the water and ran so fast that men on foot could not escape it, though horsemen could. In the story, some Amangwane lie in wait for the creature at a pool, cut off its head as it emerges, and its body retreats into the pool, which then dries up so that water ceases to flow. When men wonder why the water has stopped, others explain that they killed a serpent there the previous day; the hunters describe its fiery head and say they found a soft stone inside it, suggesting that they go to the Dutch to see whether they know about such a serpent. A footnote compares the drying of the pool to a Bechuana belief that killing a sacred water-snake in a fountain causes it to dry up, and suggests that the \"soft stone\" probably refers to a bezoar or similar intestinal concretion.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The editor connects this tale with a previously mentioned monstrous serpent and calls it a recent \"myth of observation\" related to the arrival of the Dutch in Natal in 1836.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The editor comments that the story could have as its historical basis only a large water snake or eel and firearms, with imagination and repeated narration supplying additional details.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The editor says that the man who first related the story mentioned the snake in connection with the rainbow, which some imagine to be a large snake, and asked whether the snake killed by a Dutchman might have been a rainbow living in the river.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The narrator states that when he was a boy he heard men say that at the time of the Dutch arrival there was a fiery serpent that came out of the water and ran very fast.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The men said that a man on foot could not run away from the fiery serpent, but horsemen could outdistance it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Some Amangwane came, lay in wait for the serpent at a pool, and cut off its head as it was coming out of the pool.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After the serpent’s head was cut off, its body went back into the pool, which then dried up so that water ceased to flow from it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Some men asked why the water had ceased, and others replied that they had killed a serpent at that place the previous day.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Those of the Amangwane said that the serpent had a fiery head and that they found a soft stone inside it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Amangwane suggested going to the Dutch to see whether they knew about this serpent and the soft stone found in it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A footnote states that the notion of a fountain drying when a water-snake is killed is similar to a Bechuana superstition that The attackers demand that the man dismount from the ox he is riding, but he replies that he does not walk on the ground. Her mother, father, brother, and sister follow the beast, resting where he rests and continuing after him in the morning. The mother goes weeping; the father, brother, and sister grow tired and turn back, but the mother continues with the beast. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l25291-l25511","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"UMDHLUBU  NESELESELE. / IZINGANEKWANE. / UMDHLUBU  NESELESELE. / IZINGANEKWANE.; lines 25291-25511","start":"25291","end":"25511","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A messenger informs the king that his child Umdhlubu, believed dead, is alive again. The father threatens the messenger if the report is false, but orders him to spread the news and have the people gather large oxen. The messenger announces that the princess, the king’s child who was dead, has come, and the people rejoice, take their shields and oxen, bring presents, and slaughter many cattle, even along the way, so that old men, old women, and the sick who cannot reach the princess’s home may eat. The father comes and calls to his child to come out; she is silent until he repeatedly slaughters groups of oxen, after which she appears at the doorway, stands, and then comes out. He invites her into the cattle-kraal to dance for her because he had thought she was dead but she is alive; after he slaughters more oxen she enters the kraal. They dance for her greatly, though the other side of the kraal does not rejoice or dance with that side. The father goes with her into the house, sits with her, and orders a fat young ox to be killed and cooked so they may eat and rejoice, for she was dead and has risen from death. All the people rejoice; the child returns to her royal position; the father resumes living at the kraal and ruling royally, having previously stayed away because he remembered his dead child. Her mother and the children of her house rejoice together. The father asks how she came there; the child says she was brought by a frog, and points out where he A man enters the house with a pole, finds the snake’s head, ties a rope around its neck, and leads it out. The people drag the snake—identified as a boa constrictor—to a pool, throw it into the water, and wash themselves to remove its evil influence, since it is considered an ominous prodigy. The king then commands his people to flee to another country, leaving the snake’s mother behind as one who has borne a monster. They settle, build houses, and their children grow up and marry. After many years, the mother of the snake sets out to follow the king. She meets people who question her; she explains that her offence was giving birth to a beast, a boa constrictor carried for many years and cast into the water, and that the people fled because she had a prodigy with her. I am taking Umdhlubu to her own country.\" Hearing this, they leave it and go on. The frog continues its journey and again meets a string of men who call others to see the huge frog and suggest killing it; the frog repeats the same declaration and is again allowed to pass. Later, the frog encounters boys who are herding cattle. They see the frog; one boy, identified as a son of the damsel's father (her half-brother), exclaims \"By Umdhlubu the king's child!\" and urges the others to come and kill the great frog, telling them to run and cut sharp sticks to pierce it. The mother, not recognizing her, asks where she comes from. The girl answers that she is merely travelling. The mother then tells the visitor that other women are happy with such fine children, but she herself is troubled because her child was lost; she left the child in a valley where she believes the child died. The visitor questions why the mother left the child and suggests it was because she did not love her. The mother explains that queens distracted her and prevented the nurse from carrying the child, so she forgot the child, and that she was not used to carrying a child herself. The girl insists that no woman can forget her own child and repeats the accusation of lack of love. The mother looks closely at the girl and realizes she is her lost child. She rejoices and praises her child with laud-giving names. Footnotes explain that the queens distracted the mother from her child, clarify the custom of laud-giving names for warriors and beloved or remarkable children, give an example of a youth named Untiye whose praise-names liken him to a valuable but thorny unganu tree and to an adder blocking a doorway, and note that in the tale Umdhlubu is lost but not forgotten, for her brothers swear by her name and her mother invents praise-names for her.","language":"English (translation of Zulu, with Zulu terms)","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A young woman enters content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l23691-l23809","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / UBONGOPA-KAMAGADHLELA. / IZIKGANEKWANE. / UBONGOPA-KAMAGADHLELA.; lines 23691-23809","start":"23691","end":"23809","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this segment of the Ubongopa-kamagadhlela tale, a boy repeatedly calls on Ubongopa, an ox, urging it to stand, let him mount, and then go, because thieves of another tribe are killing them. The boy mounts the ox and commands it to set out. As Ubongopa goes, the houses, gardens, cattle pen, and all the things of the village follow, so that observers say the whole country is moving. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l16211-l16281","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CANNIBALS. / IZINGANEKWANE. / APPENDIX. / CANNIBALISM.; lines 16211-16281","start":"16211","end":"16281","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An appendix to Callaway's collection discusses cannibalism among African peoples and in other sources. It notes a common opinion among local natives that cannibalism is of recent origin, arising in famine, and that cannibals such as the Marimo and those in Zulu legends speak of men as \"game.\" Various reported forms of cannibalism are listed: eating one's own dead (e.g., the Amanganja), selling and exchanging corpses as food between tribes, buying people of other tribes with one's own wives and children for food during famine, eating witches condemned to death (with some objecting as unwholesome), devouring prisoners of war as a sign of triumph, and \"professional\" cannibals who hunt men as game. The author then cites Herodotus's account of the Padseans, who kill sick men and women for food despite their protests and sacrifice rare old men to their gods before eating them. Winwood Reade's suggestion that cannibalism may be an extension of sacrificial ceremonies is mentioned, and the possibility that cannibalism sometimes originated in human sacrifice is raised. It then focuses on \"little birds\" whose speech can be understood by specially gifted people, a belief linked to the English proverb \"a little bird told me.\" The editor notes that Zulu legends and some recent individuals claim such powers, treating birds as prophets. Umpengula relates the case of his brother Undayeni, a highly sensitive man whose prophetic dreams and visions, and his ability to interpret bird language, appeared after a near-fatal struggle with a leopard and a dispute among family spirits over his vocation as a diviner. In a cattle-pen, a wagtail tells people (through Undayeni) to cultivate extensively so they can buy cattle and later warns of an approaching drought; Undayeni’s companions hear only twittering and remain skeptical, though the account notes that in that year Ungoza arrived and they bought many cattle from his people.","language":"English and Zulu","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In the \"legend-producing\" period, some birds such as the crow and raven were regarded as birds of evil omen, and auguries future.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Umpengula describes his brother Undayeni as a highly sensitive man with a nervous system that put him in rapport with the spirit-world, subject to dreams and visions that were realised and sometimes saved himself and his family from danger.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Undayeni's peculiar powers are said to have appeared after a prolonged contest with a leopard lasting most of a day, which nearly killed him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Undayeni's friends believed the spirits had chosen him to be a diviner, but attributed his failure to become one to a dispute between the spirits of his own house and those of his maternal uncle, so that he remained merely a wise man and interpreter of dreams, \"half-way between divining and not divining.\"","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Along with his dream and vision powers, Undayeni is said to have understood the language of birds.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the cattle-pen, Undayeni heard the wagtail (umvemve) \"speaking\" and saying that people should dig extensively that year because they would buy cattle with the resulting corn, and he reported this message to others, affirming its truth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Undayeni's listeners regarded his report of the wagtail's words as absurd, asking how he could have heard a bird speak, but he said the bird would return and say something further.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"After some days, while they were again in the cattle-pen, the wagtail returned and twittered; Undayeni asked his companions to listen, then explained that the bird had said that the coming year would be very dry, although the others only heard twittering.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The prediction of a dry year from the wagtail's speech alarmed the listeners.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"According to Umpengula, the wagtail spoke many messages to Undayeni, but when he relayed them people were amazed and content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l31255-l31351","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"UNTOMBI-YAPANSI. / IZINGANEKWANE. / UNTOMBI-YAPANSI. / IZINGANEKWANE.; lines 31255-31351","start":"31255","end":"31351","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this portion of the tale, Untombi-yapansi allows the imbulu to try on all her possessions. The imbulu puts them on, mounts Untombi-yapansi's ox, and praises how they suit her. When Untombi-yapansi later asks the imbulu to dismount and return her things so she can ride, the imbulu refuses and proposes a test: they will cross at some stones and see whose feet get wet. The imbulu, still mounted, leaps on the stones while Untombi-yapansi, on foot, walks through the water and gets wet. After crossing, the imbulu declares that Untombi-yapansi's feet are wet, renames her Umsila-wezinja (Dog's Tail), and claims the name Untombi-yapansi for herself. The true Untombi-yapansi remains silent and follows on foot while the imbulu rides the ox. They then reach the village where Untombi-yapansi's sister is married, enter the village and go to its upper part. At a house, the imbulu tells Untombi-yapansi not to come inside but to hold the ox, and then sits down inside the The narrator links this belief to Crusader times, describing Saracen horror at a fanatic group called the Tafurs, rumored to eat the corpses of enemies. He then cites an early English romance in which King Richard I (Cœur de Lion) hosts a gruesome banquet for Saracen ambassadors, serving boiled heads of slain Saracens and boasting that his army can Scott.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Turkish children are described as being taught that Franks are content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l30138-l30183","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / THE  GREAT  FIERY  SERPENT. / THE  RAINBOW. / UTINGO  LWENKOSIKAZI.; lines 30138-30183","start":"30138","end":"30183","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains that when it rains and the rainbow appears, called \"the queen's bow\" and \"the rod of the queen,\" people say the rain will clear up, and the text affirms that the rain stops and the sky clears even after heavy rainfall. A translator's footnote then remarks that a distance of more than 500 yards mentioned in the narrative is a modest exaggeration compared with a Scottish tale from Campbell's West Highland Tales in which an eel's body passes a fishing rock from morning until dusk. The note further compares this to a Muslim legend from Weil's Biblical Legends of the Mussulmans where Moses' staff becomes a gigantic serpent, as large as a camel, which lifts Pharaoh's throne to the ceiling and declares that, if Allah willed, it could swallow Pharaoh, those present, and the entire palace without any visible change in itself.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"When it rains and the rainbow appears, men say that it is going to clear up because the \"rod of the queen, the bow\" is seen.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The rainbow is named \"utingolwenkosikazi,\" glossed as \"the queen's bow,\" and is described as the queen's rod or bow.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage states that even when it rains much, once the bow appears the rain stops and the sky clears.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A footnote refers to a distance of more than 500 yards in the narrative and comments that it is a very modest fish on a rock and sees the head of an eel pass.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In the Scottish tale, the eel continues passing for an hour while the man fishes, length.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Scottish eel story is identified as coming from Campbell's West Highland Tales, volume II, page 370.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The footnote further compares the exaggeration to a Muslim legend in which Moses flings his staff on the ground and it is instantly changed into a serpent as huge as the largest camel.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In the Muslim legend, the serpent glances at Pharaoh with fire-darting eyes, raises Pharaoh's throne aloft to the ceiling, and opens its jaws to proclaim that, if it pleased Allah, it could swallow Pharaoh, all present, and even his palace and all it contains without any visible change in itself.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Muslim legend of Moses' serpent is identified as drawn from Weil's Biblical Udalana moves from her own watch-house to Untombi-yapansi’s and asks where she has eaten, pointing out that there is no refuse of sugar-cane where she should have eaten. At sunset they return home; the chief asks whether there were birds, and Untombi-yapansi reports there were very many. The imbulu then explains that it is Umsila-wezinja’s habit to sit idly on the ground while birds destroy the garden, and afterwards claim she has been defeated by the birds. The next morning, as they go again to watch the garden, Untombi-yapansi refuses to go first through the gateway because the dew would wipe off the substance she has smeared on her body to keep her brass-coloured skin from glistening and being recognised by people. Udalana enters first; when they sit in the garden and see the birds, Untombi-yapansi again speaks of the birds which devour her sister’s garden, adding that although she is not truly her sister now, The father of the chief son is head of the village. A son whose mother was married with the father’s own cattle leaves the hereditary village and forms his own, though he may inherit the chief position if no heirs remain in the chief house. The chief house may use its own cattle to acquire wives, and children of such marriages (especially daughters) are reckoned to the chief house; their dowry cattle later return to that house and can be used again to take wives. An example is given: Uzita’s chief wife bears his chief son Ubabazeleni. Later, cattle belonging to Ubabazeleni’s house are used to marry the mother of Unsukuzonke, who becomes Ubabazeleni’s brother and is designated to inherit if Ubabazeleni and his offspring die, preventing disputes among Uzita’s children.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The father of the son who is recognized as chief heir is the hereditary estate but leaves to have his own village.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Although the son from the father’s cattle is inferior to the son of the house.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When that daughter is married, the son of the chief house can take a wife with the cattle that have come as the The chief of the Amadhlungundhlebe sends some of his people to fetch a large ox, which is brought and slaughtered. After this, Umkxakaza comes out of the cave carrying her blanket, sleeping mat, pillow, and rod, and wearing a petticoat decorated with brass beads. She sets her bedding at the doorway and rests on her rod and mat. The chief tells her to turn her back and then to turn around, and she obeys. The Amadhlungundhlebe remark that she is pretty but complain about her two legs, saying she would be pretty but for them. They tell her to go back into the cave and then depart. Later, many Amadhlungundhlebe are summoned. In the morning they go to Umkxakaza carrying a special veil through which, when worn, the wearer’s body can be seen. They sit in the shade and take snuff; when she sees them she fears they have come to kill her. They go to the tobacco garden, pluck tobacco and put it outside, then enter the cave, call her out, give her the veil, and she puts it on. A heading states that the Amadhlungundhlebe take away Umkxakaza.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"While Umkxakaza is in the cave, people Numerous birds habitually devour the crops. As the birds come when they enter, Udalana throws stones at them and calls them \"Umsila-wezinja.\" Untombi-yapansi tells her not to, saying those birds devour her sister’s garden, though the other girl is not truly her sister anymore because she herself is now Umsila-wezinja and had previously been Untombi-yapansi. At her word the birds immediately depart and no birds return for the whole day, which greatly surprises Udalana, who is used to being troubled by them daily. At midday Untombi-yapansi asks Udalana to keep throwing stones while she goes to bathe. She goes to the river, enters a pool, washes, and comes out with her whole body shining like brass, holding a brass rod. She strikes the ground and commands the people of her father, the cattle of her father, and her food to come out. Many people, many cattle, and her food then emerge from the earth. The parents remark that the child knows a blood-relation by the navel and recognize the visitor as one of their own. This is said to illustrate what it means \"to know by the navel.\" A second example involves an older person traveling in a distant country. Overtaken by sunset near a village where he knows no one, he decides to stay the night, greets the householder, and is received like a stranger at first, with no sympathy in the eyes. The villagers ask where he comes from, feed and treat him kindly as if he belonged to them, refusing him nothing. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l5481-l5578","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"UZEMBENI. / UZEMBENI;46 / IZIXGAXEKWAXE. / UZEMBENI.; lines 5481-5578","start":"5481","end":"5578","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Towards sunset the dust appeared. They said, 'Lo, she is now coming.' The toe came first; she came after it. As soon as she came, she laughed to herself ... saying, 'Eh, eh! in my house here to-day there is a delicious odour. My children, what have you done? Whence comes this odour?'\"","summary":"Usikulumi visits a group of girls, having left his pack of dogs in a bed of reeds. Fearing that a being associated with Long-toe will pursue him if they send him away, the girls dig a pit in the floor of their house, hide Usikulumi inside it, cover it, and sit over the concealed pit. Towards sunset a cloud of dust signals the approach of Uzembeni; her long toe arrives first, then she herself. On entering, she laughs, rolls on the ground, and remarks that there is a delicious odour in her house, asking her \"children\" what they have done and where the scent comes from. She enters the house, continues laughing and patting them, and insists on searching, while the girls deny any knowledge of anything they could have obtained. An editorial footnote identifies Uzembeni as a gigantic ogress who scents out prey and longs for human flesh, and compares this episode to European tales of giants who smell human blood and to Polynesian myths where powerful beings sniff the air to detect nearby humans.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Usikulumi comes to the girls     "summary": "Umbadhlanyana rebukes a cannibal for eating his ukcilo (a morsel of food) and threatening to eat him as well, telling the cannibal there is another morsel that will completely satisfy his hunger.   },

      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "A cannibal eats Umbadhlanyana's ukcilo, a morsel of food belonging to Umbadhlanyana.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "Umbadhlanyana asks the cannibal why he ate his ukcilo and then said he would eat Umbadhlanyana himself.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "Umbadhlanyana tells the cannibal that there is another morsel which will quite fill him.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },

      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "All the cannibals see that Umbadhlanyana has gone into the nostrils of one cannibal.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "When they see Umbadhlanyana go into the cannibal's nostrils, all the other cannibals flee.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },

Hungry, she roasts meat anyway, and other cannibals follow the delicious odour to the rock. One asks the rock to open so he may enter, but the girl recognizes that he is not the owner and refuses him, telling the long-haired cannibal to depart. That cannibal goes away, roughens his voice with a hoe so that it resembles the owner’s, returns, calls to the rock again and is admitted. Knowing he will return and eat her, the girl escapes, taking sesamum in a calabash. When the cannibal comes back and the rock does not open, he realizes she has gone, summons many cannibals, and they pursue her. The king’s praises recall that he ‘ate’ a particular man without suffering harm, emphasizing that he consumed the man’s body, not just his cattle. She is so weak that it seems as if death has already come to her, but she answers that she intended to depart and her limbs failed. She is told she will soon see Ugungqu-kubantwana. She then goes to a river, kneels, and drinks an entire pool until the mud at its bottom appears, and then sits down. At the pool are oribes (identified as officers of Ugungqu-kubantwana) and hyenas. Ugungqu-kubantwana orders that the old woman be eaten; the hyenas agree, but the oribes argue she should first become fat and then postpone the eating until morning because it is dark. That night all the animals sleep, though some delay sleep because they want her to be eaten. Near midnight all are asleep except four oribes, who get up, take the old woman, lift her, place her on the backs of three of them, and the fourth carries a water-vessel as they run off with her. The story continues with Uthlakanyana fleeing and being pursued by a doe. He reaches a full river, transforms into an upper millstone, and allows the doe to pick him up and throw him across, while she remarks that if it were really he she would kill him. The woman offers them all she possesses and specifically offers food—amabele (native corn), which they say they do not eat, and then amadumbi (tubers). Pretending to help them cross, Usitungusobenthle plaits a very long rope, throws it across the water, and invites many of the soldiers to hold onto it so she can pull them over. Having also obtained a sharp stone, she pulls them out to the middle of the sea and then cuts the rope so they are swept away by the water and drown, while she feigns distress over the fate of the king’s people. She repeats the stratagem with further groups, again cutting the rope in midstream and pretending the rope had slipped from her hand. Editorial notes compare this episode to a Hottentot tale of Heitsi Eibip, to a Highland legend of Maol a Chliobain who drowns a pursuing giant from a hair-bridge, and to a Zulu tale of Ulangalasenthla and Ulangalasenzantsi, all sharing the pattern of conversation across a river in which pursuers naively trust the pursued and perish.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Usitungusobenthle and her children go through the sea and sit down on the other side.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The army of the Amajubatente arrives at the sea, sees Usitungusobenthle sitting on the opposite shore, and is astonished to find her there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Usitungusobenthle plaits a very long rope and throws it across the sea.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Usitungusobenthle calls to the army, saying, “Come along, I will cross you over,” but this is described as her merely chaffing them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Usitungusobenthle has found a sharp stone before carrying out her stratagem.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Usitungusobenthle tells many of the soldiers to lay hold of the rope; many grasp it, and she pulls them until they are in the middle of the sea.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"When the soldiers on the rope are in the middle of the sea, Usitungusobenthle cuts the rope, and they are carried away by the sea.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"After cutting the rope, Usitungusobenthle cries out \"Woe is me! They then have her turn her back, scarify her loins in two places, and declare that she will now have a child. After they depart and she returns home, she becomes pregnant and rejoices. The narrator explains that she had long been treated as a wife of no consequence because of her barrenness, while the other wives bore children described as \"crows\" whose behavior at her hearth caused trouble. Umkxakaza, a royal daughter, has lived hidden for uncounted years in an inner enclosure (umgonqo), known only to the maidens who refuse others entry. After a long time the people decide that, before she comes out, they will all go together to work in the king’s royal garden (umbutiso), expecting that once she emerges there will be beer and celebration throughout the tribe. When she is about to come out, beer is in preparation in every part of her father’s village. All the people rise early and go to the distant royal garden, leaving at home only Umkxakaza and her sister Ubalatusi. After their departure, thunder sounds and the earth shakes even in the house where the sisters sit. Umkxakaza sends Ubalatusi to see what is happening; Ubalatusi finds that a forest now stands at the entrance of the village, obscuring the gate, and that part of the fence has fallen and lies on the ground. The old woman stays behind while the brothers drive the cattle away with their hunting dogs. As they travel through a scorched, waterless land, they reach the top of a precipice. The elder asks to be tied with a rope and lowered to the bottom so he can drink water there, and the younger lowers him down so he can drink.     "summary": "A woman whose children have been eaten by an elephant repeatedly asks \"Mother\" to point out the elephant that devoured them. Inside its stomach she finds a vast interior world with forests, rivers, high lands, rocks, villages, many people, dogs, cattle, and her own children sitting there. She gives the children amasi (milk) and learns they have eaten nothing since being swallowed. She urges them to roast the elephant’s flesh; they fear this will kill them, but she explains the beast will die and they will not. She lights a great fire, cuts the liver, roasts it, and eats with her children. They cut and roast more flesh and eat. Questioned why his mother’s dwelling is at the gateway, he explains that it is because of affliction, since she gave birth to a snake. The father then instructs the whole nation to gather his cattle. Ten oxen are brought and given to Untlilatu-yesiziba, who dismounts; another ten are given to his sister, who also dismounts. The remaining people are told to dismount of their own accord, because the chief children have received gifts. Editorial headings note that the father acknowledges them, gives them cattle, gives everything into his son’s hands, and makes Untlilatu-yesiziba king. The mother rejoices. The father takes Untlilatu-yesiziba by the arm and invites him to go to the house at the head of the village, but the son refuses, saying he will go into his mother’s house instead. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l36688-l36795","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ABATWA  UKWESABEKA  KWABO. / THE  HYRAX. / FABLES. / IZINGANEKWANF.; lines 36688-36795","start":"36688","end":"36795","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains a Zulu saying about the hyrax, whose ‘loitering’ and lack of a tail are used as a proverb. People quote a phrase glossed as ‘Do you bring it for me’ to criticize those who do not attend to work that others undertake and who ask others to act for them. The saying warns that another will not bring anything when there is only enough for those present and concludes, ‘The hyrax went without a tail because he sent for it… go for yourself.’ The narrative clarifies that the hyrax did not literally speak; rather, the expression arose because other animals have tails while the hyrax has none, and it is as if he lost his tail by sending for it. The hyrax is also described as fearing a cloudy sky and staying in his hole unless there are gleams of sunshine. The tale is applied to people who are disinclined to work in foul weather and who ask others to fetch things for them; one who refuses such a request answers ‘by the hyrax’ so that the requester cannot later complain. The storyteller is named Umpengula Mbanda. An editorial footnote notes that other peoples have fables explaining the tailless condition of animals and cites a Norse tale in which a Bear, prompted by a Fox, fishes with his tail, presenting this as a parallel to the Zulu myth of the hyrax.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that the loitering of the hyrax is now a widely used saying among \"black men,\" who use the words of the hyrax.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"This saying is addressed to people who do not trouble themselves about what others like and who tell others to act for them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The key expression is reported as a phrase equivalent to \"Do you bring it for me,\" indicating a request that another fetch something.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage declares that another person does not bring anything for a man when there is only enough for those present.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The proverb includes the statement that the hyrax went without a tail because he sent for it, linking his tailless condition with sending someone else.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Speakers advise listeners not to act like the hyrax, saying they will not get anything by asking others and should go for themselves.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The narrator says, \"Such then is the tale of the hyrax,\" and explains that the hyrax did not actually speak the request \"Do you bring it for me\" with his He is called a chief or king whose people are supported by him, but at first they dispute his authority because he appears to do nothing. He replies that if he simply sits and looks at the ground the land will become desolate; the people will fall into precipices and pits, be eaten by wild beasts they do not see, and die of famine because they cannot find food. He says they are blind because they dispute him. Afterwards the people recognize him openly as their king so that they may live, reasoning that their own claimed majesty will end if they die of famine. He is then acknowledged as chief, reigns, and the country is peaceful. Her caretakers cannot hide her, demand repayment for raising her, the brother pays them, and his sister returns to him. The narrator then introduces another, historically grounded matter resembling this \"navel\" case. He recounts how, when their family lived among the Zulus, they were scattered after Udingane could not prevail in battle against the Dutch. The narrator had two uncles younger than his father; the youngest, Umagushu, married the sister of the Manjanjas, children of Unthlambela. After about four months of marriage, as the country was being desolated, the family fled to the country of the whiteman. On the way, Umagushu’s wife Umanjonga deserted him and returned to her own people while already pregnant. In the general confusion, the husband could not find her. It will not cross a river of its own accord; to make it cross, men must push it hard, choosing shallow water where the bottom can be seen, because in deep water it can hide and disappear from view. The bullock has only one permitted use: it may be eaten only when used to pay off a man's debt, and this is said to be its only work. It is very fierce and dangerous when being pushed uphill, so the men driving it warn each other to be careful not to be gored, especially because they are below and the animal is above. The men remind him that he now has no position and that Unsilane will take the headship, and Umatongo yields. The passage then explains inheritance in a polygamic household: in a particular house, all children born after the first girl belong to that house, while the first girl goes to the chief (great) house. The children do not follow the girl to the chief house, but they remain part of its potential heritage if all heirs of the chief house die. While heirs of the chief house live, it cannot take their property, although they remain \"under\" the chief house because their mother belongs to its polygamic establishment, having been taken to wife by its cattle. The return of the bridewealth cattle to the chief house through the first girl does not break this tie. If the chief house dies out, these children inherit the whole heritage. Heritage is taken in the order of houses according to the times of marriage; it cannot pass by any house to one outside the chief house's polygamic establishment until all such houses are extinct, and finally the last male child belonging to the great house enters on the heritage.","language":"English (translation from In the Middle Ages, Europeans knew only the name of the founder, Zoroaster, who was reimagined as a magician and master of hidden sciences. During the Renaissance, Barnabe Brisson collected information on ancient Persian religion from Greek and Roman sources. In the seventeenth century, Italian, English, and French travellers such as Pietro della Valle, Henry Lord, Mandelslo, Ovington, Chardin, Gabriel du Chinon, and Tavernier encountered Zoroaster’s followers (Parsis) in Persia and India, reporting their existence, customs, and beliefs; du Chinon saw their books and realized the original holy script was no longer understood except through translations and commentaries in another language. In 1700 Thomas Hyde, an Oxford Orientalist, attempted the first systematic history of the old Persian religion using Muslim writers and what he believed were genuine ancient Persian monuments, though these were actually late compilations; despite his lack of critical judgment, his work provided the first complete picture of modern Parsiism and encouraged further inquiry. Hyde urged travellers to procure the Parsis’ sacred books at any price. In response, George Boucher obtained a manuscript of the Vendidad Sadah from Parsis in Surat, brought to England by Richard Cobbe in 1723, but the manuscript remained unread, treated as a ‘sealed book’ and hung by an iron chain on the wall of the Bodleian Library as a curiosity. A Scotsman named Fraser later tried to obtain both Parsi books and an understanding of their contents but largely failed. In 1754, the young scholar Anquetil Duperron saw a facsimile of four leaves of the Avestan text. A note explains that Hyde identified Abraham as the first lawgiver of ancient Persia, saw Magism as a Sabean corruption of a primeval faith, and regarded Zoroaster as a reformer who relearned forgotten truth from exiled Jews in Babylon.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"During the Middle Ages, European knowledge of Mazdeism was content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l3145-l3267","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"C   2 / XXXVI  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X; lines 3145-3267","start":"3145","end":"3267","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"The Good was centred in the supreme god, in Ahura Mazda, the bright god of Heaven, the all-knowing Lord, the Maker... In front of him and opposed to him slowly rose the evil Spirit, Angra Mainyu.\"","summary":"The passage explains how Iranian religion developed a sharp moral dualism between Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu and illustrates this through several Indo-Iranian storm and dragon myths. Mithra is portrayed as a solar and judicial deity of truth who punishes oath-breakers and judges in hell with Rashnu. The text contrasts Indian and Persian attitudes toward demons, then presents parallel Vedic and Avestan myths: Indra versus the serpent Ahi over dawns and waters, Atar versus the dragon Azi Dahaka over the royal light (khvarenah) at the cosmic sea Vouru-kasha, Trita and Thraetaona as dragon-slaying heroes, and Tishtrya versus the drought demon Apaosha in a battle for rain empowered by sacrifice from Mazda. A note explains khvarenah as the heavenly light of sovereignty that makes and unmakes kings, illustrated by Yima’s fall and Azi Dahaka’s usurpation. A brief footnote compares Mithra to the Greek sky-father Zeus besieged by the Titans.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Mithra is described as the god of heavenly light, lord of vast luminous space and the wide pastures above, and later as the god of the sun.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Because light and truth are treated as equivalent for bodily sight and mental perception, Mithra becomes the god of truth and faith.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Mithra punishes the Mithra-drug, defined as the one who lies to Mithra or to the contract, and acts as a judge in hell together with Rashnu.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Rashnu is called \"the true one,\" the god of truth, and is described as an offshoot of Mithra in his moral character.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Zeus is presented as Mithra’s Greek counterpart, the god of heaven and father of gods and men, who when besieged by the Titans calls Thetis, Prometheus, and the Hecatonchires to help him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In India, fiends are pushed into the background and, under the influence of a metaphysical outlook, gods and fiends become fleeting manifestations of an everlasting, indifferent Being.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In Persia, demons are taken in earnest, feared and hated, and the vague Indo-Iranian dualism becomes sharply defined and forms the structural frame of Mazdeism.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The conflict between Good and Evil is depicted as an open and never-ceasing warfare that rages through all avenues of space and time, not only in passing storms.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Good is centered in the supreme god Ahura Mazda, described as the bright god of heaven, the all-knowing Lord, the Maker, and as the \"good Spirit\" Spenta Mainyu.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Opposed to Ahura Mazda there rises the evil Spirit, Angra Mainyu.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The war in nature is said to be waged in the storm, and the Vedas describe it as Indra, armed with lightning and thunder, fighting a serpent, Ahi.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The serpent Ahi has carried off the dawns or the rivers, described as goddesses or milch cows, and keeps them captive in the folds of the cloud.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In the Avesta this myth appears as a fight for the possession of the light of khvarenah between Atar and Azi Dahaka.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Atar means \"fire\" and is both a thing and a person, sometimes described as the weapon of Ahura Mazda and usually as his son, like fire springing from heaven either flung or born from it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Azi Dahaka is called a fiendish snake and a three-headed dragon who strives to seize and extinguish the khvarenah, but Atar frightens him away and recovers the light.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The battle between Atar and Azi Dahaka takes place at the sea Vouru-kasha, a sea from which all waters fall to earth with the winds and clouds, interpreted as the sea above in the atmospheric field of battle.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Another Vedic version describes Trita or Traitana Aptya, the \"son of waters,\" killing a three-headed, six-eyed fiend and letting loose the cows.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The title \"son of waters\" is in both Vedas and Avesta a name of the fire-god as born from the cloud I  8; lines 14610-14704","start":"14610","end":"14704","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This passage from the Vendidad prescribes ritual and legal responses to a woman with an issue of blood. The woman must sit in a designated \"place of infirmity\" for successive four-to-nine-night periods while her bleeding is monitored. If she still sees blood after nine nights, the condition is declared a work of the Daevas done for their worship and glorification. In response, worshippers of Mazda must clear a path through wood to the Barashnum-gah, dig three holes in the earth, wash the woman with gomez (cattle-derived liquid) in two holes and with water in the third, and kill specified numbers of Khrafstras (harmful creatures) made by Angra Mainyu. The text then turns to legal penalties: a worshipper who suppresses a woman’s issue of blood is classified as a Peshotanu and condemned to heavy corporal punishment using ritual instruments. Another set of penalties, increasing with repeated offenses, is laid out for a man who again and again wilfully touches and lies with a woman during her issue of blood, altering the normal pattern of her bleeding.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A woman who continues to see blood is required to sit in a \"place of infirmity\" for four nights, with the period extended successively to five, six, seven, eight, and nine nights if bleeding persists.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The woman’s condition is evaluated at the end of each specified nighttime period to determine whether she still sees blood.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"If the woman still sees blood after nine nights, the text states that this is a work of the Daevas performed for their worship and glorification.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Worshippers of Mazda are instructed to clear the way of the wood, including both growing trees and logs, leading to the place where cleansing occurs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"As part of the ritual response, three holes are to be dug in the third.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Participants in the ritual must kill Khrafstras: two hundred corn-carrying ants in summer or two hundred of other Khrafstras made by Angra Mainyu in winter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Khrafstras are described as creatures made by Angra Mainyu.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Angra Mainyu is associated with harmful creatures whose destruction forms part of the cleansing rite.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A worshipper of Mazda who suppresses the issue of blood of a woman, whether out of the ordinary course or at the usual versa.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"For repeated contact with the impure woman, penalties escalate: thirty stripes with each instrument for the first time, XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X; lines 2617-2712","start":"2617","end":"2712","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Scholarly commentary explains that the Avesta term for priest is Athravan, meaning \"fire-man,\" while Magu/Magi originally designated a Median tribe rather than the priestly function and could carry hostile overtones in Persian usage. An adversary of the priests in Avesta-related tradition is called \"hater of the Magi\" and, in Pahlavi, \"one who hates the Magu-men.\" A Bundahis tradition briefly described here portrays an enemy figure who prays to Ahriman by the Sipit Rud river, whose adversary Feridun is born in Ghilan, and who is bound to Mount Damavand. The section then summarizes that the Avesta was composed in Media by priests of Ragha and Atropatene, not by Persians. A footnote cites Yasna IX, 24, where the sacred being Haoma overthrows Keresani when he attempts to seize royalty and prevent Athravans from teaching freely. The commentator identifies this struggle as an old Indo-European myth and equates Keresani with Vedic Kriśanu, who seeks to keep Soma from humans; in the Avesta Keresani becomes an anti-Magian king, possibly Darius, and the name is later used as a title for the Christian Kaisars of Rum. Another footnote discusses Professor Oppert's debated interpretation of the Behistun inscription as evidence that Darius compiled an Avesta-like collection of religious law, commentary, benedictions, and translations.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The proper word for a priest in the Avesta is Athravan, literally meaning \"fire-man.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The word Magu originally denoted a member of the Median tribe of Magi rather than the priestly function, although Persians commonly designated their priests as Magi.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Persians often referred to priests by the tribal name Magi, sometimes with an implication of spite or scorn, whereas the Magi themselves preferred functional titles like Athravan.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In the Avesta, an enemy of the priests is called Moghu-zbi, \"hater of the Magi,\" instead of the expected Athrava-zbi, \"hater of the Athravans.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Pahlavi renders the hostile phrase as \"one who hates the Magu-men,\" and another term, mageus meaning \"holiness, godliness,\" was later confused with Magi, contributing to the Greek idea that magos could mean both \"priest\" and \"god.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A Bundahis tradition describes an unnamed hostile figure who addresses prayers to Ahriman by the banks of the Sipit Rud; his adversary Feridun is born in Ghilan, and the hostile figure is bound to Mount Damavand near Rai.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The of Persia.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"These Median Avesta texts express the ideas of the sacerdotal class under the Achaemenian dynasty, but the author back.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ahura Mazda is depicted answering questions about where Drug-Nasu rushes in relation to various parts.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The good waters are described as reaching a series of body parts in order: left content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l13774-l13876","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VIII. / FARGARD    XIII.  I  63 / FARGARD    XIV.  1 65 / FARGARD    XIV.  1 67; lines 13774-13876","start":"13774","end":"13876","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage prescribes that a man must kill immense numbers of animals classed as noxious—dog-shaped \"snakes\" (identified with cats), tortoises, land and water frogs, several kinds of ants, earthworms, and horrid flies—and fill ten thousand holes used for washing the unclean. Commentary explains that such creatures (Khrafstras) are hated and associated with pollution, disease, or theft. The text then requires the man to godly and piously give twice seven sets of fire implements and a set of priestly instruments to godly men as an atonement to the soul of the \"water dog.\" The implements include materials for the sacred fire, a broom for the fire-vessel, tongs, bellows, cutting tools, and ritual vessels, among them the Paitidana mouth-veil and the Khrafstraghna instrument for killing snakes and similar creatures. Further commentary states that everything issuing from a person, especially breath, is unclean, so priests and even laymen must wear a mouth-veil during ritual and eating; a parallel is drawn with a Slavonian priest at Arkona who must leave the temple to breathe so as not to pollute the god's presence. A poetic protest by Firdusi against killing the corn-carrying ant, preserved by the high-priest Moola Firooz, introduces a contrasting attitude of compassion toward small creatures.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man, referred to as \"he,\" is commanded to kill ten thousand of various creatures: dog-shaped snakes, tortoises, land frogs, water frogs, corn-carrying ants, biting and hole-digging ants, earthworms, and horrid flies.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The same man is ordered to fill up ten thousand holes associated with the unclean.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The term \"Mar banak snakes\" is explained as dog-like because they sit on their hindparts, and the commentary suggests that the cat is the animal intended and is counted among Khrafstras to be killed to redeem a sin.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"G. du Chinon reports that the Gaures have horror of serpents, snakes, lizards, toads, frogs, crayfish, rats, mice, and especially the cat.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Commentary says that certain frogs and toads foul the waters where they live, causing diseases and ultimately death among humans, and that the more such creatures exist in a country, the more the waters cause sickness and death.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Commentary explains that corn-carrying ants are persecuted because they are seen as stealing by carrying away heaps of grain more than they need for their own food.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Firdusi is quoted as protesting against the proscription of the corn-carrying ant, saying that it is a living thing and its life is dear to it, and Moola Firooz records these lines in his Pand Namah.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The list of creatures to be killed includes earthworms and horrid flies, with commentary identifying \"corpse flies\" among them.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The holes to be filled are explained as \"the holes at which the unclean are washed,\" linking them to ritual washing of impure persons.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The man must godly and piously give to godly men twice seven sets of implements for the fire as an atonement unto the soul of the water dog.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Fire implements include proper materials for the fire, a broom, a pair of tongs, round bellows, an adze, and a saw, which worshippers of Mazda use to procure wood for the fire of Ahura Mazda.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Commentary suggests the \"proper materials for fire\" are two loads of wood and two loads of incense to burn upon the wood.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The broom is used to cleanse the Atash-dan or fire-vessel.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Worshippers of Mazda procure wood for the fire of Ahura Mazda using tools such as the adze and saw.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The man must godly and piously give to godly men a set of priestly instruments—Astra, meat-vessel (possibly milk-vessel), Paitidana, and Khrafstraghna—as an atonement unto the soul of the water dog.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The Khrafstraghna is described as an instrument for killing snakes and similar creatures.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Commentary states that everything that goes out of a person is unclean and that human breath defiles all it touches, so priests and even laymen must wear the Paitidana mouth-veil while on duty, praying, or eating.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The Paitidana (Parsi Penom) is described as two pieces of white cotton cloth hanging loosely from the bridge of the nose to at least two inches below the mouth, tied with two strings at the back of the head.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A Slavonian priest in Arkona is said to be enjoined to go out of the temple whenever he wants to draw breath so that the presence of the god is not defiled by contact with mortal breath.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The commentator notes that the principle about breath not defiling the divine presence is not peculiar to the Zoroastrian Aryans and illustrates it with the Arkona example.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"penitent man","description":"Unnamed individual dog.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"water dog","description":"Animal whose soul the prescribed acts of killing and gifting are meant to C- / FARGARD    IV.  33; lines 7055-7167","start":"7055","end":"7167","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"'The law of Mazda, O Spitama Zarathustra! cleanses the faithful from every evil thought, word, and deed, as a swift-rushing mighty wind cleanses the plain.'","summary":"The passage concludes a teaching that the law of Mazda removes even heavy penalties of sin and cleanses the faithful from every evil thought, word, and deed, like a swift, mighty wind that purifies a plain. Ahura Mazda exhorts Zarathustra to make all his deeds good, since full atonement for his sin is effected through this law. A new section (Fargard IV) outlines regulations on contracts and outrages. It declares that a man who does not restore property lent to him is a thief and robber, continually stealing the neighbor's property as long as he keeps it. An interlocutor asks Ahura Mazda how many contracts there are; Ahura Mazda replies that there are six, the first being the word-contract. Commentary elaborates on contract classification, equates non-restoration of a loan with bad-faith indebtedness, cites Herodotus on Persian abhorrence of lying and debt, and quotes a Pahlavi text in which Hormazd says the worst sin is breaking one's word when only he is witness.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The text states that \"it\" takes away the heaviest penalties of sin and any sin that may be committed, even for deeds for which there is said to be no atonement.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The law of Mazda is said to cleanse the faithful from every evil thought, word, and deed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The law of Mazda's cleansing is compared to a swift-rushing mighty wind that cleanses the plain, which the commentary glosses as cleansing the plain from chaff.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Zarathustra is addressed by name and told that all his future deeds should be good.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"It is stated that full atonement for Zarathustra's sin is effected by means of the law of Mazda.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A heading entitled \"Contracts and Outrages\" outlines that Fargard IV treats contracts (classification, damages for breach, responsibility of kinsmen, and penalties) and outrages (menaces, assaults, blows, various kinds of wounds, broken bones, manslaughter, and false oaths).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"An editorial note states that certain clauses about contracts and praise of physical well-being seem misplaced and proposes a corrected sequence for the chapter.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The law declares that a man who does not restore a thing lent when it is asked back steals the thing and robs the man from whom it was borrowed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"It further states that as long as such a man keeps his neighbor's property in his house as though it were his own, he steals it anew every day and every night.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A commentary note explains that a man is a thief when he takes with a view not to restore, and a robber when, being asked to restore, he replies that he will not.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A note cites Herodotus that among Persians the basest thing is to lie and the next basest is to be in debt, because a debtor is likely to end up lying.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The same note clarifies that the debtor in question is a debtor of bad faith who asks for something promising to restore it at the proper time while inwardly resolving not to restore it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"An interlocutor addresses \"Maker of the material world, Holy One\" and asks Ahura Mazda how many contracts he has.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that there are six contracts and identifies the first as the word-contract.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A commentary note states that the contracts are classified in two ways: the first two by mode of being entered into, and the last four by their amount, and that the exact amount signified by the first two is uncertain to the commentators.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Another note defines the word-contract as a contract entered into by simple word of mouth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A Pahlavi quotation reports that the immortal Zarturt Isfitaman asked the good, beneficent Hormazd which sin is worst, and Hormazd replied that no sin is worse than when a man, having given his word to another with no witness but Hormazd, breaks his word and denies knowledge of it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"A commentary note suggests that a phrase in the preceding context may refer to \"the sin of usury\" and explains that while it is lawful to take high interest in general, it is not lawful to do so from the faithful.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura Mazda / Hormazd","description":"The deity addressed as Maker of the material world and Holy One, giver of the law of Mazda, who answers questions about contracts and declares which sin is He must also supply small cattle, rear whelps, build bridges over canals, repair stables, cleanse dogs of disease, and feast groups of godly men. This complex penalty is said to atone for the deed: if the offender undergoes it, he enters the world of the holy ones; if not, he falls into the dark world of the wicked. The next section (Fargard XV) introduces five sins which, if neither confessed nor atoned for, make a person a Peshotanu; the first is knowingly teaching one of the faithful a foreign, wrong creed and law.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"As atonement for the soul of the water dog, an unnamed man must godly and piously give godly men a can be watered on both sides by such a rill.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"He must procure for godly men a house with ox-stalls and with nine hathras and nine The coming forth and processing of barley, corn, and wheat causes the Daevas to start up, faint, groan, and finally be destroyed and driven from the house, as if plenty of corn were like red-hot iron in their throats. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l15314-l15407","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    XVIII.  193 / FARGARD    XVIII. / O    2 / FARGARD    XVIII.  1 97; lines 15314-15407","start":"15314","end":"15407","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"He does thereby as thoroughly destroy the fruit of my womb as a four-footed wolf does, who tears the child out of a mother's womb.\"","summary":"The passage presents a dialogue between the holy Sraosha and the female Druj demon. Sraosha, with his club uplifted, questions the demon about the human males who belong to her and the acts by which they make her conceive demonic progeny. She names a man who urinates onto his foot and a man who emits seed during sleep, saying that such men make her conceive as males do their females. For each offense, the demon prescribes ritual counteractions: charitable giving of stored riches to the faithful, and specific sequences of recited formulas and offerings after rising and stepping away or after waking from sleep. These acts are said to destroy the fruit of her womb as thoroughly as a four-footed wolf tearing a child from a mother's womb. Finally, Sraosha declares that he will deliver the man to Spenta Armaiti and asks that she return him on the mighty day of resurrection as one who knows the Gathas; a footnote identifies Spenta Armaiti as the genius of the earth and compares related purity regulations in other texts.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A counteracting act is defined as when a man, unasked, kindly and piously gives to one of the faithful some part, however small, of the riches he has stored up.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker states that by performing the counteracting act, the man thoroughly destroys the fruit of the demon’s womb as a four-footed wolf tears a child out of a mother’s womb.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:6","ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sraosha, described as holy, repeatedly asks the Druj demon with his club uplifted against her, calling her wretched and wicked, to identify her second and third males and the acts that counteract them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:7","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Druj demon, called guileful, identifies her second male as the man who, while urinating (“making water”), lets it fall along the upper forepart of his foot.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The demon says that this man makes her conceive progeny as other males make their females.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"To counteract the urinary offense, the demon prescribes that the man rise, step three steps further away, say three Ahuna-Vairya, two humatanam, three hukhshathrotemam, then chant the Ahuna-Vairya and offer up one Yehe hatam.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The demon identifies her third male as the man who emits seed during his sleep and again says that such a man makes her conceive progeny as other males make their females.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"To counteract the nocturnal emission, the demon prescribes that when the man has risen from sleep he should say three Ahuna-Vairya, two humatanam, three hukhshathrotemam, then chant the Ahuna-Vairya and offer up one Yehe hatam.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In each case, the standing.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sraosha","description":"A holy, tall-formed figure who questions the Druj demon with his club First, Ahura Mazda is said to forbid wasting even a tiny amount of thread, and anyone who throws clothing on a corpse is described as impious, excluded from the happy realm, and destined instead for a dark world of fiends, a dismal realm to which sinners are delivered by their own deeds and souls. Commentary elaborates that the dead should be clothed only in old, well-washed garments and that every unnecessary thread of a shroud becomes, in the other world, a black snake that clings to the heart of the one who made it; the dead person is said to rise against this wrongdoer. The commentator contrasts this with Greek custom of dressing the dead in their finest clothes, while noting that in Zoroastrian belief rich garments are offered to the soul once it is in heaven. The text then turns to Fargard VI, where Ahura Mazda answers Zarathushtra’s questions about how long ground where a dog or a man has died must lie fallow (a year) and forbids worshippers of Mazda to sow or water that part of the field during that period. Sowing or watering such ground within the year is equated with bringing dead matter to water, earth, and plants and incurs the status of Peshotanu with a set number of stripes from two instruments. To make the ground fit again, the worshippers must inspect it for bones, hair, flesh, dung, or blood; failing to do so brings the same heavy penalty. A separate rule states that throwing even a small bone of a dead dog or man onto the ground, if grease or marrow flows from it, brings a lesser but still substantial beating.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ahura Mazda is said not to allow people to waste anything of value, not even as much as a tiny laid on the dead; every unnecessary thread placed on the corpse will in the other world become a black snake clinging to the heart of the shroud-maker, and the dead will rise against him, seize him by the skirt, and accuse him that the shroud has become food for worms and vermin.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The commentary notes that after the fourth day,
