content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l7682-l7780","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    IV.  39 / FARGARD    IV.  4 1 / FARGARD    IV.  43 / FARGARD    IV.  45; lines 7682-7780","start":"7682","end":"7780","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage sets out rules for agreements among men of the same faith concerning the transfer of goods, a wife, or knowledge, with knowledge identified as teaching of the holy word. It prescribes an intense regimen of study and prayer for the learner, continuing day and night until he can recite all the words spoken by former teaching priests (Aethrapaitis). It then returns to contracts and oaths, forbidding anyone, before water and blazing fire, to deny receiving an ox or garment from a neighbor. Another section ranks the man with a wife, house, children, and riches above those without such things. Translator’s notes illustrate this with Persian customs and later Zoroastrian teaching that a childless man is barred from the bridge of paradise and questioned by angels, and compare this to a Brahmanical doctrine that a man without a son falls into hell for lack of family worship. The text further asserts that the man who fills himself with meat is much more filled with the good spirit than the one who does not, calling the latter almost dead and valuing the former more highly. Commentary links the good spirit with Vohu Mano and contrasts Zoroastrian ‘fasting from sin’ with other religions’ fasting from bread. Finally, the text states that this well‑nourished man can strive against the onsets of Asto-vidhotu, a hostile being mentioned by name.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Men of the same faith, whether friends or brothers, may come to an agreement so that one obtains from the other either goods, a wife, or knowledge, and each type is to be appropriately delivered, received, or taught.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Knowledge in this context means being taught 'the holy word' by a teacher.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The learner is instructed to study during the first and last parts of the day and of the night so that his mind may increase in knowledge and grow strong in holiness.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"While studying, the learner is to sit up giving thanks and praying to the gods for increased knowledge, resting only in the middle parts of day and night.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The learner must continue this pattern until he can recite all the words that former Aethrapaitis have said; a note identifies an Aethrapaiti as a teaching priest.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"An injunction states that before water and blazing fire, no one should dare to deny having received an ox or a garment from a neighbor; a note explains that water and fire are the elements before which oaths are taken against false oaths.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The text declares that a man who has a wife is far above one who begets no sons, a man who keeps a house is above one who has none, a man who has children is above a childless man, and a man who has riches is above one who has none.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A note cites Herodotus that in Persia the king gives prizes to those who have the most children, and cites the Saddar that a man without a child is barred from the bridge of paradise, where angels ask whether he has left a substitute; if not, they pass by and he remains at the head of the bridge in grief and sorrow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The same note explains that, according to a Brahmanical doctrine, a man without a son falls into hell because no one performs the family worship for him.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The text states that of two men, the one who fills himself with meat is filled with the good spirit much more than the one who does not, that the latter is almost dead, and that the former is above him by the worth of an Asperena, a sheep, an ox, and a man.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A note suggests that the 'good spirit' may be Vohu Mano, and another note quotes later Zoroastrian teaching that while some people abstain from meat or strive to pass a day without eating, Zoroastrians abstain from sin in deed, thought, or word and 'fast from sin' rather than from bread.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The text says that 'this man'—apparently the one who eats meat and is filled with the good spirit—can strive against the onsets of Asto-vidhotu, a named hostile power.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Speaker addressing Zarathustra","description":"An content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l16481-l16581","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"KARGARD    XIX.  2M / FARGARD    XIX.  215 / FARGARD    XIX.  21  7 / FARGARD    XX.  210.; lines 16481-16581","start":"16481","end":"16581","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An introductory commentary explains that Thrita is the first healer, having driven back death and disease after Ahura Mazda brought him from heaven ten thousand healing plants that grew around the tree of eternal life, the white Horn or Gaokerena. Thrita is identified with Thraetaona and compared with Vedic Trita Aptya, a priest of Haoma and serpent-killing hero, and Thraetaona is described as inventor of medicine whose Fravashi is invoked against diseases and plagues created by the serpent. Disease is said to be understood as a kind of poisoning from the serpent, and this theory is linked to the prominence of serpents in the cult of Asklepios. The Vendidad section then narrates Zarathustra asking Ahura Mazda who first among the healthful men of old drove back sickness and death and turned away weapons and the fire of fever from mortals; Ahura Mazda answers that it was Thrita, who asked for a source of remedies and obtained it from Khshathra-Vairya to withstand sickness, death, pain, fever, and rottenness, including the use of a knife and herbs.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage begins with the formula \"Ashem vohu: Holiness is the best of all good.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Thrita is described as the first who drove back death and disease.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Ahura Mazda is said to have brought down from heaven ten thousand healing plants to Thrita.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"These healing plants had been growing around the \"tree of eternal life,\" identified as the white Horn or Gaokerena.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Thrita is mentioned elsewhere in the Avesta as one of the first priests of Haoma.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Haoma is described as a source of life and health, and its first priests are said to have been the first healers.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Thrita is said to have been originally the same as Thraetaona.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In the Rig-veda, the great feat of Thraetaona is ascribed to Trita as well as to Traitana.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Trita Aptya, called \"the son of the waters,\" is described as both a celestial priest who pours Haoma into rain and a celestial hero who kills the snake in storms.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"According to Hamza, Thraetaona was the inventor of medicine; formulas of exorcism against sickness (Tavids) bear his name, and the Avesta invokes Thraetaona's Fravashi against various fevers and plagues created by the serpent.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The commentary states that disease was understood as coming from the serpent and considered a kind of poisoning, so the killer of the serpent was invoked to act against it; thus Thrita-Thraetaona has a double right to the title \"first of the healers\" as both priest of Haoma and conqueror of the serpent.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A note adds that in the Vedas Trita had been a healing god.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The \"healthful\" are glossed as those whom no weapon could wound, compared to Isfendiar.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The phrase \"drove back sickness to sickness, drove back death to death\" is explained as \"kept sickness in bonds, kept death in bonds.\"","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Khshathra-Vairya is said to preside over metals and to have given Thrita a knife whose point and base were set in gold; Thrita is described as the first who healed with the knife and also with herbs, alongside healing with the holy word mentioned elsewhere.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The theory that disease comes from the serpent is said to account for the large role of the serpent in the worship of Asklepios, since sickness and healing may both come from him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda who first among the healthful, wise, happy, wealthy, glorious, strong men of old drove back sickness to sickness and death to death and turned away the point of the poniard and the fire of fever from the bodies of mortals.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that Thrita was that first healthful, wise, happy, wealthy, glorious, strong man of yore who drove back sickness to sickness and death to death and turned away the point of the poniard and the fire of fever from mortals.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The text states that Thrita asked for a source of remedies and obtained it from Khshathra-Vairya to withstand sickness, death, pain, fever, disease, and rottenness.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura Mazda","description":"Described as the most beneficent Spirit, Maker of the material world, the Holy One, who answers Zarathustra and brings healing plants from heaven.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:11","ev:12","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Thrita","description":"Presented as the first healer and first of the healthful, wise, and as a priest of I  I  3; lines 11097-11198","start":"11097","end":"11198","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage consists of a series of questions addressed to Ahura Mazda about what reward a man will receive after his soul has parted from his body if he brings various types of fire to the Daityo-gatu. These fires include ones in which excrement or cowdung has been burnt, fires from brick-makers' and potters' kilns, the fire of the reapers, and the fires of a goldsmith and a silversmith. Ahura Mazda replies that each act will yield a reward equivalent to having brought a specified number of fire-brands to the Daityo-gatu, with different numbers for each type of fire. A commentary note identifies the Daityo-gatu as the Bahram fire, composed of many fires, the earthly representative of heavenly fire, described as a sacred centre to which every earthly fire longs to return; it adds that the more a fire has been defiled by worldly use, the greater the merit in liberating it from such defilement.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An unnamed inquirer repeatedly addresses Ahura Mazda as 'Maker of the material world, Holy One' and asks what a man's reward will be after his soul has parted from his body if he brings particular kinds of fire to the I  99; lines 15410-15508","start":"15410","end":"15508","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes a wise person who knows the Yasna and the revealed law and is called the Word incarnate; this figure’s name is to include the word \"Fire\" (e.g., Fire-creature, Fire-seed, Fire-offspring, Fire-land). The holy Sraosha, armed with an uplifted club, questions the female demon Druj about the fourth category of her \"males.\" Druj explains that this category consists of any man or woman over fifteen years of age who walks without wearing the sacred girdle and shirt. The Daevas are said to wither such a person at the fourth step and grant them power to destroy the world of the holy spirit, in a manner likened to Yatus and Zandas; Druj states there is no way to counteract this. In a new section, Ahura Mazda invites the upright Zarathustra to ask questions so that he may become better and happier. Zarathustra asks who grieves and pains Ahura Mazda most, and Ahura Mazda answers that it is the courtesan Cahi, an incarnation of the female demon Gahi, who goes whoring after all categories of people (faithful and unfaithful, worshippers of Mazda and of the Daevas, wicked and righteous). Ahura Mazda describes Cahi’s look as drying up one third of the mighty floods that run from the mountains and withering one third of the beautiful growing plants and the grass, and a note adds that she becomes guilty of death after being with three men.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A wise and clever man who knows the Yasna and the revealed law is described as the Word incarnate.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The name of this figure is commanded to include the word \"Fire,\" with suggested titles such as \"Fire-creature,\" \"Fire-seed,\" \"Fire-offspring,\" and \"Fire-land.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sraosha, described as holy and tall-formed, confronts the female demon Druj with his club uplifted against her and asks who the fourth of her males is.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Druj, called wretched, wicked, and guileful, answers that her fourth male is a person, either man or woman, more than fifteen years of age, who walks without wearing the sacred girdle and the sacred shirt.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A note identifies the sacred girdle and shirt as the Kosti and the Sadar, and describes walking several steps without the Kosti as a graded sin that becomes a tanafuhr sin from the fourth step.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Daevas are said to wither such a person at the fourth step, even to the tongue and the marrow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The withered person then goes with power to destroy the world of the holy spirit and destroys it like the Yatus and the Zandas.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sraosha asks Druj what can counteract this destructive condition.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Druj replies that there is no means of counteracting it and repeats that when an adult walks without the sacred girdle or shirt, the Daevas wither them and they destroy the world of the holy spirit like the Yatus and Zandas.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Ahura Mazda addresses an upright questioner, identifying himself as the Maker, the best of all beings, the most knowing, and the most pleased in answering what is asked of him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Ahura Mazda says that demanding answers from him will make the questioner better and happier.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda who grieves him with the sorest grief and pains him with the sorest pain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that the courtesan Cahi, who goes whoring after the faithful and the unfaithful, Mazda-worshippers and Daeva-worshippers, wicked and righteous, is the one who grieves and pains him most.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A note describes Cahi as a courtesan and an incarnation of the female demon Gahi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Ahura Mazda states that Cahi’s look dries up one third of the mighty floods that run from the mountains.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Ahura Mazda states that Cahi’s look withers one third of the beautiful, golden-hued growing plants and one third of the grass.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A note indicates that when Cahi has been with three men, she is guilty of XV11; lines 931-1024","start":"931","end":"1024","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage from Darmesteter’s introduction describes Meiners’ hostile critique of books ascribed to Zoroaster that contain numerous unfamiliar names, exalt figures like Horn and Jemshid as divine heroes, and recount many tales of demons, yet also notes resemblances between Parsi, Brahman, and Muslim ideas. The author reports later scholarly conclusions that Parsiism contributed elements to Mohammed’s formation of Islam and that the old religions of India and Persia share a common source. Meiners’ remarks about shared demon tales and remedies with Indian priests are called a germ of comparative mythology. The passage goes on to recount how Anquetil and especially Kleuker defended the authenticity of the Avesta, compared it with Plutarch’s account of Magian religion, debated Meiners’ claim of a mythical identity between Mount Alborz and Mount Meru, and discussed the reversed meaning of a demon-related term in Persia and India. Kleuker’s philological arguments that Zend and Pahlavi lack Arabic elements (except in books considered modern) and Tychsen’s eventual support of the Avesta’s authenticity are also summarized.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Critics are said to ascribe to Zoroaster books containing numerous names of trees, animals, men, and demons unknown to ancient Persians.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"These books invoke an incredible number of pure animals and other things that, according to the silence of ancient writers, were not known or at least not worshipped in Persia.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The fabricators of the disputed rhapsody highly praise figures such as Horn and Jemshid as divine heroes, although no Greek writer is said to mention them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Meiners observes that there are many points of resemblance between the ideas of the Parsis and those of the Brahmans and Musulmans.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Meiners interprets these resemblances as proof that Parsiism is a medley of Brahmanical and Musulman tales.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Modern scholarship, as summarized in the passage, concludes that Parsiism was one of the elements out of which Mohammed formed his religion.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The same modern scholarship also concludes that the old religions of India and Persia flowed from a common source.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Meiners reports that the author of the criticized text tells the same tales of numberless demons of valid.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Kleuker replies that Mount Alborz is a real mountain name borne by two actual mountains, one in Persia and another in XXXI X / CHAPTER  V. / XC  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    V.  XC1; lines 4813-4858","start":"4813","end":"4858","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage discusses Zoroastrian ritual impurity associated with childbirth, especially when the child is still-born. Although the mother has increased life and enlarged Ormazd's realm, she is treated as unclean due to contact with death and the presence of a \"death-fiend\" in her. For a still-birth, she must drink gomez to wash the \"grave\" in her womb and is forbidden to drink sacred water except at risk of death, incurring penalty for defiling it. In practice, similar treatment is extended to women after live births because mother and child are considered in great danger for three days, during which a great fire is lit to ward off fiends who try to kill them. A note from the Saddar prescribes continuous fire during pregnancy and three days of candle or fire after birth to keep Devs and Drûgs from harming the child. Ethnographic and classical notes add a Persian custom of brandishing a sword around the birthing place to deter the fairy Aal, and a Roman practice where deities Intercidona, Pilumnus, and Deverra guard the threshold to keep Sylvanus from harming the mother. A following section explains that sickness, sent by Ahriman, is treated as a form of demonic possession and uncleanness, to be cured by washings and especially by spells, which are regarded as the most powerful medicine, though surgery and drugs are also used. A commentator remarks that, unlike knife and physic, spells at least do no harm if they fail.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A woman who has given birth is described as ritually unclean, even though she is said to have increased life in the world and enlarged the realm of Ormazd.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Vendidad specifically examines the case of a woman delivered of a still-born child, who is considered unclean because she has been in contact with a dead creature.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The woman with a still-born child must drink gomez to wash over the \"grave\" in her womb.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The postpartum woman is forbidden to drink water, the sacred element, unless she is in danger of death; even XC1X / VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    V.  CI; lines 5234-5345","start":"5234","end":"5345","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Parsi tradition is found in the Pahlavi Commentary ...\"","summary":"In this closing part of his introduction to the Vendidad, James Darmesteter explains the sources and methods he used for his translation. He notes that Parsi tradition is preserved in the Pahlavi Commentary, whose understanding was aided by a Gujarathi translation by Aspendiarji and a Persian transliteration and translation from the Haug collection in Munich, with help from Professor von Halm. He also drew on the Ravaets and the prose Saddar, and on European scholars such as Spiegel and Haug. Darmesteter follows Westergaard’s Avesta text and paragraph divisions while indicating Spiegel’s divisions in brackets. He discusses how quotations from the Pahlavi Commentary that entered the Vendidad Sadah are often rejected as spurious, though lack of a Pahlavi translation alone is not decisive, and he describes how untranslated passages may be admitted in brackets. He explains his non-traditional division of Fargards, the ways his translation differs from earlier ones, and his limited space for justificatory notes. He thanks E. W. West for revising the manuscript and improving the English, dates the introduction to Paris, November 1879, and adds notes on leaving some formulae untranslated, earlier complete Vendidad translations, and abbreviations for key sources such as Aspendiarji’s translation, the Bundahis, the Pahlavi Commentary, the Grand Ravaet, and Ormazd et Ahriman.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Parsi tradition for the Vendidad is accessed through the Pahlavi Commentary, whose understanding was helped by a Gujarathi translation and paraphrase by Aspendiarji and by a Persian transliteration and translation from the Haug collection in Munich.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The editors were indebted to Professor von Halm, Director of the State Library in Munich, for access to the Haug collection manuscript.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Ravaets and the prose Saddar frequently provided valuable information about the traditional meaning of doubtful passages, and the prose Saddar differs considerably from the Saddar in verse translated by Hyde.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Aspendiarji’s Gujarathi translation was published in Bombay in 1842 in two volumes, and it closely accords with the Persian translation in the Haug collection, including shared mistakes such as misreading the Pahlavi transliteration of Zend a-vastra as a verb meaning ‘he who wishes.’","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The editors are indebted to Professor Spiegel’s Commentary on the Avesta and to translations in the second edition of Martin Haug’s Essays as key European scholarly sources.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The translation follows the Avesta text and paragraph divisions given by Westergaard, while bracketed references provide the corresponding divisions of Professor Spiegel’s edition, and quotations refer to Spiegel’s text as corrected from the London manuscript.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Many passages in the Vendidad Sadah are quotations from the Pahlavi Commentary that have entered the Sadah text and are generally treated as spurious because they are not translated in the Commentary and are not connected with the context, so they are excluded from the edited text.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Although lack of a Pahlavi translation often marks a passage as spurious, the editors note that translations may be lost or omitted when repeated, and when they judge this to be the case they admit the untranslated passages into the text in brackets.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The principal Fargards are divided by the editors into several sections according to subject matter in an attempt to resolve the Vendidad into primitive fragments, but they acknowledge that only the paragraph divisions have traditional authority from the manuscripts.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Darmesteter’s translation often differs substantially from earlier published translations, and although space prevents full justificatory notes, explanatory notes are intended to account to scholars for the new meanings, with the expectation that a fresh reading of the original text will justify the translation.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Formulae and enumerations in the Vendidad are often left untranslated, even though they are considered part of the text, and this practice is illustrated with references to several Fargards.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Earlier complete translations of the Vendidad were published by Anquetil Duperron in French, by Professor Spiegel in German, and by Canon de Harlez in Belgium, and Spiegel’s translation was later translated into English by Professor Bleeck, who added information from unpublished Gujarathi translations.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The volume uses specific abbreviations for major sources: Asp. for The text then turns to scholarly discussion of Zarathustra's status (divine or human) and argues that Mazdeism continues the old Indo-Iranian religion rather than reacting against it. Finally, it analyzes the semantic history of divine names such as Asura, Yazata, and Daeva, showing how some terms for gods in the shared Indo-Iranian tradition later came to denote demons in Indian content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l2715-l2805","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"C   2 / XXXVI  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X; lines 2715-2805","start":"2715","end":"2805","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Fire, earth, and water had always been considered sacred things, and had received worship.\"","summary":"This scholarly introduction to part of the Vendidad argues that the Avesta’s liturgical texts and priestly traditions already existed under the Achaemenian kings. It describes how the Magi’s sung rituals, comparable to those of the Brahmans, formed a sacred corpus transmitted to later Mobeds, and how the liturgical Avesta functioned as a sacred book for Persians, chanted in Zend before a Persian-speaking audience, akin to Latin liturgy among European peoples. The author discusses the relative age and co-ordination of Avesta texts, the symmetrically arranged enumerations of gods, and references to seven Arch-Devs and seven Amshaspands, noting that a full contrast between these groups came later. The passage also notes that only the germs of a theory of time and space as first principles appear in the Avesta, compared with its fuller development in Greek philosophy (Eudemos, disciple of Aristotle). Finally, it examines Magian observances, especially the doctrine of elemental purity: fire, earth, and water are revered as sacred and must not be polluted by corpses, leading to prohibitions on cremation and burial that distinguish Magian practice from other Iranians and are eventually enforced under the Sassanian state religion.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Magi sang songs to their gods during sacrifice, and no sacrifice could be performed without their assistance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Magi are said to have possessed rites, prayers, and hymns that were well composed and arranged.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The rites, prayers, and hymns of the Magi are described as \"not unlike\" those of the Brahmans.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"There is said to have been a collection of formulae and hymns forming part of the Avesta.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Herodotus may have heard the Magi sing in the fifth century B.C. the same Gathas that Mobeds in Bombay sing in the present day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The liturgical part of the Avesta is described as a sacred book for the Persians, which had not been written by them but was sung for their benefit.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Zend hymns sung before a Persian-speaking people are compared to Latin words sung by French, Germans, and Italians, with Zend noted as closely related to Persian.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The present Avesta texts are said to be derived from texts already existing under the Achaemenian kings.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Gathas are considered older than the rest of the Avesta because they are often quoted and praised in the Yasna and the Vendidad.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Yasna, Visperad, and Vendidad contain long, symmetrically elaborated enumerations of gods.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Plutarch’s account of Mazdeism is said to show that the work of co-ordination of the Avesta was already completed by the end of the Achaemenian period.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Greek accounts of the Achaemenian period are described as presenting a later stage of thought and a stronger sense of symmetry than the Avesta.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Passages at the end of the Zamyad Yast and in Vendidad X, 9 seq. show that, when they were composed, the seven Arch-Devs were not yet contrasted with the seven Amshaspands.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The theory of time and space as first principles of the world is said to be present only in germinal form in the Avesta and fully developed in the time of Eudemos, a disciple of Aristotle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The extent to which Magian dogmatical conceptions were accepted by the whole Iranian population, and the process by which they spread, are described as unknown because of lack of documentary evidence.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Magian observances are said to be better known, allowing an idea of how and in what particulars they differed from other Iranians.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The Magi are described as introducing or developing a principle concerning the purity of the elements.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Fire, earth, and water are described as sacred things that had always received worship.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"From the principle of elemental purity, the Magi drew the conclusion that burying or burning the dead defiled a god.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"By the time of Herodotus, the Magi had succeeded in keeping fire free from pollution by corpses, and cremation was a capital crime.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Earth continued to be defiled by corpses until, under the Sassanians when Mazdeism became the state religion, this practice was stopped.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The religious difference between the Persians and their Medic priests is described as chiefly a matter of observances.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The sacerdotal class is said to have drawn stricter conclusions from popular religious principles by logic, in a puritan spirit.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"A footnote asserts that Darius caused additional inscriptions to be engraved and wrote other edicts and religious formulae.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Magi","description":"Priestly class who sang songs to their gods during sacrifice, possessed a body of rites, prayers, and hymns, and developed the doctrine of elemental purity affecting treatment of the dead.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:9","ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Mobeds in Bombay","description":"Later Zoroastrian priests in as not unlike those of the Magi.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Herodotus","description":"Greek historian who may have heard the Magi sing the Gathas and whose time is used as a reference point for the prohibition of cremation and preservation of fire from pollution.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Plutarch","description":"Greek author whose account of Mazdeism is cited as evidence that the co-ordination of the Avesta was complete by the end of the Achaemenian period.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Darius","description":"A king mentioned in a footnote as causing other inscriptions to be engraved and writing edicts and religious formulae.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Achaemenian kings","description":"Dynastic rulers under whom earlier Avesta texts are said to have existed and among whom the co-ordination of the Avesta was completed.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Philip","description":"A historical figure used as a chronological marker; some Avesta passages are said to have possibly been composed long before his time.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Eudemos","description":"A disciple of Aristotle in whose time the theory of time and space as first principles of the world is described as fully developed.","role_refs":["role:5","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Aristotle","description":"Philosopher identified as the teacher of Eudemos in connection with the developed theory of time and space as first principles.","role_refs":["role:5","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Iranian population","description":"The broader Iranian populace whose acceptance of Magian dogmatical conceptions is said to be uncertain.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:13","name_or_label":"Other Iranians","description":"Non-Magian Iranians whose observances are compared with those of the Magi.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:14","name_or_label":"Sassanians","description":"Dynasty under which Mazdeism became the state religion and the prohibition on defiling earth with corpses was successfully enforced.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:15","name_or_label":"Mazdeism","description":"Religious system described in Plutarch’s account and later made the religion of the Sassanian state.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Medic priests","description":"Priests of the Persians, identified as differing from the Persians chiefly in observances and associated with the sacerdotal class.","role_refs":["role:1","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:17","name_or_label":"Sacerdotal class","description":"Priestly group that drew strict conclusions from popular religious principles by logic and developed observances in a puritan spirit.","role_refs":["role:2","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:18","name_or_label":"Seven Arch-Devs","description":"Group of content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l6250-l6343","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    II.  I  I / FARGARD    II.  I  3 / FARGARD    II.  I  5 / FARGARD    II.  I  J; lines 6250-6343","start":"6250","end":"6343","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“Therefore make thee a Vara, long as a riding-ground on every side of the square, to be an abode for men… Thither thou shalt bring the seeds of men and women… and the seeds of every kind of tree and fruit… All those seeds shalt thou bring, two of every kind, to be kept inexhaustible there… That Vara thou shalt seal up with the golden ring, and thou shalt make a door, and a window self-shining within.”","summary":"Ahura Mazda instructs Yima to construct a square Vara, as large as a riding-ground, furnished with water, evergreen banks, dwellings, and the seeds of the best kinds of humans, animals, trees, fruits, and fires, two of each kind, to be preserved there in ideal, disease-free conditions; the Vara is to be laid out in streets, sealed with a golden ring, and lit by a self-shining window. Yima wonders how to build it, is told to crush and knead the earth like a potter, does so, and completes the Vara, bringing in the seeds. A translator’s note compares this to the Shah Namah story of Gamshid teaching the Divs to knead clay and build palaces, and notes that Muslims identified him with Solomon as a wise king and builder.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A Vara is to be made as long as a riding-ground on every side of a square, to serve as an abode mortals.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Vara is to be divided into parts with streets: nine streets in the largest part, six in the middle part, and three in the smallest part.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"To the streets of the largest part a thousand seeds of men and women are to be brought; to those of the {"record_id":"batch.motif.sufi-omar-khayyam-sufistic-quatrains-gutenberg-l14435-l14622","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/sufi/project-gutenberg/sufistic-quatrains-omar-khayyam.md","passage_locator":{"label":"QUATRAINS OF OMAR KHAYYAM / MONSIEUR J.B. NICOLAS / THE QUATRAINS OF KHAYYAM / THE QUATRAINS OF OMAR KHAYYAM; lines 14435-14622","start":"14435","end":"14622","translation":"The Sufistic Quatrains of Omar Khayyam","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In these quatrains the poetic voice identified as Khayyam repeatedly urges an unnamed listener to turn away from mosque, prayer, fasting, and concern over the inconstant world, and instead to seek wine, the tavern, and sensual and mystical companionship. Human bodies and their dust are imagined as future cups, bowls, pitchers, and tavern dust soaked in wine. Blooming roses, zephyrs, and the nightingale illustrate fleeting beauty, while cypress and lily exemplify freedom by remaining mute and empty-handed. The speaker describes gatherings of lovers who, having emptied the cup of God’s love, are tranquil and drunk, beyond pain and the constraints of time. He questions the value of long life with repeated "after that?" and counsels organizing a Paradise here below with cup and wine, doubting the attainability of a future Paradise. 

Wine is praised above empires and royal regalia and portrayed as a nectar and chain binding fools and sages alike. The speaker confesses regret over lawless living and failure to obey divine commands, yet claims trust in God’s benevolence, which he says makes those who have done nothing equal to those who have done much. God is said to have fashioned people from creation’s crucible so that they cannot be better than they are. The community of drinkers claims to have broken vows, closed the door of what is called good and bad, and to be drunk with the wine of love, beyond reflection, intelligence, and reason. The inconstant world and the inevitability of annihilation are contrasted with present enjoyment of wine and a caressing mistress.

The dead are described as embedded in the dust of pride and as insubstantial as wind, prompting further calls to drink. A filthy, gender-ambiguous figure in a shirt of Hell-smoke appears and breaks the group’s wine flask, boasting of a deed "worthy of a man." The speaker addresses his heart, describing how admission to the banquet of an idol identified as the Divinity requires going out of and re-entering oneself, and tasting a wine of annihilation that separates one from beings and non-beings. He embraces his intimacy with wine and drunkenness, wonders why the world blames him, and wishes that all illegal things produced drunkenness so that sound reason would never appear. Finally, he accuses God of breaking his wine pitcher, closing the portals of joy, and pouring his clear wine on the earth, and asks whether God could have been drunk.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker tells an addressee to stop speaking of the mosque, prayer, and fasting, and instead to go to the tavern and intoxicate himself, even asking alms for that purpose.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker says that the earth from which the addressee is composed will be made into cups, bowls, and pitchers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The world is compared to a palace of brief being, and a wise man is urged to give himself up to rose-colored wine.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker says that each atom of the drinker’s dust, carried away by the wind, will fall on the sill of the tavern, saturated with wine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Zephyrs are said to make roses bloom, whose fragrant beauty gladdens the nightingale; the flowers quickly depart from the earth and often do not return.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The speaker tells the addressee to rest in the shadow of the flowers before they depart.","category":"speech","evidence

Notes clarify the nine-foot distances between gomez and water holes and between holes and furrows, and explain that the steps prevent the foot of the unclean one from touching the earth.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg; Zend-Avesta Part I: Vendidad."},{"id":"ev:7","type":"summary","locator":"11660-11603","quote_or_summary":"The unclean one is instructed to walk to the holes, while Zarathustra is told to stand outside by the furrow and recite the prayer NemasH ya.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg; Zend-Avesta Part I: Vendidad."}],"confidence":{"extraction":"medium","motif_candidates":"medium","comparison_claims":"uncertain","notes":"Ritual actions and spatial arrangements are clearly described, but the broader motif classification, especially regarding initiation, is interpretive and should be reviewed by a specialist."},"reviewer_status":{"status":"needs_review","reviewer":"","reviewed_at":"","notes":""},"extracted_by":"atlas-llm-gpt4o-2026-07","extracted_at":"2026-07-18","notes":"Extraction focuses on ritual structure, demon-expulsion function of the kesh, and the role of spells and holy liquids; motif links are provisional."}

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.sufi-omar-khayyam-sufistic-quatrains-gutenberg-l14624-l14819","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/sufi/project-gutenberg/sufistic-quatrains-omar-khayyam.md","passage_locator":{"label":"QUATRAINS OF OMAR KHAYYAM / MONSIEUR J.B. NICOLAS / THE QUATRAINS OF KHAYYAM / THE QUATRAINS OF OMAR KHAYYAM; lines 14624-14819","start":"14624","end":"14819","translation":"The Sufistic Quatrains of Omar Khayyam","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A sequence of quatrains reflects on human mortality, divine mystery, fate, and the tension between worldly religion and inner trust in the divine. The speaker addresses a human friend, God, his own heart, the Wheel of Heaven, a potter, a cupbearer, a mullah, and various personified images such as Rose, Fortune, and a china cup. He complains that God lays snares yet judges humans, affirms confidence in divine pity, and questions why he was separated from his true self and thrown into the world. The heart is urged to free itself from material grief and ascend to the heavens. The potter is warned that human clay bears the touch of revered figures. Repeated images of wine, gardens, cups, skulls as pitchers, spring and autumn, flowers, and green turf express the brevity of life and the hope for inner rebirth. Wine is praised as an antidote to grief and a means of joyful companionship with a divine or beloved friend, contrasted with hypocrisy, midnight religious alarms, and accusations from a mullah. The speaker insists that only the divine can open the door and show a safe way, while human guides are perishable.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker tells a human addressee that they are the result of the four elements and the seven heavens, are perplexed among these, and should drink wine because once they depart they will not return.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker accuses the divine Thou of raising ambushes, spreading snares that lead people to death, and then calling those who fall into them rebels.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The divine essence is described as impenetrable to intelligence, and the divine Thou is said to care no more for human obedience than for human faults.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker states that he is drunk with sin but that his confidence in the divine Thou makes this acceptable, and he counts on divine pity.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker imagines that if worldly things were only based on show and threats did not exist, each person could reach their desires without fear.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Wheel of Heaven is addressed as constantly filling the speaker's heart with woe, killing the germ of joy by loading the air with water and turning the water he drinks into mud.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The speaker tells his heart that if it frees itself from the grief inherent in matter it will become a pure soul, ascend to the heavens, and dwell in the firmament, and that it should feel shame at inhabiting the earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The potter is urged to use reason and not abase man when moulding his clay, which is said to be the finger of Feridoun and the hand of Kai-Khosrou placed on the wheel.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The rose is likened to the face of a ravishing youth, wine to a ruby whose brightness delights the soul, and fateful fortune to a being that appears ever more strange yet somehow familiar.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The world is compared to a kitchen from which the addressee absorbs only smoke, while he sorrows in searching for being and annihilation; attachment to the world is said to bring only loss, whereas disregarding this loss brings benefit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The speaker refuses to torment sleeping people by making them cry out 'O my God! O my God!' at midnight and warns that riches and beauty quickly disappear, both being lost during the night.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The speaker asks the divine Thou why, if from the beginning He wished to make the speaker known to himself, He later separated him from this self and threw him amazed into the midst of the world.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The speaker wishes there were a place of repose and a road with a settled end, and hopes that after a very long time the heart might have a new birth on earth, like green turf being born again.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"While drawing a horoscope in the 'book of love', the speaker hears words from the burning heart of a wise man, saying that happy is he who has in his house a friend as beautiful as the moon and expects a night as long as a year.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The sequence of spring and autumn is said to make the leaves of human existence disappear, and sages are cited as saying that grief is a poison and its antidote is wine.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The heart is urged to drink wine in a garden, enjoy the presence of its friend identified as the Divinity, renounce hypocrisy and show, and, if following Ahmed's doctrine, to draw a cup of wine from the fountain into a bowl that Ali, in his round of cupbearing, will serve.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The speaker recounts drunkenly breaking a china cup against a stone, and imagines the cup saying that it has been like the speaker and that the speaker will in turn be like it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The cupbearer is called to bring wine when flowers are in blossom, to leave acts of worship, and to rejoice with ruby wine and the sweet presence of the divine friend before the angel of death sets a watch.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The cupbearer is told to rise from his bed and pour limpid wine before human skulls are made into pitchers, pouring wine from pitcher to bowl.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The speaker complains that pervasive hypocrisy wearies his heart and tells the cupbearer to cheerfully bring wine, even by pawning the prayer-rug and turban, hoping this will give his arguments a solid basis.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The listener is urged to examine what they brought at the beginning and what they will carry away at the end, and is told that death is inevitable whether or not they drink wine.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:20"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The speaker prays to the divine Thou alone to open the door and show a way of safety, refusing to give his hand to any other guides because all are perishable while the divine is eternal.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:21"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The speaker tells a mullah that his words come from hatred, that he constantly accuses the speaker of irreligion, and that the speaker remains convinced of his own stance and questions the mullah's right to lecture him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:22"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The angel of death is described as one who will 'put a watch upon us', limiting the time available for rejoicing with wine and the friend.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Human skulls are imagined being turned into pitchers after death, in contrast to present use of pitchers to serve wine.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Divine 'Thou' / God / Friend [the Divinity]","description":"The transcendent being addressed as 'Thou' and 'friend [the Divinity]', portrayed as creator, judge, source of snares, mysterious essence, giver of pity, and the only eternal guide who can open the door and show a way of safety.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:11","ev:15","ev:17","ev:21"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Speaker / poet","description":"The first-person voice who urges drinking wine, questions God and fate, admonishes his own heart, recounts breaking a cup, argues with religious figures, and reflects on mortality and self-knowledge.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:10","ev:16","ev:19","ev:22"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Cupbearer","description":"A person addressed repeatedly to rise, leave worship, pawn religious items if necessary, and pour or bring wine to the speaker and his XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X; lines 4190-4289","start":"4190","end":"4289","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Scholarly introduction discussing how Mazdean dualism evolved gradually from an Indo-Iranian background into Magian dualism and then toward monotheism, including speculative systems that derive two opposing principles from a single first principle (Space, Infinite Light, Boundless Time, or Fate), and later allegorical interpretations of Ahriman and the Tahmurath myth as inner moral struggle.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Vedic and Avesta religions are presented as different but linked traditions that both derive from a common source.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The author asserts that there was no single religious revolution in the Avesta tradition; instead, belief changed through a long and slow movement.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Indo-Iranian religion is described as having a vague and unconscious dualism that developed into the sharply defined dualism of the Magi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Mazdeism is said to express the ideas of a sacerdotal caste and to have arisen from the long elaboration of successive generations of priests rather than from one man or one day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Mazdeism’s characteristic symmetry is described as still imperfect in the Avesta, illustrated by the absence of the opposition of six arch-fiends to six arch-gods in some Avestan texts and by the stars not yet being members of Ormazd’s army in earlier Yasts.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The text emphasizes a continuing reflective spirit in the tradition that produced new religious systems over time.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After the Magi accounted for the existence of evil by positing two principles, a question arose about how two principles could exist, leading to a longing for unity and the idea that both derived from one principle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Different sects are said to have identified the single first principle as either Space, Infinite Light, Boundless Time, or Fate.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A footnote explains that Space, Infinite Light, Time, and Fate are abstract forms of Ormazd in his naturalistic character as the Heaven God, with heaven being Infinite Space and Infinite Light whose movement gives rise to Time and Fate.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Time is described as twofold: a limited time that measures the 12,000-year duration of the world, called the 'Sovereign Time of the long period,' and a 'Boundless Time' called Zrvan akarana.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Vendidad XIX, 9 is taken to indicate that the Zervanite system, centered on Boundless Time, already existed or was at least nascent when that passage was composed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The author notes that monistic systems based on a single principle leave little direct trace in the Avesta but were already in existence by the time of Aristotle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Eudemos is reported as knowing Chronos and Zervan as the first principles of the Magi, and Berosus presents Boundless Time as a legendary hero.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In a 19th-century controversy, some Parsis are said to deny Ahriman any real existence and to interpret him as a symbolical personification of bad instincts in man.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Rev. Dr. Wilson is described as showing that the symbolic view of Ahriman held by some Parsis is at variance with their sacred books.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"European critics are said to have viewed the Parsi reinterpretation of Ahriman as progress in rationalism akin to that of Voltaire and Gibbon.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The author argues that the rationalizing interpretation of Ahriman is not due to European influence and predates Parsi contact with Europe and Christianity.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Commentators interpret the myth of Tahmurath riding on Ahriman as on a horse for thirty years as symbolizing the curbing of evil passion and restraining 'the Ahriman in the heart of man.'","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The idealistic interpretation of the Tahmurath and Ahriman myth is reported as current at least by the fifteenth century and prevalent among most Dasturs.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The author notes that it is difficult to determine to what extent this reinterpretation was influenced by Islam and suggests there are indications it began while the old religion was still flourishing.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The gradual change from dualism to monotheism is described as a slow process that cannot be ascribed to a single person or time and is deeper and wider than the prehistoric movement from an imperfect to a more perfect dualism.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ormazd (Heaven God)","description":"The supreme deity of Mazdeism, described in a footnote in his naturalistic character as the Heaven God, with Space, Infinite Light, Time, and Fate as abstract forms of him and with an army that later includes the stars.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ahriman","description":"A being whom some Parsis regard as real but others reinterpret as a symbolical personification of bad instincts in man; in the Tahmurath myth he is ridden like a horse and is said to dwell in the human heart as evil passion.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Magi","description":"A priestly group associated with the sharply defined dualism of the tradition and with explaining the existence of evil by positing two principles, later linked to systems of first principles such as Time or Space.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Mazdeism","description":"The religious system that expresses the ideas of a sacerdotal caste, characterized by a largely symmetrical dualism whose exact symmetry is still imperfect in the Avesta.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Boundless Time (Zrvan akarana)","description":"A principle called Boundless Time, presented as a possible single source from which the two principles derive, as an abstract form of Ormazd, and later as a legendary content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l3269-l3402","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"C   2 / XXXVI  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X; lines 3269-3402","start":"3269","end":"3402","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Commentary on Indo-Iranian and Mazdean mythology: a brief mention of movement \"down the seven Karshvare\" led by winds, the son of the waters, and the light dwelling in the waters; then an analysis of the storm-god type in Vedic Indra Vritrahan and his Iranian counterpart Verethraghna (Bahram), worshipped as a protective fire. The atmospheric god Vayu is described as both the physical atmosphere and a bright, fiend-smashing deity in a golden car, invoked by Ahura Mazda against Angra Mainyu, and also known as Rama Hvastra, originally a pastoral god of good pastures associated with Mithra and later reinterpreted as a giver of good flavour to food. As atmosphere, Vayu is the meeting place of god and fiend, leading to a doctrine of a void space, Vai, between Ormazd and Ahriman and eventually to a distinction between good and bad Vai, personified as good and bad Fate bringing life and death. The serpent demon Azi sometimes conquers, seizing the sky and darkening the light, stealing the sovereign light (khvarenah) from Yima Khshaeta, and later appears in legend as the usurper Zohak (Dahaka), a king with two snakes' heads on his shoulders who overthrows and kills Jemshid (Yima) but is himself overthrown by Feridun (Thraetaona). Zohak cannot be killed and is bound on Mount Damavand until the end of the world, when he will be released and then slain by Keresaspa; the fiend is said to be as long-lived as the world and to reappear after each defeat. The name Azi is also reinterpreted as an abstraction meaning 'want', yet he still fights Atar (sacred fire) and, with the demonesses Pairikas, tries to carry off the rain-floods, like the Indian serpent Ahi. The passage notes Mazdeism's many demons, including the Yatus, preserved from Vedic tradition as shape-shifting demon-wizards, a term also applied to human sorcerers (Yatu-man), often associated with the Pairikas (Paris).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A movement is described \"down the seven Karshvare,\" led by the winds, by the son of the waters, and by the light that dwells in the waters.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In the Vedas, Indra Vritrahan is praised as a god that conquers light and as a fiend-smiter.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Verethraghna is presented as the Iranian brother of Indra and eventually becomes the genius of Victory, known as Bahram.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Verethraghna retains the mythical features of a storm god and is worshipped on earth as the Bahram fire, believed to be an emanation from the fire above and a powerful protector of the land against foes and fiends.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In Indo-Iranian mythology, Vayu denotes both the atmosphere and a bright god who fights and conquers within it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In Mazdeism, Vayu is a god-conqueror of light, a smiter of fiends, made entirely of light, who moves in a golden car with sonorous rings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Ahura Mazda invokes Vayu for help against Angra Mainyu.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Another name of Vayu is Rama Hvastra, originally meaning a god of the resting-place with good pastures; the clouds in the atmosphere are compared to a herd of cows, and the Indian Vayu is described as a good shepherd.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Rama Hvastra is connected with Mithra, who is called the lord of the wide pastures.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Due to a later linguistic misunderstanding, Rama Hvastra comes to be regarded as a god who gives a good flavour to foods.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"When considered as the atmosphere, Vayu is the place where god and fiend meet, with one part belonging to the good and another part to the evil.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A later doctrine posits a void space, Vai, between Ormazd and Ahriman where their meeting takes place.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"There is a distinction between two Vai, a good one and a bad one, which develop into the good Fate and the bad Fate, Destiny bringing good and evil, life and death.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Azi is described as a serpent who sometimes conquers, seizing the sky and darkening the light, and carrying off the sovereign light (khvarenah) from Yima Khshaeta.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Over time, Thraetaona, Yima, and Azi Dahaka become historicized; a legend tells how King Jemshid (Yima Khshaeta) was overthrown and killed by the usurper Zohak (Dahaka), a man with two snakes’ heads on his shoulders, and how Zohak was later overthrown by a prince of royal blood, Feridun (Thraetaona).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Zohak, though vanquished, cannot be killed; he is bound to Mount Damavand until the end of the world, when he will be released and then killed by Keresaspa.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The fiend is said to be as long-lived as the world, appearing again as dark and fearful as ever whenever he is vanquished.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The word azi is later identified with a similar word meaning ‘want,’ making the demon into an abstraction, but he remains the same being as the serpent Azi in that he fights against Atar, the fire, and strives to extinguish it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:19

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l6052-l6145","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    I. / IO  VENDIDAD. / FARGARD    II.  I  I / FARGARD    II.  I  3; lines 6052-6145","start":"6052","end":"6145","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Under the rule of Yima, the earth repeatedly becomes so full of men, animals, and red blazing fires that there is no more room. Each time, an unnamed first-person speaker warns Yima of the overpopulation. Yima then steps toward a luminous southern space to meet the sun, invokes Spenta Armaiti, and uses a golden ring and a poniard to make the earth grow larger, first by one-third and later by two-thirds, so it can bear more flocks, herds, and men at his will. Translator’s notes connect Yima’s journeys to the sun with later traditions about a figure called Gemachid who walks daily in the heaven of the sun to gain astral knowledge, with a dream of Cyrus grasping the sun as an omen of kingship, and with the idea that the sun is the source of royal power; they also note later portrayals of Yima as a founder of civilisation.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The earth is repeatedly described as filled with flocks, herds, men, dogs, birds, and red blazing fires so that there is no more room for flocks, herds, and men.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:9","ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A first-person speaker states several times, \"I warned the fair Yima\" that the earth has become full and that there is no more room for flocks, herds, and men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:10","ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Yima steps forward towards a luminous space, southwards, to meet the sun before acting on the earth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Yima presses the earth with a golden ring and bores it with a poniard as part of his action.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Yima speaks to Spenta Armaiti, asking this being to \"kindly open asunder\" and \"stretch\" to bear flocks, herds, and men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Yima makes the earth grow larger by one-third, and later by two-thirds, compared to its previous size.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After Yima enlarges the earth, flocks, herds, and men come as many as he wishes, at his will and wish.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Under the sway of Yima, periods of six hundred and then nine hundred winters pass while the earth is replenished with flocks, herds, men, dogs, birds, and red blazing fires, leading again to lack of space.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The text says that these long periods pass \"under the sway of Yima,\" associating him with rule over the earth during these times.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9","ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Red blazing fires are listed alongside men, dogs, birds, flocks, and herds as part of what fills the earth.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:9","ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Spenta Armaiti is glossed in a note as \"the genius of the earth.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A note reports a tradition recorded by G. du Chinon about a great personage called Gemachid who walks every day in the heaven of the sun and brings back knowledge of the stars after visiting them closely.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The note states that Yima goes three times to the sun to take from it royal power for three times three hundred years, and compares this to a tale where Cyrus in a dream sees the sun at his feet and tries three times to seize it as it rolls away.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In the cited dream story, the Magi interpret Cyrus’s three attempts to seize the sun as presaging a reign of thirty years.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The note explains that in Aryan mythology the sun is the symbol and source of royalty, and that Persian kings are described as \"the brothers of the sun.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Another note says that the happiness Yima made reign on the earth is described elsewhere in the Avesta, and that in the Shah Namah he is depicted as the founder of civilisation, social order, arts and sciences, and the first builder.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The speaker claims to have warned Yima whenever the earth became completely full of living beings and fires.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:10","ev:14"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Yima","description":"Referred to as the fair Yima, son of Vivanghat/Vfvvanghat; under his sway long periods of winters pass while the earth is filled with living beings and fires. I  27 / FARGARD    IX.  I  29 / I30  VENDIDAD. / FARGARD    IX.  I3I; lines 11995-12087","start":"11995","end":"12087","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“Sweetness and fatness will never come back again to that land and to those fields…until that ungodly Ashemaogha has been put to death, and the holy Sraosha has been in that place, offered up a sacrifice…”","summary":"Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda what should be done when a man who does not know the rites of cleansing attempts to cleanse the unclean, and how to fight the Druj who rushes from the dead upon and defiles the living. Ahura Mazda replies that the demon Druj Nasu, along with sickness and death, becomes stronger in such a case. Zarathustra then asks the penalty for the ignorant cleanser, and Ahura Mazda prescribes that the worshippers of Mazda bind him, strip him, flay him alive, cut off his head, and give his corpse to corpse-eating birds and ravens, while declaring that he has repented; his repentance remits his evil deeds. A note further explains that the man is taken to a desert place, nailed, skinned, and beheaded, and that if he has performed Patet he goes to paradise, but if not he remains in hell until the day of resurrection. Zarathustra asks who threatens to take away fullness and increase from the world and to bring sickness and death; Ahura Mazda identifies the ungodly Ashemaogha, who cleanses the unclean without knowing the rites. Before this, sweetness, fatness, health, and growth of corn and grass flowed from the land and fields. Zarathustra asks when these blessings will return, and Ahura Mazda answers that they will never return until Ashemaogha has been put to death and the holy Sraosha has been in that place offering a sacrifice. A note explains that this sacrifice, called zanda ravan, makes the soul living and enables it to enter heaven, probably when combined with the sinner’s
