content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l4533-l4641","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"XXXVI  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X / CHAPTER  V.; lines 4533-4641","start":"4533","end":"4641","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"[The dog] at the head of the Kinvat bridge, which leads from this to the next world, and with his barking drives away the fiend from the souls of the holy ones, lest he should drag them to hell.\"","summary":"The passage explains Zoroastrian ideas about death, impurity, and sacred elements. Dogs (and even birds of prey) are used in the Sag-did ritual to smite the death-demon (Nasu). A four-eyed dog stands at the head of the Kinvat bridge to the next world, where its barking drives away fiends from the souls of the righteous, and ritual dogs repeatedly traverse the corpse’s path while priests recite spells to blow death’s deadly breath to hell. The use of gomez (urine, especially of a bull) for purification is linked to myths of storm-floods, imagined as the urine of a heavenly animal whose waters cleanse the sky and drive fiends away from gods and humans, freeing them from the death-demon. Uncleanness is defined as contagion of death, strongest at the moment life departs; Nasu then defiles those around the corpse, but the corpse no longer defiles after a year as the demon’s power wanes. Because the corpse is the focus of contagion, it must be disposed of without spreading death; unlike earlier Indo-European customs of cremation and burial, the Avesta deems both sacrilegious due to the extreme holiness of the elements fire, earth, and water. These elements were already holy in Indo-Iranian times and are worshipped as divine in the Vedas, where fire carries the dead to heaven and mediates between humans and gods. In Persian belief, fire is an earthly form of eternal divine light that must remain free of death and uncleanness and serves only to repel fiends; Parsis therefore maintain an everlasting Bahram fire. A commentary adds myths of dogs who guard earthly and heavenly regions and of a yellow-eared dog created by Ormazd to protect the first man Gayomart from Ahriman and the fiends, who flee to hell at the dog’s terrifying bark.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Sag-did ritual may be performed by various kinds of dogs—such as a shepherd's dog, a house dog, a Vohunazga dog, or a young dog four months old—and, when no dog is available, by birds of prey, which are said to be as fiend-smiting and Nasu-smiting as dogs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Birds of prey are explicitly described as \"fiend-smiting\" and \"Nasu-smiters\" like dogs.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A dog is said to stand at the head of the Kinvat bridge, which leads from this world to the next, and with his barking he drives away the fiend from the souls of holy people so that the fiend cannot drag them to hell.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Wherever a corpse passes, from the house to its final resting-place, death is described as walking with it, and along that route a spirit of death breathes and threatens the living.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"No man, flock, or being belonging to the world of Ahura is allowed to pass along the corpse’s route until the deadly breath that blows through it has been driven away to hell.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A four-eyed dog is made to go along the corpse’s way three, six, or nine times, while a priest strengthens the dog’s gaze with spells that are dreaded by the fiend (Drug/Druj).","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The use of gomez (urine) in cleansing the unclean is said to be derived from ancient mythic conceptions about storm-floods that cleanse the sky of dark fiends.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"These storm-floods are described as the urine of a gigantic animal, specifically a bull, in the heavens.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Floods from the heavenly bull are said to drive the fiend away from the god and from humans, making a person \"free from the death-demon\" while the death-fiend flees toward hell pursued by a fiend-smiting spell that commands the Druj to perish and never again deliver the living world to Death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Uncleanness is defined as nothing other than the contagion of death and is at its greatest intensity when life is just departing.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"At the moment of death, the Nasu demon defiles ten persons around the corpse, but after a year the corpse no longer causes defilement.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The corpse is said to be less unclean when rotten than when it is still almost warm with life; death defiles least when the body looks most hideous and most when it might still appear majestic, because the death-demon’s power lessens over time.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Because the corpse is the focus of contagion, it must be disposed of in a way that prevents death from spreading; whereas Indo-Europeans either burned or buried the corpse, the Avesta regards both cremation and burial as sacrilegious.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The elements fire, earth, and water are described as holy, and were already considered holy in the Indo-Iranian period; in the Vedas they are worshipped as godlike beings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"In Indian (Vedic) practice, despite the holiness of fire, the dead are burned; fire is said to kindly carry the dead to their heavenly abode on its undecaying, flying pinions, killing demons, and acting as a god who travels from earth to heaven and from man to god, being the deity most friendly to humans.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In Persian belief, fire is seen as an earthly form of the eternal, infinite, godly light, so that no death or uncleanness may enter it; fire is called the purest offspring of the good spirit and the purest part of creation, and its only function is to repel fiends with its bright blazing.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Wherever Parsis are settled, they keep an everlasting Bahram fire, preserved with more than Vestal care.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"A commentary states that there are dogs who watch over the earthly regions and others who watch over fourteen heavenly regions.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs

This worldview contains both latent monotheism and unconscious dualism, which were later diminished in Indian developments but retained and intensified in Mazdeism. The Heaven God is described as the greatest, all-knowing sky deity who created and encompasses everything and sees all through the sun, moon, and stars as his eyes. He is known by names such as Varana (all-embracing sky), Asura (Lord), Asura Mazdha (Lord of high knowledge), and in the Avesta as Ahura Mazda, while Varana/Varuna in India becomes a name for the material heaven and for a mythical region, Varena, where a storm god fights a storm fiend. The god’s former bodily sky-nature persists in depictions of him as bright, immense, clothed in the starry heaven, with heavenly rivers as his spouses and the fire of lightning as his son, dwelling in infinite luminous space that is both his place and body. Herodotus reports that Persians invoking Auramazda as creator of earth and heaven called the vault of the sky Zeus. Alongside the Heaven God, many natural forces—sun, wind, lightning, thunder, rain, prayer, sacrifice—are personified as gods, some of which might rival him in power. XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X; lines 2191-2293","start":"2191","end":"2293","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage is a scholarly discussion of Mazdean (Zoroastrian) doctrine and its historical witnesses in Greek and Persian sources. Drawing on Theopompos, it outlines key Avesta tenets: two opposing principles, the good Ormazd and the evil Ahriman; their antithetical creations and the division of all beings into two classes; the limited duration of the world; the final defeat and destruction of the evil principle; the resurrection of the dead; and everlasting life. A comparative note links the idea that resurrected humans will have no shadow with broader traditions in India and Persia, where gods, a deified figure named Rashidaddm, and the plant of eternal life, Haoma, likewise lack shadows. The author argues that these doctrines were already formed by the Achaemenian period, though the Avesta as such may not have been the state sacred book. Avestean Magism is said to be characterized by belief in two principles and by prohibiting burial of the dead, practices apparently confined to the priestly Magi rather than general Achaemenian Persia. The text examines the absence of Ahriman’s name in royal inscriptions of Darius and Xerxes and in Herodotus’ account, cautioning against arguments from silence. Herodotus is said to describe Persian customs—such as worship of Zeus on mountain summits and calling the whole heavens Zeus—and this is interpreted as an allusion to Ormazd. A further practice, the religious duty to persecute and kill noxious animals as creatures and incarnations of the evil principle, is taken as indirect evidence that belief in Ahriman and dualism existed at least among the Magi.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Mazdean belief is described as teaching two principles, a good one named Ormazd and an evil one named Ahriman.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The two supreme powers are said to have antithetical creations, and all beings in nature are divided into two corresponding classes aligned with each principle.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Mazdean doctrine includes the limited duration of the world and an end to the struggle between Ormazd and Ahriman through the defeat and destruction of the evil principle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The resurrection of the dead and everlasting life are listed as tenets of the Avesta.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A comparative note states that men, when raised from the dead, shall have no shadow; that in India gods have no shadows; that in Persia Rashidaddm was recognised as a god because he produced no shadow; and that the plant of eternal life, Haoma, has no shadow.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Avestean Magism is said to be characterised in belief by the admission of two principles and in practice by the prohibition of burying the dead.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The author notes there is no evidence that Achaemenian Persia accepted the dualistic doctrine and evidence that it did not follow the prohibition on burial, while these belief and practice existed among the Magi as a sacerdotal class.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In rock inscriptions at Persepolis and Naqsh-i Rustam, Darius and Xerxes invoke Auramazda in a manner said to resemble the Avesta but do not mention Ahriman, and the author argues that such silence does not prove ignorance of Ahriman.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Herodotus’ account of Persian religion is described as treating religious customs rather than doctrines and as mentioning no explicit tenets; he appears not to name Ormazd.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Herodotus reports that Persians worship Zeus on the summits of mountains and call the whole circle of the heavens Zeus, and the passage states that this agrees with the character of Ormazd.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A duty is described for the faithful to persecute and kill noxious animals because they are creatures and incarnations of the evil principle; Herodotus’ wording makes this appear a custom peculiar to the Magi, and the author takes it as evidence that belief in Ahriman and dualism existed at least as a Magian article of faith.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ormazd / Auramazda","description":"The good principle and supreme god in Mazdean belief, equated with the whole circle of the heavens and with Zeus in Herodotus’ report.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ahriman","description":"The evil principle opposed to Ormazd in Mazdean dualism and associated with noxious creatures persecuted by the faithful.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Resurrected humans","description":"Men who are raised from the dead in Mazdean eschatology, described as no longer possessing shadows.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Indian gods (Nala XC1; lines 4704-4811","start":"4704","end":"4811","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"the corpse is laid on the summit of a mountain, far from man, from water, from tree, from fire, and from the earth itself\"","summary":"A scholarly introduction to the Vendidad explains how Persian funerary practice shifted from burial to exposing corpses on mountain-top Dakhmas under Magian influence, in order to avoid defiling divinized elements such as earth, fire, and water. The passage describes the Dakhma (Tower of Silence) architecture and its ritual separation from the ground, and notes the doctrinal importance of corpses remaining in the sun, as if life were prolonged by beholding it. It then outlines Vendidad purity rules: only corpses of beings belonging to Ahura's world defile, while those of Ahrimanian creatures do not and may be killed as a pious act. The text extends impurity to \"partial death\"—breath, hair, nail clippings, and bodily changes are treated as demonic property that can pollute especially fire. Menstruation is said to be sent by Ahriman; menstruating women are considered possessed and must be secluded from people and fire, with restricted food passed on a long leaden spoon. The author suggests such notions arise from universal physiological instincts and notes parallels in Leviticus and Pliny, though in Persia they are integrated systematically into the religious Killing such beings, including an Ashemaogha or a Khrafstra, is said to be a pious act equivalent to killing Ahriman himself.","figure_refs":["fig:8","fig:9","fig:10","fig:11","fig:12","fig:13"],"symbol_refs":["sym:2","sym:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"scene:4","label":"Partial death: breath, hair, and nails as demonic property","summary":"The text extends the notion of impurity from actual death to \"partial death\": everything that leaves the human body is treated as dead and claimed by the demon. Parings of nails and cuttings or shavings of hair are unclean and can be turned into weapons by demons unless safeguarded by appropriate rites and spells. Bodily changes are generally viewed as works of the demon that render the person unclean.","figure_refs":["fig:9","fig:10","fig:13"],"symbol_refs":["sym:2","sym:8","sym:9","sym:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"scene:5","label":"Menstrual impurity and seclusion","summary":"A major topic is the impurity of menstruating women, whose menses are said to be sent by Ahriman, especially when abnormally prolonged. Her food intake is restricted so that any additional strength would not aid the fiends, and food is passed to her from a distance using a long leaden spoon. HI; lines 12478-12533","start":"12478","end":"12533","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage gives ritual instructions: the practitioner is told to recite \"fiend-smiting\" and healing words, chanting the Ahuna-Vairya formula eight times and using prayers that speak of the Lord's will as the law of holiness and ask Mazda to appoint a protector, to identify the one who will smite the fiend, and to keep worshippers from their hater. HI / I42  VENDIDAD. / FARGARD    XI.  H;; lines 12583-12678","start":"12583","end":"12678","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"'Away art thou driven, O mischievous Angra Mainyu! from the fire, from the water, from the earth, from the cow, from the tree, from the faithful man and from the faithful woman, from the stars, from the moon, from the sun, from the boundless light, from all good things, made by Mazda, the offspring of the holy principle.'","summary":"The passage contains liturgical instructions in Fargard XI for driving Angra Mainyu and other fiends away from all good creations of Mazda—including fire, water, earth, animals, plants, heavenly bodies, and faithful humans—by chanting specific formulas such as the \"Mazda ad moi\" prayer, the Airyama-ishyo, and multiple Ahuna-Vairyas. These prayers ask Mazda to teach excellent words and works, to make the world thrive forever under his sovereign rule, to provide protection, and to condemn the fiendish Drug, its brood, and the world of the fiend to perish and be banished to the northern regions, so they can no longer give death to the living world of the holy spirit. An attached scholarly commentary introduces Fargard XII, explaining that its (now partly lost) regulations concern near relatives of the dead, who are considered ritually unclean by mere relationship and must stay in a special place (Armešt-gâh) apart from the faithful and all clean objects, expressing a view that death enters all members of a family.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Angra Mainyu is described as \"mischievous\" and is driven away from the fire, water, earth, cow, tree, faithful man, faithful woman, stars, moon, sun, boundless light, and all good things made by Mazda.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Fire, water, earth, cow, tree, faithful man, faithful woman, stars, moon, sun, boundless light, and all good things are said to be made by Mazda and called the offspring of the holy principle.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Mazda is explicitly named as the maker of all good things and is associated with a \"holy principle.\"","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The practitioner is instructed to say \"fiend-smiting and most-healing words\" and to chant \"Mazda ad moi\" four times, asking Mazda to teach excellent words and works so that, through good thought and the holiness of the one who praises him, Mazda may make the world thrive forever under his sovereign rule.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A formula in the ritual states, \"I drive away Aeshma, I drive away the Nasu.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Another formula repeats, \"I drive thee away, O mischievous Angra Mainyu! from the fire, from the water,\" with further elements indicated as in earlier sections.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The practitioner is told to chant the Airyama-ishyo four times, including the invocation, \"May the beloved Airyaman come hither!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The practitioner must chant five Ahuna-Vairyas, including phrases such as \"The will of the Lord is the law of holiness,\" \"Whom hast thou placed to protect me?\" and \"Who is he who will smite the fiend?\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A prayer asks, \"Keep us from our hater, O Mazda and Armaiti Spenta!\" and pronounces repeated curses: \"Perish, O fiendish Drug! Perish, O brood of the fiend! Perish, O world of the fiend!\" and commands the Druj to perish and rush away to the regions of the north, never again to give death to the living world of the holy spirit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The \"living world of the holy spirit\" is mentioned as something the Druj must never again give unto death, in contrast to the \"world of the fiend\" which is commanded to perish.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The commentary states that Fargard XII is found only in the Vendidad Sadah and missing in the Zend-Pahlavi Vendidad due to apparent loss of folios in a key manuscript.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The directions in the preceding chapter are described as general, whereas the directions in Fargard XII are special and apply only to the near relatives of the dead, determining how long their period of \"staying\" (upaman) should last.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The word upaman is said to usually indicate the staying of the unclean in the Armešt-gâh, apart from the faithful and every clean object.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"From the use of upaman, the commentator infers that relatives of a dead person were considered content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l6578-l6763","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"I ZING  AN  E E WANE. / UNTOMBINDE. / UNTOM13IND3. / IZIXG  ANEXWANE.; lines 6578-6763","start":"6578","end":"6763","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A devouring being called Isikguk^umadevu is stabbed by a man and dies, and all the cattle, dogs, men, and Untombinde that it had swallowed come out of its body alive. Untombinde returns to her father Usikulumi, son of Uthlokothloko, and is taken by Unthlatu, son of the king Usibilingwana, to be his wife. She goes to stand in her bridegroom’s kraal to be acknowledged, but the people there say that Unthlatu, the king’s only son, was lost when a boy. The king’s wife weeps over her lost child. The king lets Untombinde remain, saying she can marry one of his other sons, and a separate house is built for her in the kraal. The mother refuses to have her stay with her and insists on the house. The mother then places sour milk, meat, and beer in the house; she says she used to put these there even before Untombinde came. That night Unthlatu, elsewhere described as a boa-man with snake-like, bright slippery skin, comes secretly, eats the meat, drinks the beer, and takes from the sour milk, and then departs. In the morning Untombinde finds that all the food and drink have been consumed and fears she will be blamed for eating what her mother placed. Editorial footnotes explain Unthlatu’s serpent-like nature, the Zulu marriage custom of a girl standing silently at the bridegroom’s kraal, and compare these elements to Polynesian practices and the European tale \"The Serpent\" in the Pentamerone.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man comes forward and stabs the lump-like being called Isikguk^umadevu, and it dies.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After Isikguk^umadevu dies, cattle, dogs, a man, all the men, and Untombinde herself come out of its dead body.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Once released, Untombinde returns to her father, Usikulumi, who is described as the son of Uthlokothloko.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"On her arrival at her father’s place, Untombinde is taken by Unthlatu, son of Usibilingwana, to be his wife.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Untombinde goes to her bridegroom’s kraal and stands at the upper part of the kraal without speaking, in accordance with a described custom.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The people of the kraal ask Untombinde whom she has come to marry; she answers Unthlatu, and they reply that he is not there, explaining that the king once had a son who was lost when still a boy.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The king’s wife, referred to as the mother, weeps and says she bore only one child, who was lost, and that there was no other.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Untombinde remains at the kraal; the king asks why she has stayed, the people advise that she depart, but the king decides she should remain because he has other sons and she will become their wife.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A house is built for Untombinde in the kraal, and she stays there instead of living with the mother, who insists that a separate house be built for her.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When the house is ready, the mother places sour milk, meat, and beer inside it; Untombinde asks why, and the mother replies that she used to place such things there even before Untombinde came.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"At night Unthlatu comes to the house, takes from the sour milk, eats the meat, drinks the beer, stays a long time, and then goes out.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In the morning Untombinde examines the sour milk, meat, and beer and finds that they have been eaten or taken.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Untombinde expresses concern that her mother has put these things in the house to be eaten and that people will say she herself has eaten them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A footnote explains that In/datu means a boa-constrictor and Un/datu means the boa-man, and that Unthlatu had a peculiar snake-like appearance, with bright, slippery skin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The same footnote compares Unthlatu’s form and role to the prince in the tale \"The Serpent\" in the Pentamerone, who spends seven years in the form of a serpent and in that form loves and woos a king’s daughter.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Another footnote describes a Zulu custom: when a young woman is going to be married, she goes to the bridegroom’s kraal and stands silently; if the people approve of her they acknowledge her by killing a goat and entertaining her; if not, they give her a burning piece of firewood to signify that there is no fire for her there and she must kindle a fire elsewhere.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The same footnote notes that among Polynesians it is also customary for the young woman to \"run away\" to the bridegroom as the first step towards marriage, citing Grey.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"A footnote mentions the Maori hero Whakatau misleading Hine-i-te-iwaiwa about his whereabouts, indicating an editorial comparison to an episode of trickery in this Zulu tale.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Untombinde","description":"Young woman who has been swallowed by Isikguk^umadevu, emerges alive when it is killed, returns to her father Usikulumi, is given as wife to Unthlatu, goes to stand at the bridegroom’s kraal, remains there when Unthlatu is said to be lost, receives a separate house, and experiences Unthlatu’s nocturnal visits and the disappearance of food placed in her house.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4","role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Isikguk^umadevu","description":"A lump-like devouring being that has swallowed cattle, dogs, men, and Untombinde; it is stabbed by a man and dies, releasing all those it had devoured.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Unnamed slayer of Isikguk^umadevu","description":"The man who comes forward at the cry \"Forward!\" and stabs Isikguk^umadevu, killing it and enabling the release of its victims.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Usikulumi","description":"Untombinde’s father, described as the son of Uthlokothloko, who receives her when she returns from the monster’s body.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Uthlokothloko","description":"Ancestor figure mentioned as the father of Usikulumi.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Usibilingwana","description":"A king whose son is Unthlatu; his kraal is where Untombinde goes to stand as bride; he is said to have had only one son who was lost as a boy but now has other sons who may marry Untombinde.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Unthlatu (Un/datu, boa-man)","description":"Son of the king Usibilingwana, originally the intended bridegroom of Untombinde. He is said to have been lost when a boy. A footnote describes him as the boa-man, associated with a boa-constrictor and having bright, slippery, snake-like skin. Later he secretly comes at night to Untombinde’s house, eats and drinks the provisions, and departs.","role_refs":["role:7","role:9","role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"The mother at the kraal","description":"The king’s wife and mother of the lost son Unthlatu; she weeps over having borne only one child who was lost, insists that Untombinde have a separate house rather than stay with her, and places sour milk, meat, and beer in Untombinde’s house, apparently anticipating Unthlatu’s nocturnal visits.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"People of the kraal","description":"The group of people at Usibilingwana’s kraal who question Untombinde, explain that the king’s son was lost, advise the king to send her away, and later say she should remain with her mother.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Cattle released from Isikguk^umadevu","description":"Cattle that come out of the dead body of The mother weeps over her lost child. The people suggest sending Untombinde away, but the king decides she should stay, since he has other sons who could marry her. A separate house is built for her at the kraal, and she resides there instead of with the mother. A footnote elaborates on the Zulu custom of a prospective bride standing at the bridegroom’s kraal, and compares it with a similar Polynesian practice.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:6","fig:7","fig:8","fig:9"],"symbol_refs":["sym:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"scene:3

{"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l5782-l5875","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"UZEMBENI. / IZINGANEKWANE. / UZEMBENI. / IZINGAXEKWANE.; lines 5782-5875","start":"5782","end":"5875","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In the conclusion of a Zulu tale, when a tree creaks the dogs tear off Uzembeni’s head and limbs, each dog carrying a piece to a rock by the river. Using large pebbles they grind her flesh to powder, then cast the powdered flesh into the water, and Uzembeni dies. Usikulumi and a beautiful damsel, who had been in the tree, come down, flee to Usikulumi’s people, and are followed by the dogs. On his unexpected return home, Usikulumi’s people, who had thought him dead, greet him with a funeral lamentation, slaughter oxen, rejoice greatly, and ask where he found such a beautiful damsel.

An editorial comparison then cites a Polynesian story of Rata, who fells a very tall straight tree to make a canoe. The insects, birds, and spirits of the forest, called the offspring of Hakuturi, are angered, restore the tree by replacing every chip and shaving while chanting for the pieces to fly together and for the tree to stand upright, and eventually tell Rata he had no right to fell the forest god but promise to build the boat for him.

A further note explains that among the Zulus a person who has been absent and supposed dead is greeted on return with a funeral lamentation, followed by a great feast. The editor observes a similar custom in Polynesia, citing examples in which Rehua laments on Rupe’s approach and Rupe laments in reply, Ngatoro-i-rangi weeps over his niece before food is spread, old people weep loudly when Hatupatu—supposed slain by his brothers—returns, and all the people weep over Maru-tuahu on his arrival.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"When the tree creaks, the dogs tear off Uzembeni’s head and limbs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Each dog carries a limb to a rock by the river, takes large pebbles, and grinds the flesh to powder.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Usikulumi and a damsel are in the tree, then descend from it and run away to Usikulumi’s people.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The dogs cast Uzembeni’s flesh, ground to powder, into the water and then follow Usikulumi.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Uzembeni dies after her body has been dismembered, ground to powder, and cast into the water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Usikulumi returns home to his people, who greet him with a funeral lamentation, kill oxen, and rejoice greatly.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Usikulumi’s people say they thought he was dead or no longer in the land of the living and marvel at the beautiful damsel he brings.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Rata goes into the forest, finds a very tall straight tree, fells it, and cuts off its branching top intending to fashion the trunk into a canoe.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Insects, birds, and spirits of the forest, called the offspring of Hakuturi, are angry at the felling of the tree and by night raise it up again, replacing each chip and shaving while chanting an incantation for the pieces to fly together and the tree to stand upright.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The restoration of the tree happens repeatedly until Rata watches and catches one of the beings, who tell him he had no right to fell the forest god, instruct him to go home, and promise to build the boat for him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A note states that among the Zulus, when someone who has disappeared and is supposed dead unexpectedly returns, it is customary first to salute him with a funeral lamentation and then to make a great feast.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The note adds that a similar custom appears among Polynesians, citing episodes where Rehua laments on Rupe’s approach and Rupe laments in reply, Ngatoro-i-rangi weeps over his niece before food is served, old people weep loudly on Hatupatu’s return (supposed slain by his brothers), and all the people weep over Maru-tuahu on his arrival.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Usikulumi","description":"Male figure in the Zulu tale who escapes with a damsel, returns to his people after being thought dead, and is welcomed with a funeral lamentation and feast.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Uzembeni / Uzwanide","description":"Figure whose head and limbs are torn off by dogs, return.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Dogs","description":"Group of dogs who tear off Uzembeni’s head and limbs, grind the flesh to powder She calls others to witness the prodigy. An editorial note then compares this apparently absurd tale with a Christian account, reported by Mabillon from Pope Gregory I, that St. Benedict sang eucharistic hymns in his mother’s womb, content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l16691-l16784","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    XIX.  21  7 / FARGARD    XX.  210. / FARGARD    XX.  221 / FARGARD    XXI.; lines 16691-16784","start":"16691","end":"16784","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This passage combines a concluding prayer against demons and disease with the opening of Fargard XXI, titled \"Waters and Light.\" It invokes Mazda, Atar, Vohu-mano, Sraosha, and Armaiti for protection against the fiend, Druf, and various demonic beings and curses the \"world of the fiend\" to the northern regions so it can no longer bring death to the living world. The editor outlines Fargard XXI as praise of the holy bull, invocations to rain and to waters with the lights of sun, moon, and stars, and spells against disease. The text then praises a holy, beneficent bull that brings increase and gifts to the faithful but is killed by hostile beings. A footnote identifies this bull as the primeval bull created by Ormazd and killed by Ahriman, and notes older myths comparing a cloud to a bull that brings rain. Finally, Zarathustra is instructed to call the clouds to pour down rain in myriad drops to destroy sickness, death, and named beings associated with disease, and a brief spell contrasts \"death\" with the coming of \"healing\" at different times of day.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage refers to \"all manner of diseases and deaths, all the Yatus and Pairikas, and all the wicked ^ainis\" as a group of harmful entities.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Yatha ahu vairyo formula states that the will of the Lord is the law of holiness and that the riches of Vohu-mano will be given to one who works in this world for Mazda and uses the power given by Ahura to relieve the poor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A speaker asks Mazda whom he has placed to protect him while the hate of the fiend is grasping him, and answers that Atar and When Unthlatu asks what she will say to his father, she replies that she will tell him to have the whole country brew beer, a phrase glossed as assembling the whole nation. The father asks what the beer is for, and the mother answers that she will see the people, as she used to be queen. I  63; lines 13577-13672","start":"13577","end":"13672","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage first continues a condemnation of an unnamed man, describing him as a shameless eater and unfaithful keeper, repeatedly comparing him to a thief, a wild beast, a courtesan, and a child. Zarathustra then asks the Maker of the material world where a dog’s ghost goes when the dog dies with its marrow and seed dried up. Ahura Mazda replies that the ghost passes to the spring of the waters (identified in a note as the spring of Ardvi Sura, goddess of waters) and that from every thousand dogs and she‑dogs two water dogs are formed, a male and a female. A note explains that a single water dog contains as much life and holiness as a thousand ordinary dogs. The text warns that killing a water dog brings drought that dries up pastures, removing sweetness, fatness, health, and growth from the land; Zarathustra asks when these blessings will return, and Ahura Mazda answers that they will never return until the murderer of the water dog has been put to death and the holy soul of the dog has been offered up as a sacrifice for three days. How shall I drive away direct defilement? How indirect defilement? How shall I drive the Nasu from the house of the worshippers of Mazda? How shall I cleanse the faithful man? How shall I cleanse the faithful woman?’”","summary":"On a mountain by the Dareja, Zarathustra prays to Ahura Mazda and various divine beings, asking to be taught the truth and how to free the world from the Druj, Angra Mainyu, defilement, and the corpse-demon Nasu, and how to cleanse faithful worshippers. Ahura Mazda replies that Zarathustra should invoke the good law of Mazda, the Amesha Spentas who rule the seven regions of the earth, sovereign Heaven, boundless Time, Vayu, the powerful Wind made by Mazda, and Spenta Armaiti, the fair daughter of Ahura Mazda. Ahura Mazda further tells him to invoke his own Fravashi, the holy Word as his soul, and his creation. Her mother tries to catch her, but the pigeons only distress her and go off with Usitungusobenthle, while the mother follows weeping. Toward evening they reach a tree, perch with Usitungusobenthle in the top, and the mother sleeps at the foot of the tree. During the night the pigeons take Usitungusobenthle again and go away with her to their own country. In the morning the mother can no longer see them on the tree and returns home. In the pigeons’ country they declare that Usitungusobenthle shall be queen, and she becomes queen. She has a husband who is also an Ijubatente (pigeon), and gives birth to three children. I  8 / FARGARD    XVII.  1 85; lines 14707-14806","start":"14707","end":"14806","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage concludes a legal section on ritual impurity by specifying penalties for contact with an \"unclean thigh\" and equating sexual intercourse with a menstruant woman to burning the corpse of one’s own son and dropping its fat into the fire; such sinners are called embodiments of the Druj and are said to deserve death. A prose introduction to Fargard XVII explains that anything cut from the human body, especially hair and nails, is considered dead matter belonging to Ahriman and inhabited by a demon, and must be ritually protected by spells and by burial in the earth within consecrated circles. The commentator notes that this reflects a world-wide superstition about hair and nails as weapons of the evil one, citing Esthonian, South American (Gaucho), and Liègean practices, and a Norse myth of a ship built from the nails of the dead. The canonical verses then present Zarathushtra asking Ahura Mazda which deed most strengthens the Daevas as if sacrificing to them, and Ahura Mazda replies that it is dropping hair or nail clippings into a hole or crack without performing the proper ceremonies.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man who sits on an unclean thigh without sexual intercourse is said to owe a penalty of ninety stripes with the Aspahe-astra and ninety stripes with the Sraosho-charana, as prescribed by Ahura Mazda.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Sexual intercourse with a woman who has an issue of blood, whether at the usual time or not, is stated to be no better deed content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l5993-l6079","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGAXEKWANE. / UZEMBENI. / TORTION  OF  THE  TALE. / IZINGANEKWANE.; lines 5993-6079","start":"5993","end":"6079","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"And truly Uzembeni afterwards came to life, although the dogs had ground her to powder, and thrown her into the water. She again joined piece to piece, and came to life again.","summary":"In this portion of the Uzembeni tale, a man climbs into a tree while dogs are expected to fight Uzembeni and kill her. Uzembeni comes and cuts at the tree; when it is about to fall, the dogs tear her to pieces. They kill her again more completely, scattering her fragments, and her skin speaks, telling the man to descend because she is dead but will come to life again. Uzembeni indeed revives after being ground to powder and thrown into the water, reassembling herself and coming to life once more. She searches for those who were on the tree but cannot find them, and then returns home. A footnote compares this repeated death and revival motif with the Hottentot figure Heitsi Kabib, who \"died several times, and came to life again.\" Another footnote outlines the Italian tale of Petrosinella, a maiden confined in a tower by an ogress, who escapes with a prince using stolen gallnuts that produce a bulldog, a lion (from which the ogress hides in a jackass skin), and finally a wolf that devours the ogress. A concluding remark notes that stories where ogres have beautiful daughters courted and won by princes are common in the folklore of many nations, citing further European examples.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The dogs are expected to fight with Uzembeni and kill Six pigeons are present; one says the word \"Vukutu,\" and another repeatedly asks why he says \"Vukutu,\" this exchange taking place in the woman’s presence. Ahura Mazda tells him to go to a beautiful, high-growing tree, hail it as a good and holy tree made by Mazda while reciting Ashem vohu, and to have the faithful man cut a baresma twig of specific size, hold it in his left hand, and keep his eyes fixed on it while offering sacrifice to Ahura Mazda, the Amesha-Spentas, the golden Haomas, Vohu-mano, and good Rata. Zarathushtra then describes how Vohu-mano becomes defiled, directly and indirectly, by daevas through contact with bodies they have smitten, and asks that Vohu-mano be cleansed. Ahura Mazda prescribes a purification ritual using gomez (bull’s urine) from a legally qualified ungelded bull, performed in a field made by Ahura where furrows are drawn. The purifier must recite one hundred Ashem vohu and two hundred Ahuna Vairya formulas praising holiness and Mazda’s will, and then wash Vohu-man four times with gomez from the ox and twice with water made by Mazda. Darmesteter’s notes explain that Vohu-mano can denote the faithful person or his clothes, the bull must be entirely white, the cleansing field is the Barashnum-gah, and Parsi practice emphasizes keeping one’s gaze on the baresma during sacrifice.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Zarathushtra asks Ahura Mazda what kind of sacrifice he should perform to worship and promote the creation of Ahura Mazda.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Ahura Mazda instructs Zarathushtra to go to a specific tree described as beautiful, high-growing, and mighty among the high-growing trees, and to address it with a greeting that hails it as a good, holy tree made by Mazda while reciting the Ashem vohu formula.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The tree that Zarathushtra is to approach is explicitly characterized as beautiful, high-growing, and mighty among high-growing trees, and as made by Mazda.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The faithful man is instructed to cut off a twig of baresma, specified as being as faithful worshipper must not stop keeping his eyes fixed on the baresma twig he holds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The sacrifice offered while holding excellent.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Zarathushtra addresses Ahura Mazda as all-knowing and states that Ahura Mazda is never asleep and never I  8 / FARGARD    XVII.  1 85 / FARGARD    XVII.  I  87; lines 14809-14902","start":"14809","end":"14902","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage links neglect of lawful rites with the generation of Daevas and vermin (lice) that destroy crops and clothes. Zarathustra is instructed to treat cut hair and nails as dangerous substances: they must be removed specific distances from the faithful, fire, water, and consecrated baresma, buried in holes of prescribed depth, enclosed by furrows cut with a metal knife, and accompanied by fiend-smiting formulas including the Ahuna-Vairya. A special invocation dedicates buried nails to the Asho-zusta bird so that they become weapons against the Mazainya Daevas; if they are not ritually dedicated, the nails instead become weapons in the hands of these Daevas. Translator’s notes explain a doctrine that the human body is a microcosm formed from elemental counterparts in nature (bones from earth, blood from water, hair from trees, life from fire), which return to their sources after death and will be restored at the resurrection. This doctrine is described as an old Aryan theory with parallels in Indian, Greek, and Scandinavian traditions, and notes also clarify later beliefs about the holy bird eating ritually charged nails north.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Neglect of lawful rites is said to cause Daevas to be produced in the Airyaman is asked to smite diseases, deaths, and various evil beings (Yatus, Pairikas, wicked 6ainis). A formula affirms that the will of the Lord is the law of holiness, promising the riches of Vohu-mano to one who works in this world for Mazda and uses divinely given power to relieve the poor. The bird leaves the open space, perches on the fence, and eventually flies away. When their father returns at night expecting his titbit \u0013 the bird and a pot of amasi (sour milk) \u0013 he finds the bird gone and the milk mostly finished. He questions his children; they first claim ignorance, then one child reveals that they let the bird go and ate the amasi. The father beats them and laments the loss, fearing he may die of famine, and the tale ends. An editorial footnote then notes that in this Zulu tale the power of rendering labour vain is ascribed to a bird, and compares it to a Central American legend (cited from Tylor) in which two princes He brought with him the nine twigs; he drew along nine furrows. ‘I drive away ... the disease, rottenness, and infection which Angra Mainyu has created ... all manner of diseases and deaths, all the Yatus and Pairikas, and all the wicked Gamis.’”","summary":"Ahura Mazda, described as the Holy One and Maker of all good things, recalls creating a beautiful, shining \"mansion.\" After this, the ruffian Angra Mainyu looks at him and, by witchcraft, creates an enormous multitude of diseases. An incantation follows in which the speaker repeatedly declares \"I drive away\" various named afflictions and demonic beings, including sickness, death, pain, fever, many specific disease-spirits, When they question him, he tells them to look at the mat and stick; they see them bloody and assume the meat has been taken down, while he insists on using the feeding-mat as a witness. Before he departs, the father instructs him to take the road that runs around a mountain and not the one that climbs it. At the fork where the two roads separate, Ubabuze disregards the advice and takes the forbidden road up the mountain. XXXI X; lines 2400-2506","start":"2400","end":"2506","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage discusses the hereditary nature and Media-based origins of the Zoroastrian priesthood, tracing Maubeds to King Minochihr and restricting the Dastur office to priestly families. Another tradition centers on Shiz, capital of Atropatene, with its famous fire temple of Azerekhsh visited by pilgrim kings and ascribed to Zeratusht. This tradition recounts that Zoroaster went from Shiz to the mountain Sebilan, spent time in retirement, returned with the Zend-Avesta in old Persian (requiring commentary), and then declared himself a prophet. The passage also mentions Athravans who wander from afar to bring holiness to countries, and briefly notes a Greek account in Diogenes Laertius of a long succession of Magi after Zoroaster as a dim recollection of a Magian dynasty.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The priesthood is described as hereditary: Maubeds are said to I  I; lines 5950-6049","start":"5950","end":"6049","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The editorial introduction explains that this section of Fargard II combines myths about Yima as the first dead and king of the dead in a blissful realm with eschatological myths about the end of the world. An earlier scheme portrays the world’s long span of twelve millennia ending in a dire winter (likened to the Fimbul winter), followed by an everlasting spring when humans, returned from heaven to earth, enjoy eternal earthly happiness like that experienced after death in Yima’s realm. Later Mazdean cosmology instead makes the world end by fire, so the catastrophic winter is no longer final and Yima’s Var, once a paradise that sends its inhabitants back to earth, is reinterpreted as a kind of ark. The text then narrates a dialogue in which Zarathustra asks Ahura Mazda who was the first mortal to receive the divine law; Ahura names Yima, the fair and great shepherd, as the first recipient. Ahura first calls Yima to be preacher and bearer of the law, but Yima declines, so Ahura assigns him to make the world thrive, nourishing, ruling, and guarding it. Yima accepts and promises a reign without extreme cold or heat, disease, or death. Ahura Mazda gives him a golden ring and a gold-inlaid poniard as royal regalia, and under Yima’s sway three hundred winters pass while the earth is filled with flocks, herds, and men. Footnotes compare Yima with Vedic Yama as first man and priest, note Zarathustra’s later status as titular law-giver, and identify the ring and poniard as symbols of sovereignty.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The introduction states that the second part of the section combines myths of Yima as the first dead and king of the dead, ruling in a region of bliss, with old myths about the end of the world.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The world is said to last a long year of twelve millennia and was originally to end by a dire winter, likened to the Fimbul winter.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After this dire winter there would be an everlasting spring, when men, sent back to earth from the heavens, would enjoy an eternal earthly life with the same happiness they had experienced after death in Yima’s realm.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In the definitive form of Mazdean cosmology, the world is made to end by fire, so destruction by winter is no longer the final event.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Because the world’s end is by fire, the Var of Yima, originally a paradise that returns its inhabitants to earth, is described as becoming merely “a sort of Noah’s ark.”","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Zarathustra addresses Ahura Mazda as the most beneficent Spirit, Maker of the material world, and Holy One, and asks who was the first mortal before him with whom Ahura conversed and whom he taught the law of Ahura, the law of Zarathustra.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that the fair Yima, the great shepherd, was the first mortal before Zarathustra with whom he conversed and to whom he taught the law of Ahura, the law of Zarathustra.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ahura Mazda says he told Yima, son of Vivanghat, to be the preacher and bearer of his law.","category":"speech","evidence

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l8862-l8908","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VIII. / FARGARD    V.  63 / FARGARD    V.  65 / F    2; lines 8862-8908","start":"8862","end":"8908","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A human interlocutor repeatedly addresses Ahura Mazda as 'Maker of the material world, Holy One' and asks what penalty a man should pay for throwing bones from a dead dog or dead man onto the ground so that grease or marrow flows. In the most serious case, involving a bone as large as two fingers or two ribs, the offender is called a 'Pesho-tanu' and receives two hundred stripes with each scourge.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A man is described as throwing on the ground a bone from a dead dog or from a dead man.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The bone is compared to different sizes: the top joint of the forefinger, the top joint of the middle finger, a content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l4423-l4531","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"XXXVI  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X / CHAPTER  V.; lines 4423-4531","start":"4423","end":"4531","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This introductory passage contrasts the structure of the Vendidad with the Biblical Books of Moses, noting that in the Vendidad the law is revealed as a response to man's questions to Ahura. It then explains Mazdean concepts of impurity as possession by a demon and describes how death, through the demon Drug Nasu (Corpse-Druj), contaminates the corpse and anyone who touches it. The demon is driven from the dead by the Sag-did, the \"look of the dog\" (a four-eyed or white yellow-eared dog), and from the living by washings with ox's urine and water plus the Sag-did, accompanied by spells that banish the fiend to the northern regions. Death from a single corpse is portrayed as a power threatening the whole living world, with a danger of further deaths in the same house for three days. A footnote identifies the corpse-spirit with a fly sent in the name of Ahriman. The author notes that similar feelings and rites concerning death exist among other Indo-European peoples, citing Greek water-sprinkling to drive away death and a Vedic verse that addresses Death while burning the corpse. He argues that rites expelling the Drug are performances of myths, imitations of divine acts. Finally, he discusses the Parsi reinterpretation of the \"four-eyed dog\" as a spotted dog, infers underlying myths of dogs that drive away the death-fiend, and compares the Parsi dog with Kerberos and Yama's two brown four-eyed dogs guarding the realm of death, mentioning a Parsi tradition of the yellow-eared dog watching at a threshold (cut off in the excerpt).","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The outward form of the Vendidad has been compared with that of the Books of Moses, but the author notes that in the Bible there is no conversation between God and the lawgiver: the law comes down unasked, and God gives commands but no answers.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In the Vendidad, the first cause of revelation is said to be the wish of man rather than the will of God; man must ask Ahura, who knows everything and is pleased to answer, and the law is described as \"the question to Ahura\" (ahuri frasno).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Impurity or uncleanness is described as the state of a person or thing possessed by a demon, and the object of purification is to expel the demon.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Death is stated to be the principal means by which uncleanness enters man and is described as the triumph of the demon.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When a man dies and the soul has parted from the body, the \"Drug\" Nasu or Corpse-Druj falls upon the dead from the regions of hell, and whoever thereafter touches the corpse becomes unclean and makes unclean whomever he touches.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Druj is expelled from the dead by the Sag-did, \"the look of the dog\": a \"four-eyed dog\" or \"white one with yellow ears\" is brought near the body and made to look at the dead, after which the Druj flees back to hell.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Druj is expelled from the living, whom she has seized through their contact with the dead, by washings with ox's urine and water combined with the Sag-did.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Spells accompanying the purification ceremonies address the Druj and the \"world of the fiend,\" commanding them to perish and rush away to the regions of the north and never again give unto death the living world of the holy spirit.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The death of a man is said to involve more than the death of one individual: the power of death from hell threatens from the corpse, as from a stronghold, the whole world of the living, defiling and seizing whatever comes within reach and \"from the dead defiles the living, from the living rushes upon the living.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When a man dies in a house, there is described as being a danger for three days that somebody else may die in that house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A footnote states that the Druj appears in the shape of a fly, and that the fly that comes to the smell of the dead body was thought to be the corpse-spirit taking possession of the dead in the name of Ahriman.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The author asserts that the feeling out of which these ceremonies grew was not unknown to other Indo-European peoples, and that Mazdeism carried it to an extreme and preserved a clearer sense of it while elsewhere it faded.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"As an Indo-European parallel, the author states that when a Greek goes out of a house where a dead man lies, he sprinkles himself with water from the aphaviov at the door, thereby driving death away from himself.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Another parallel describes the Vedic Indian, who, while burning the corpse in rites intended chiefly for the benefit of the dead, considers himself in danger and cries aloud, \"Away, go away, O Death! injure not our sons and our men!\" (Rig-veda X, 18, 1).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The author claims that the rites by which the Drug is expelled are performances of myths, stating that nothing in worship exists that did not exist before in mythology.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"He explains that what is called a practice is an imitation of gods, as man believes gods.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The Parsis, being unable to find four-eyed dogs, interpret the term as meaning a dog with two spots above the eyes; the services of a two-spotted dog are accepted only for want of a four-eyed dog or a white one with yellow ears.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"From this, the author infers that there were myths in which the death-fiend was driven away by dogs of that description.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The four-eyed dog of the Parsis XXV / INTRODUCTION,    II.  XXV11 / INTRODUCTION,    II.  XXIX; lines 1491-1536","start":"1491","end":"1536","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage is a methodological reflection on the study of the Avesta and Indo-Iranian mythology. It explains that religious ideas in texts are often organized by logical rather than historical sequence, so comparison is needed to recover their historical development. The \"comparative school\" of scholars is said to have developed Indo-Iranian mythology; Roth, following Burnouf, argued that Iranian epic history comes from the same source as Vedic Indian myths and highlighted the primitive identity of Ahura Mazda, Iran’s supreme god, with the Vedic supreme god Varuwa. Windischmann’s work on Mithra and Anahita is praised, while Haug’s approach is criticized for turning Mazdeism into a revolutionary movement against Vedic polytheism, reading a schism and curses against Zoroaster into the Vedas, and treating both Avesta and Veda as historical pamphlets. The passage then describes an ongoing scholarly struggle in which two parties, once divided over the Avesta’s authenticity, are now both seen as partly right and wrong, each having rendered important services. The author urges that these groups become allies, combining their methods. A footnote acknowledges Haug’s later, valuable contributions as a Pahlavi scholar, especially his work in using inscriptions to clarify manuscript Pahlavi.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that in religious texts logical order often replaces chronological order, so that the past is read into the present and historical sequence is obscured.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The author claims that only comparison can restore proper historical order and trace the birth, growth, changes, and former relations of ideas.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The \"comparative school\" is said to XX1U / XXIV  VENDIDAD.; lines 1266-1307","start":"1266","end":"1307","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A scholar (Burnouf) sought the origin of Indian languages outside India and turned to the Persian languages, beginning with Zend. Using Anquetil’s existing translation as a guide, he found it inadequate, partly because Anquetil’s Parsi dastur teachers transmitted flawed Zend and Pahlavi traditions, and partly because Anquetil lacked Sanskrit and the tools of comparative grammar. Burnouf instead relied on an older Sanskrit translation of the Yasna by the Parsi Neriosengh, based on the old Pahlavi version, and tested this material through comparison of parallel passages and the newly founded comparative grammar of Bopp. In this way he outlined the Zend lexicon, fixed its grammatical forms, and established what is called the only correct method of interpreting the Avesta. He also initiated comparative mythology between the Avesta and the Veda by asserting the identity of Vedic Yama with Avesta Yima and of Traitana with Thraetaona and Feridun. His commentary on the Yasna is praised as a model of critical insight and balanced judgment, avoiding both narrow factualism and uncontrolled comparison, and mediating carefully between tradition and Later, in Airyana Vaejo by the good river Daitya, Ahura Mazda convenes the celestial gods and Yima convenes mortals, and they assemble together. Ahura Mazda, described as the Maker, warns Yima that fatal winters will fall on the material world, bringing fierce frost and deep snow even on the highest mountains, causing three kinds of beasts to perish. Fields that once bore abundant grass for cattle will then be overwhelmed by melting snows and streaming floods, so that places where sheep’s footprints remain will seem happy lands. Therefore Ahura Mazda tells Yima to make a Vara, literally an enclosure, later known as Var-Gam-kard. A commentary explains that later tradition introduces a demon called Malakosan, associated with a destructive rain or winter that nearly annihilates mankind and other creatures, from which men, The offender must be kept at fixed distances from fire, water, consecrated bundles of baresma, and the faithful, confined in a special enclosure and sustained with coarse food and worn-out clothes until advanced age. At that point a trained executioner flays and decapitates him on a mountain top, and his corpse is given to corpse-eating creatures, especially ravens, while a formula proclaims his repentance and the remission of his evil deeds. Translator notes explain technical age terms and suggest earlier legal practice and additional afterlife punishment in hell. The latter part of the passage enumerates those who most rejoice the Earth: one who fills the burrows of creatures belonging to Angra Mainyu, and one who cultivates corn, grass, and fruit, correcting overly dry or wet ground. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l8097-l8194","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD   V.  49 / VENDIDAD. / FARGARD    V.  5  I / FARGARD    V.  53; lines 8097-8194","start":"8097","end":"8194","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A legal prescription declares that a certain trespass incurs the same penalty as murdering one of the faithful and that a corpse is to lie where it is until rain has fallen on the corpse, the Dakhma, and the unclean remains, and until birds have eaten the corpse. Zarathustra then addresses Ahura Mazda, asking whether he sends the waters from the cosmic sea Vouru-kasha down with the wind and clouds, even to corpses, Dakhmas, unclean remains, and bones, and whether those waters then flow back unseen to the sea Puitika. Ahura Mazda confirms this, saying that he sends the waters down to those unclean places, then makes them flow back unseen to the purifying sea Puitika. There the waters stand boiling in the heart of the sea, are cleansed, and then run back from Puitika to Vouru-kasha toward a well-watered tree that bears the seeds of all his plants. From these seeds he rains down plants upon the earth to provide food for the faithful and fodder for the beneficent cow. Commentarial notes explain that in later mythology Vouru-kasha and Puitika were identified with earthly seas and the tides, and further describe the tree of all seeds growing in the middle of the sea, a godlike bird Sinamru whose movements cause branches to grow or break and scatter seeds, and the rain-god Tistar who rains those seeds down on earth.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A trespass is said to incur the same penalty as the murder of one of the faithful.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A corpse is to lie where it is until the corpse, the Dakhma, and the unclean remains have been rained on, and until birds have eaten up the corpse.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Zarathustra addresses Ahura Mazda as maker of the material world and asks if he sends the waters from the sea Vouru-kasha down with the wind and clouds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Zarathustra asks whether Ahura Mazda makes the waters flow down to corpses, Dakhmas, unclean remains, and bones, and then makes them flow back unseen to the sea Puitika.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ahura Mazda answers that it is as Zarathustra has said: he sends the waters from the sea Vouru-kasha with the wind and clouds, makes them stream down to corpses, Dakhmas, unclean remains, and bones, and then makes them flow back unseen to the sea Puitika.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The waters stand boiling in the heart of the sea Puitika, are cleansed there, and then run back from the sea Puitika to the sea Vouru-kasha.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"From the sea Puitika the cleansed waters return to the sea Vouru-kasha toward a well-watered tree on which grow the seeds of all Ahura Mazda’s plants of every kind.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ahura Mazda says he rains those plants down upon the earth to bring food to the faithful and his people, and fodder to the beneficent cow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A note states that in later mythology the sea Vouru-kasha and the sea Puitika were assimilated to the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman, and the movement of waters from heaven to earth and back was interpreted as the A speaker asks Ahura Mazda how long she must remain confined and separated from other Mazda‑worshippers regarding her seat, food, and clothing, and Ahura Mazda decrees a further nine nights of separation followed by another washing with gomez and water. The speaker then asks whether her clothes, once washed and cleansed, may be used by various named priests or by any priest, warrior, or husbandman. Ahura Mazda replies that they may never be used by these pure faithful, but may serve as coverings and sheets for a woman in her sickness or a man unfit for work who must sit in the place of infirmity, until they are clean. Translator’s notes explain the sacrificial functions of the listed priests, define the status of an infirm person and the place of infirmity, mention rules about clothing defiled by the dead and Menstruous women are also purified by Ghosel. Objects are defiled to varying degrees based on their material and penetrability, with wet matter transmitting impurity more than dry, and corpses ceasing to defile after a year. The text then outlines Zoroastrian civil and penal law preserved in the fourth Fargard: contracts classified by mode (word- or hand-contracts) and by object (sheep, ox, man, field) with specified monetary values; contracts cannot be voided by one party alone, and the breaker pays the value of the next higher contract. Family and next of kin are said to be responsible for fulfilling contracts, identified as a principle of old Indo-European civil law. Assaults are divided into seven degrees, from minor menaces up to manslaughter, and repeated lesser assaults without atonement escalate to the next degree, so seven minor offenses equal manslaughter. Finally, every crime incurs two penalties, one in this world and one in the next. Earthly punishment consists of a set number of stripes with an instrument called Aspahe-astra or Sraosho-čarana; 200 stripes form the unit of heavy penalties, and those so punished are called
