content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l5131-l5179","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTION,    V.  XCV / INTRODUCTION,    V.  XCV11 / XCV111  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    V.  XC1X; lines 5131-5179","start":"5131","end":"5179","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The commentator questions whether the extremely high numbers of stripes prescribed in the Vendidad (e.g., for killing certain dogs) were ever literally inflicted. He notes that in later practice bodily punishments were converted into monetary fines, a process already hinted at in Pahlavi materials. Later Ravaets equate a fixed number of stripes (a Tanafuhr) with specific sums in various currencies, suggesting that fines may have enriched the fire-temples and influenced priests’ use of the Sraosho-karana. Pahlavi sources distinguish three types of atonement: by money (khvastak), by the Sraosho-karana (corporal punishment), and by cleansing, the last consisting of repentance expressed through confession and recitation of a formula. Footnotes compare maximum numbers of stripes in other legal traditions and explain that in later Parsiism each sin and good deed has a set monetary value that can be weighed on the scales of Rashnu so as to decide the soul’s fate. The same principle of compensation is said to have been observed by Herodotus in Persian law.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Vendidad prescribes very high numbers of stripes for certain offenses, such as the murder of a shepherd’s dog (eight hundred stripes) and of a water dog (ten thousand stripes), and the commentator doubts these were literally carried out.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In later or modern tradition, bodily punishment is converted into monetary fines, and this conversion is alluded to in the Pahlavi translation.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Ravaets state that two hundred stripes (a Tanafuhr) equal three hundred istirs, twelve hundred dirhems, or thirteen hundred and fifty rupees, making each stripe worth about six rupees.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"It is unclear whether a guilty person could choose to commute stripes into payment independently or only with the judge’s assent.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The commentator suggests that fire-temples likely gained much of their wealth from such fines, and that the sound of dirhems could cause the Sraosho-karana to fall from the Mobeds’ hands, implying a preference for monetary atonement over corporal punishment.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The system of financial penalties did not eliminate bodily penalties; Parsis are said to apply both forms.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A Pahlavi commentary explicitly distinguishes three types of atonement: atonement by money (khvastak), by the Sraosho-karana, and by cleansing.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The third type of atonement, by cleansing, is described as strictly religious and consists of repentance shown by confessing guilt and reciting a formula of repentance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A footnote compares the maximum numbers of stripes in different legal contexts: in Chardin’s time no more than three hundred, in old German law two hundred, and in Hebrew law forty.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In later Parsiism every sin and every good deed is assigned a fixed monetary value and can be weighed in the scales of Rashnu.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"According to the same note, if the number of sin dirhems outweighs the good deed dirhems, the soul is considered saved.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Herodotus is cited as having noticed the same principle of compensation in Persian law of his time.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Guilty person / offender","description":"A person subject to corporal or financial penalties whose punishment might be commuted from stripes to monetary payment and who may seek atonement.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Judge","description":"Judicial authority whose assent may be required for a guilty person to commute corporal punishment into a fine.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Mobeds","description":"Zoroastrian priests who wield the Sraosho-karana and are associated with fire-temples that may receive wealth from fines.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Parsis","description":"The Parsi community, described as applying both financial and bodily penalties in their practice of atonement.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Rashnu","description":"A figure whose scales weigh the monetary equivalents of sins and good deeds to determine the fate of the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l9714-l9759","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FARGARD    VII.  79 / FARGARD    VII.  8  I / FARGARD   VII.  83 / FARGARD    VII.  85; lines 9714-9759","start":"9714","end":"9759","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage sets out a tariff of fees for healers in terms of animals, vehicles, and food, graded by the social status of the patient (master of a house, lords of a borough, town, and province), their wives, and the son of a borough lord, as well as for healing valuable and less valuable livestock. A blessing associated with the healer’s work is said in commentary to make a person holy and lead to paradise, with no monetary equivalent. Another rule describes several healers offering themselves together before Spitama Zarathustra: one heals with the knife, one with herbs, and one with the holy word, which the commentary glosses as spells and compares with healing practices in Homer’s Odyssey and in the Greek tradition of Asclepios as described by Pindar.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The healer is instructed to heal the master of a house, the lord of a borough, the lord of a town, and the lord of a province, each in return for a different payment: an ox of low value, an ox of average value, an ox of high value, and a chariot and four.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The healer shall heal the wife of the master of a house for the value of a she-ass, the wife of the lord of a borough for the value of a cow, the wife of the lord of a town for the value of a mare, and the wife of the lord of a province for the value of a she-camel.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The healer shall heal the son of the lord of a borough for the value of an ox of high value.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The healer is also expected to heal animals—oxen of high, average, and low value, and sheep—in exchange for lesser payments: healing an ox of high value for an ox of average value, an ox of average value for an ox of low value, an ox of low value for a sheep, and a sheep for a meal of meat.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A blessing is associated with the healer’s work, and commentary explains that through it a person becomes holy and goes to paradise, with no equivalent in money.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Commentary reports that some say the blessing is given when the priest has not three thousand stirs.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A borough is explained in commentary as a group of several houses, with some translators glossing it as a street.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Commentary states that the value of a chariot and four is seventy stirs.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The schedule of healer fees is compared in commentary to a tariff of fees for a cleanser in another fargard of the Vendidad.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The passage describes several healers offering themselves together before Spitama Zarathustra: one who heals with the knife, one who heals with herbs, and one who heals with the holy word.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Commentary glosses healing with the holy word as healing by spells.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Translator’s commentary connects the classification of healers here with Asclepios, who is said to relieve Angra Mainyu’s counter-creations are described as vices and plagues, often unrelated to the lands they oppose. The mention of the Seven Rivers, associated with the Indus basin, is used to date the first Fargard to the reign of Darius I. In the cited verses Ahura Mazda speaks to Spitama Zarathustra, saying he has made every land dear to its dwellers so that, even if their lands lack charms, the whole living world would not abandon them and invade Airyana Vaejo. Commentary adds that everyone thinks their birthplace is the best land, that Airyana Vaejo is the first of the good lands with uncertain location, and that an alternative account of creation has Ahura Mazda creating delightful lands followed by an unnamed being described as ‘he who is all death’ bringing counter-creations against them.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The description of lands is said to be cosmological rather than historical and is arranged to migrations, from this description would be a mistake and would convert cosmology into history.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The counter-creations of Angra Mainyu content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l4644-l4701","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X / CHAPTER  V. / XC  VENDIDAD.; lines 4644-4701","start":"4644","end":"4701","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains the Zoroastrian view of fire, water, and earth as holy and not to be defiled by corpses or careless treatment. Fire, when ritually tended with perfumes and dry wood, is said to kill thousands of fiends like Bahram in heaven. Fire used for ordinary purposes is only a temporary exile and must be returned to its proper altar (Daityo Gatu, the Bahram fire). Gratuitous degradation of fire—such as blowing on it with one's breath—is a crime, and burning the dead is described as a heinous, even capital, offense and a sin without atonement. Water is regarded in the same way: bringing dead matter into it is as bad as defiling fire, and the Magi are said to have overthrown a king for building bath-houses, caring more for the purity of water than for their own. Earth likewise becomes holy through the presence of the goddess Spenta Armaiti; corpses must not defile her, and burying the dead, like burning them, is counted as a deed for which there is no atonement. though atonement and cleansing are requested.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The text describes clothes \"of skin or woven\" being This absolute condemnation applies if the sinner is a professor of the law of Mazda or has been taught it; if he has not, the law of Mazda can remove his sin when he confesses it and resolves never again to commit such forbidden deeds. The law of Mazda is said to take away the bonds of sin, including breach of trust, murdering one of the faithful, burying a corpse, sins previously held to have no atonement, and the heaviest penalties of sin, cleansing any sin that may be sinned. It also cleanses the faithful from every evil thought, word, and deed as a swift rushing mighty wind cleanses the plain, and Zarathustra is exhorted to make his future deeds good, as full atonement is effected through this law. Zarathustra then asks who is truly a Daeva or worshipper of Daevas, in various male and female forms, and who is a Daeva before death and becomes one of the unseen Daevas after death. Ahura Mazda answers that the man who lies with mankind in the manner of intercourse between man and womankind, or as woman lies with mankind, is that Daeva in all these senses and becomes an unseen Daeva after death. Later commentary explains the term 'vispo-daeva' in relation to older practices of invoking all the gods, the development of a class of fiends in Mazdeism, and views that demons are restless souls of XXXI X; lines 3528-3666","start":"3528","end":"3666","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains that sacrifice in Mazdean religion is more than worship: it strengthens the gods, who require food, drink, and praise, and without it they are weak against their foes. A myth recounts how the god Tutrya (Tistrya), defeated by Apaosha, gains the strength of horses, bulls, mountains, and rivers through a sacrifice offered by Ahura Mazda and then drives Apaosha away. Sacrifice consists of offerings (holy water, holy meat, and especially the sacred intoxicant plant Haoma) and spells. Two forms of Haoma are described: the earthly yellow/golden Haoma, king of healing plants, and the white Haoma Gaokerena, a world-plant growing in the middle of the sea Vouru-kasha among ten thousand healing plants; drinking Gaokerena at the resurrection makes humans immortal. Prayer or spell is said to be as powerful as offerings: Ormazd once confounded Ahriman by reciting the Honover (Ahuna Vairya), and human prayers travel between earth and heaven to smite various fiends. Several divinities are said to spring from the altar hearth and ritual exchange, many with Vedic counterparts: Piety (Aramati), associated with the altar fire (Agni/Atar); the fire messengers Nara-śansa and Nairyo-sangha; personified riches Rata, Ashi, and Pareñdi (sister of Vedic Puramdhi); and the personified cosmic order Asha Vahuta, corresponding to Vedic Rita. Sraosha is portrayed as the priest god who first prepared the ritual Baresma, offered sacrifice to Ahura, and sang the hymns; his weapons are sacred formulas (Ahuna Vairya and the Yasna). He descends thrice daily and nightly to smite Angra Mainyu and demons, protecting both the living world from nocturnal terrors and the dead from demonic assaults. At the end of time, Ormazd as Zoti and Sraosha as Raspi will perform a decisive sacrifice that will forever vanquish and nullify Ahriman. The author concludes that Mazdeism’s individual elements resemble those of Vedic and Indo-European traditions, though reorganized in a distinctive Damsels return to her, and people at home, seeing them come to plunder, cry out that the king’s child is of age. At the family home, the girl's mother feeds the cannibal and has him beat the bag; the girl's voice is heard again, so the mother summons the king, her father. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l7547-l7635","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / UNTOMBINDE. / APPENDIX. / MONSTERS.; lines 7547-7635","start":"7547","end":"7635","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Appendix discussing monster lore. Callaway cites Tylor’s view that tales of giants and monsters, often linked to fossil bones, occur worldwide. He notes that Zulu legends imply belief in former giants and include the great river monster Isikgukgumadevu and a many‑headed monster friendly to the hero Usikulumi; these beliefs do not seem based on fossils. Isikgukgumadevu is compared to the Basuto Kammapa. Callaway then lists parallels from many traditions: Greek Hydra, Minotaur, and the sea monster slain by Perseus; a Neapolitan dragon killed by Minuccio; a Highland three‑headed loch monster; a German seven‑headed dragon; a Polynesian monstrous cuttlefish fought by Kupe; the American Indian sturgeon Mishe‑Nahma that swallows Hiawatha; the Hindu tale of Hari as a gigantic saving fish who tows Satyavrata’s ship through a cosmic deluge, plus world‑supporting tortoise and elephant; a Muslim legend of a gigantic, speaking camel from a mountain that gives milk; an Ojibwa legend of an immense dormouse shrunk by the sun; the Norse world‑encircling serpent Jormungand and the wolf Fenrir bound by the magical chain Gleipnir whose foam forms a river; and further monstrous beasts like the Nemean lion, a great bear of the mountains, and the huge serpent that slays Cadmus’s companions and bends an oak with its weight.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Tylor is quoted as saying that tales of giants and monsters, connected with the discovery of great fossil bones, are widespread in world mythology.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Zulu legends imply, but do not clearly state, a belief in the former existence of giants.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Zulu beliefs in giants and monsters are said not to have arisen from observing huge fossil remains.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Isikgukgumadevu is described as the great monster of the Zulu tales.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Isikgukgumadevu is a river monster that is also capable of living on land.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Isikgukgumadevu is said to answer to the Kammapa of the Basuto legends.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In the tale of Usikulumi there is a many‑headed monster that is usually destructive but proves friendly to Usikulumi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The many‑headed Hydra of antiquity is recalled and is described as being slain by Hercules.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Minotaur is recalled as a monster slain by Theseus.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A sea monster sent by Neptune to ravage Ethiopia is recalled; Perseus turns it into a rock using the magical power of Medusa’s head.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In a Neapolitan tale, Minuccio kills a monstrous dragon with an enchanted leaf; the dragon can tear with claws, crush with its head and tail, bite with its teeth, poison with its eyes, and kill with its breath, and is said, like Isikgukgumadevu, to make nothing of an army.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A Highland tale features a three‑headed monster of the loch that is about to devour the king’s daughter but is killed by the fisherman’s son.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"German folk‑lore has a tale of a seven‑headed dragon killed by a young huntsman.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In Polynesian mythology, Kupe is attacked by a monstrous cuttlefish that raises its arms above the waters to catch and devour his canoe and its men, but Kupe kills it with an axe.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"American Indian lore includes the monstrous sturgeon Mishe‑Nahma, king of fishes, which opens its great jaws and swallows both a canoe and Hiawatha.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In Hindu mythology, Hari, the preserver of the universe, assumes the form of a small fish to save the holy king Satyavrata and in that form asks for the king’s protection.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Hari’s fish form grows rapidly to an immense size, leading the king to suspect a divine incarnation; the god reveals himself and promises preservation in an approaching deluge that will plunge the three worlds into water.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"On the appointed day, Hari appears as a gigantic golden fish with a stupendous horn; Satyavrata ties his ship to the horn with a cable made from a vast serpent.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Hindu tradition also includes a myth of a world‑supporting tortoise and elephant.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"In Muslim legend, a camel one hundred cubits high comes forth from a cleft mountain in answer to the prayer of Salih, can speak, and when touched by Gabriel’s flaming sword gives birth to a similar young camel.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The miraculous camel visits people’s dwellings daily, calls them by name, and supplies them with milk.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"An Ojibwa legend portrays the dormouse as originally the largest animal in the world, appearing like a mountain when it stood up, but it is reduced to its present size by the heat of the sun while being freed from a snare.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"In Norse mythology, Jormungand or Midgard’s Serpent is cast by All‑father into the deep ocean surrounding all lands and grows so large that it encircles the whole world and bites its own tail.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The wolf Fenrir, offspring of Loki and Angurboda, is almost as large as Midgard’s Serpent; after breaking the chains Laeding and Dromi, he is finally bound by the chain Gleipnir, made from six improbable materials, and the foam from his mouth forms the river Von.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"The Greeks are said to have the Nemean Lion and American Indians a ‘great bear of the mountains’ as examples of huge monstrous beasts.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"A huge serpent in the story of Cadmus kills all his companions, withstands a rock powerful enough to shake city walls, and bends a lofty oak by its weight.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Isikgukgumadevu","description":"The great monster of the Zulu tales, a river monster capable of living on land.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Kammapa","description":"A monster from Basuto legends to which Isikgukgumadevu is said to correspond.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Many-headed monster in the tale of Usikulumi","description":"A many-headed monster that is usually destructive but becomes friendly to Usikulumi.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Usikulumi","description":"Hero of a Zulu tale who is befriended by a many-headed monster.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Hydra","description":"A many-headed monster of antiquity slain by Hercules.","role_refs":["role:4","role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Hercules","description":"Hero who slays the Hydra.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Minotaur","description":"A monster of Greek myth slain by Theseus.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Theseus","description":"Hero who slays the Minotaur.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Sea monster sent by Neptune","description":"Sea monster sent to ravage Ethiopia as punishment for Cassiope’s vanity; turned into a rock by Perseus using Medusa’s head.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Neptune","description":"God who sends a sea monster to She protests, explaining that when she properly eats amasi many oxen will be slaughtered and the milk will be given to her ceremonially, but the leaves urge her to eat immediately, and she takes a spoon and together they finish all the amasi. A footnote explains the Zulu puberty rite in which a girl in seclusion (umgongo) may not eat amasi until she is called out by her father, when a bullock is slaughtered, ritual acts are performed, and she then may eat amasi. The narrative comments that the leaves spoil the village and that Ueilosimapundu devours everything there. The leaves then go to a house near the gateway, remove pots of beer, boiled meal, mats, and vessels, and carry everything to the gateway. They empty all the houses in the village. When they reach the house of Umkccakaza’s mother, Umkccakaza asks them to leave a small pot in the upper part of the house, sealed with cowdung. things.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The leaves tell Umkccakaza-wakoginggwayo that they already knew she was of age and that she did Inside the cave is Umkxakaza, a female being, who sees the many people approaching and says that the day has come on which she will be killed. When the people reach a tree near the cave, they sit in its shade, as they usually do when they go to pluck tobacco and take snuff. They then go into a tobacco garden, pluck tobacco, and place it outside the garden, following the chief’s standing order that his cave must be regularly swept and that anyone going to sweep it must first pluck tobacco and put it outside. The people ask the two men exactly where they saw the mysterious being, and are told it appeared in the cave. The two are then sent to look through the cave doorway to see if it is still there; they approach stealthily, being afraid, and look inside. They cannot see clearly because Umkxakaza’s body glistens, and they return to say there is one glistening being which they cannot make out. The chief tells everyone to shout together, asking whether the being is a man or a beast, and they do so. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l21927-l22036","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / UMKXAKAZA-WAKOGINGQWAYO. / IZINGANEKWANE. / UMKXAKAZA-WAKOGINGQWAYO.; lines 21927-22036","start":"21927","end":"22036","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A deformed being called Ukandakulu, with a very large, fearful head, walks with a princess (the king’s sister) to a dancing-place. They enter the village, where she stands at the doorway while he bows to his chief, and people wish to drive her away for her deformity. An editorial footnote compares this Zulu episode to several Northern (Norse) tales in which a damsel guided by a white bear breaks a forest taboo and unleashes attacking beasts, a very old woman or That night Uzembeni secretly rises intending to seize and eat Usikulumi, but each time the skin wakes him and he escapes her surprise. At dawn the skin tells him to depart because Uzembeni has already set out, so he flees with a damsel from the house. By day she goes out to dig in her garden, sitting until sunset and wondering whether her children can live, while lamenting that other women jeer at her and are described as giving birth not to human beings but to crows. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l6878-l6985","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"UNTOM13IND3. / IZIXG  ANEXWANE. / IZINGANEKWANE. / UNTOMBINDE.; lines 6878-6985","start":"6878","end":"6985","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this portion of the tale of Untombinde, a mysterious bridegroom has been visiting the girl at night, speaking to her although she cannot see him. Each morning he departs, yet the wicker door of the hut remains closed as she left it, and he continually refuses to allow her to light a fire. After one such departure she feels the door and finds it still shut, wondering how he went out. The next morning her mother enters, questions her about whom she was speaking with and who has been eating the food, but the girl denies any knowledge, and they themselves eat the food. For a third time food and drink are prepared—beer, meat, and sour milk. That evening the visitor, named Untlilatu in the translation, arrives again, touches the girl’s face and wakes her, then instructs her to feel his body from his feet to his head so she can know what he is like. She finds his body slippery and impossible to grasp. He then asks if she wants him to tell her to light the fire; when she agrees he first asks for snuff, takes a pinch from her hand, and sniffs it. An editorial footnote explicitly compares this pattern of an unseen nocturnal visitor to the story of Cupid and Psyche and to the Neapolitan tale \"The Myrtle\" in the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l3389-l3487","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"UHLAKANYANA. / IZINGANEKWANE. / UHLAKANYANA. / IZINGANEKWANE.; lines 3389-3487","start":"3389","end":"3487","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“Two cows made their appearance—one white, the other black…. ‘Let your cow be killed first, my uncle, which is white outside and in, that we may just see if it is, as you said, white also inside.’… They found it lean…. It was killed, and found to be very fat…. ‘You see the sky, that we shall get wet.’”","summary":"A cannibal thanks his sister’s child, Uthlakanyana, for helping him when he was very hungry, and they eat meat together. Two cows then appear, one white and one black. The cannibal claims them as his, but Uthlakanyana claims the black cow for himself, while the cannibal insists the white cow is his and is white (fat) outside and inside. At Uthlakanyana’s suggestion they build a house so they can live comfortably and eat their cattle. Uthlakanyana then advises that the cannibal’s white cow be killed first to see if it is as good inside as claimed. When it is killed and skinned, it is found to be lean, and Uthlakanyana refuses to eat it, asking that his own black cow be killed instead. The black cow proves to be very fat. The cannibal praises his nephew’s wisdom in seeing at once that his cow was fat. Later, many cattle and men arrive at the village in the afternoon, leading the villagers to think they are an army that has made a raid. The men leave some cattle outside, bring others into the kraal, drive them into the cattle-pen, and respectfully ask the father—described as a king—for his daughter. Ahura Mazda, the Maker of all good things, summons his herald Nairyo-sangha and sends him to the mansion of Airyaman with a message. The leopard later explicitly entrusts her children to Uthlakanyana’s care while she goes out, and he secretly builds a house with a very small doorway, digs a long burrow with a distant outlet, and prepares four assagais. The leopard returns bringing a buck and calls his name, and he answers, but the episode breaks off before the outcome is told.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Uthlakanyana tells the leopard to suckle one child first and promises to give her the other when the first has come back to him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The leopard refuses Uthlakanyana’s suggested way of nursing, saying she does not suckle in that to come out, skin her buck, and cook its flesh as he had said he would do.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Uthlakanyana skins the leopard’s buck and boils its morning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A narrative heading states that Uthlakanyana eats the leopard and her cubs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The leopard instructs Uthlakanyana to stay and keep things safe, explicitly entrusting her children to his care and telling him to preserve them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Uthlakanyana builds a house and completes it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The house Uthlakanyana builds has a very small content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l821-l880","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VOL.  I. / IZINGANEKWANE. / IZINGANEKWANE. / INTRODUCTION  TO  THE  ZULU  NURSERY  TALES.; lines 821-880","start":"821","end":"880","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this 1866 introduction, H. C. explains that the Zulus, like other peoples, have nursery tales, but these have not previously been collected and are mostly preserved by women and grandmothers, with men usually recalling them only dimly. He notes that it was difficult to obtain the tales and that many are merely fragments of fuller narratives, which he considers often ridiculous and seemingly unworthy of preservation, yet potentially useful. He argues that publishing them can reveal unsuspected points of contact with other peoples, offer clues to Zulu origins, and demonstrate that Zulus share common thoughts and similar traditional tales with others, supporting their place in \"our common humanity.\" He also proposes that these familiar tales will be eagerly read by young Zulus, in contrast to the difficult and alien Bible-based translations they currently read with loathing, criticizing the practice of teaching reading solely from religious texts. Instead, he wants to use the traditional tales of their forefathers, in the same words heard around hut-fires, as inducements to literacy. He concludes by announcing that the first tale will recount the travels and adventures of Uthlakanyana, described as a kind of Tom Thumb.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Zulus are said to have their own nursery tales, like most other peoples.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The nursery tales have not previously been collected and their existence is thought to be suspected only by a few.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Women are described as the depositaries of the nursery tales, while it is uncommon to meet a man well acquainted with them or willing to speak of them, except as something dimly remembered from his grandmother.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The author states that it was not easy to obtain the tales, describing the process as having to 'drag out' the following tales.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The collected tales are said to be largely fragments of more complete narratives.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The author characterizes much of the material as 'supremely ridiculous' and apparently unworthy of being perpetuated when considered by itself.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Despite calling the tales ridiculous and worthless in themselves, the author asserts that they will be useful in many ways.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The author believes the tales will help uncover As a man is walking, the bird appears before him, chirping loudly. Believing his hunger will be satisfied because the bird is calling him \"for a reality,\" he responds to it and praises it as the honey-bird that calls women when they are digging. The bird cries loudly in the bushes and acts as a guide, going ahead while the man follows without asking where he is going. Because the bird flies and the man must force his way through undergrowth, the bird sometimes goes far ahead and then returns to meet him. When the man stops hearing its cry, he repeatedly asks where it has gone and shouts loudly to show he is looking for it, remaining at the spot where it left him. The bird returns there, making a great noise, and the man cheers it. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l236-l317","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"TRUBNER  AND  CO.,  60,  PATERNOSTER  ROW. / NATAL / PRINTED  AT  SPRINGY  ALE  MISSION  STATION. / PREFACE  TO  THE  FIRST  VOLUME.; lines 236-317","start":"236","end":"317","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this preface segment, the missionary-collector reflects on collections of Zulu children’s tales, arguing that although now told to children they are not childish inventions and, when compared with other peoples’ legends, reveal unexpected relationships and the essential mental unity of humankind. A footnote notes that, with an ingenuity like that of Rev. G. W. Cox in interpreting Greek literature as solar myths, many of these tales could likewise be read as solar myths, linking Greek and Zulu traditions or an even earlier period. The author then quotes Elizabeth Cookson, who compares customs and creeds to fossil remains for historians, and popular tales and superstitions to clock hands and atmospheric reflection that preserve and reflect past modes of thought. Cookson argues that fables mirror the minds of less scientific ancestors, that belief in fairies and spectres shows how strongly phenomena impressed them, and that living in a marvellous world led people to question until dark diviners and interpreters arose, seeking light and answers to life’s enigma. Returning to the Zulus, the author concludes that their tales show them to be a degenerated people who have declined from an earlier legend-producing period, like relics of giant buildings pointing to a mightier past, yet also that their lore shows real intellectual power and tender feeling, so that with culture they could develop the finest human traits. He argues that such collections are practically useful because one cannot reach a people without deep knowledge of their language and traditional lore, citing Sir George Grey’s experience in New Zealand, and stating that his own study of these tales aids his work translating the Bible and Prayer Book into the Zulu language.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The author states that the collected Zulu children’s tales are not the invention of a child’s intellect and not all invented merely to gratify a child’s fancy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"He claims that careful study and comparison of these tales with corresponding legends among other peoples will reveal unexpected relationships.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"He argues that such relationships will increasingly force recognition of a great truth: that humans everywhere, regardless of country, climate, skin color, or social and intellectual condition, share essential mental qualities, tendencies, emotions, and passions.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In a footnote he remarks that, using ingenuity similar to that employed by Rev. G. W. Cox on ancient Greek literature, many of these Zulu tales could readily be converted into solar myths, thereby connecting Greek and Zulu traditions or both with a period earlier than either.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Elizabeth Cookson, as quoted, states that customs and creeds are to the historian what fossil remains are to the geologist—landmarks of the extent and progress of intelligence and civilization.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Cookson says that popular tales, songs, and superstitions are not profitless but, like the fingers of a clock, point to the time of day, and that they preserve and reflect modes of thought which would otherwise have sunk into darkness, as atmospheric reflection can occasionally bring objects below the horizon back into view.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Cookson asserts that fables are facts insofar as they mirror the minds of less scientific ancestors.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Cookson argues that the solemn belief of people in fairies, spectres, and many kinds of superstition testifies to the vivid impression that physical and mental phenomena made on their minds.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Cookson describes people as placed in a world of marvels, questioning the marvellous until dark diviners and interpreters arose who, though bewildered and bewildering, strive after light, seek to solve the enigma of life, and try to cast off from the soul the burden of an unexplained existence.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Reflecting on Zulu tales, the author concludes that they clearly show the Zulus to be a degenerated people who are no longer in the intellectual or physical condition they had during an earlier legend-producing period, having sunk from a higher state.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"He likens Zulu tales to discovered relics of giant buildings in Asia and America, which seem to speak of a mightier and better past that may be lost forever.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"He suggests that although the tales themselves may be powerless to retrace successive generations’ footsteps, it is reasonable to suppose that under influences reaching them from without the Zulus are capable of regeneration.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"He states that Zulu legendary lore contains evidence of intellectual powers not to be despised and that the tales are filled with evidences of tender feeling, gentleness, and love.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"He argues that in dealing with the Zulus, even if they are called savages, one is dealing with ‘savage men’ who only need culture to develop in them the finest traits of human nature.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"He claims that a chief practical use of the collection is to provide means of bringing culture to bear upon the Zulus.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"He maintains that one cannot reach any people without knowing their minds and mode of thought, which in turn cannot be known without thorough knowledge of their language beyond loose colloquial study.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"He cites Sir George Grey’s view that rightful government of the people of New Zealand required not only thorough knowledge of their language but also of their traditional lore.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"He says that an earnest and intelligent missionary feels an even greater need for such linguistic and traditional knowledge to handle questions requiring a subtler use of words than matters concerning only external relations.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"He notes that scarcely a day passes without his finding the value of such knowledge, and that the lighter study of children’s tales has prepared him to undertake the more serious task of translating the Bible and Prayer Book into the native tongue with greater confidence.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Missionary-author / collector","description":"The first-person narrator who collects and For then thou wilt turn gray.”

“Return, return, unhappy bride,

Within this den the murderers hide.”","summary":"The passage discusses the recurring figure of a little bird in various cited European tales that aids female protagonists: it warns an enchanted damsel not to look at the blue billows lest she turn gray, warns a betrayed bride that murderers hide in a den, exposes the deception of a false bride, and restores a forgotten bride to the prince’s recollection. The author then introduces an account of the real honey-bird’s remarkably intelligent-seeming habits, as reported by a native informant and corroborated by white men who have been led by the bird to deposits of honey. He suggests that many bird-related superstitions may originate in such manifestations of apparent animal intelligence and argues that a “childlike mind” does not sharply distinguish human from animal intelligence. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.african-nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-archive-l1693-l1778","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zulu/project-gutenberg/nursery-tales-traditions-histories-zulus-callaway.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IZINGANEKWANE. / UHLAKANYANA. / IZINGAXEKWANE. / UHLAKANYANA.; lines 1693-1778","start":"1693","end":"1778","translation":"Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus, in Their Own Words","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage opens with a remark on Uhlakanyana, described as a man whose powers in childhood allowed him to speak impressively and to overpower old men, exemplified when he took a leg of beef. The text then gives an Irish changeling story: Mrs Sullivan’s baby has wasted away and cries incessantly, leading her and her neighbours to believe that fairies have taken the child and put one of themselves in its place. On Ellen Leah’s advice, Mrs Sullivan makes a ‘brewery of egg-shells’ by boiling eggshells in a pot on a fierce fire to test whether the infant is a fairy. The child in the cradle watches the fire and pot attentively, then speaks in the voice of an old man and, when told egg-shells are being brewed, shrieks that he has been fifteen hundred years in the world and never seen such a thing. As Mrs Sullivan rushes with a red‑hot poker to attack the imp, she slips; when she reaches the cradle intending to throw the wicked being into the boiling water, she finds instead her own child sleeping peacefully. The story is cited as coming from Croker’s Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland, and a note directs readers to Thorpe’s work for other methods of detecting an imp that has replaced a child.","language":"English (with some Zulu)","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Uhlakanyana is described as a man who, while still a child, could speak impressively and was strong enough to get the better of old men, as shown when he took a leg of beef.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Mrs Sullivan’s baby had wasted away physically and never stopped squalling and crying.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Mrs Sullivan and her neighbours believed that fairies had taken a fancy to her baby and had placed one of themselves in its stead.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Because of this belief, the changeling was nearly subjected to deadly tests such as being griddled alive or other experiments intended to determine whether it could be destroyed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ellen Leah advised Mrs Sullivan to make a ‘brewery of egg-shells’ to see whether the crying child would reveal itself as a fairy, and only then to cram a red‑hot poker down its throat.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Mrs Sullivan followed the advice and put a pot on the fire, with plenty of fuel, boiling the water very fiercely.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The child lay unusually quiet in the cradle, watching the great fire and the big pot on it, and looked attentively at Mrs Sullivan as she broke eggs and put the shells into the boiling water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The child spoke with the voice of a very old man, asking his mother what she was doing and what she was brewing.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Mrs Sullivan, while hearing the child speak, put a poker into the fire to heat it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When Mrs Sullivan said she was brewing egg-shells, the child exclaimed that he was fifteen hundred years in the world and had When this has been done, all the women are ordered to come and leap over the pit, in which milk has been placed, and the bride is called to join them. This is done because it is said that when the Imbulu sees the milk, it will throw itself in to eat it. They go to the kraal; the bride says she is afraid to enter the cattle-pen of strangers but is told to go and does so. The other women leap over the pit; the bride is told to leap and is about to do so when the passage ends. When she uncovers the pot in the ninth month, the clot has become a child. The pigeons tell her to put the child in a bag, wrap him, hide him at the back of the house from other women, and feed him abundantly so that he grows quickly, which he does. When her husband comes home in the evening, unaware of the child, she brings the child forward, sets his food before him, and calls him her child. The husband is astonished and asks whose child it is. She explains that he is the child of a clot of her blood and of the pigeons that taught her wisdom by telling her the procedure. The husband rejoices that she now has a child, and the clot-born child grows up.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Pigeons tell the woman A proclamation ascribed to Khosrav Anosharvan states that the collection of Avesta fragments began under the last Arsacides and was completed under Shapur II. King Valkash ordered surviving fragments of the Avesta, whether preserved from Alexander’s ravages or by oral tradition, to be sought out and collected. Ardeshir Babagan, the first Sassanian king, made the Avesta the sacred book of Iran and established Mazdeism as the state religion. Under Shapur II, Adarbad Mahraspand purified the Avesta and fixed the number of the Nasks, and Shapur proclaimed to the heterodox that, having recognised the ‘law of the world here below,’ infidelity would not be allowed. The author then notes that the authenticity of this record has been questioned, especially because it assigns a major role to an Arsacide prince, which seems at odds with common views of the Sassanian revolution. Most Parsi and Muslim writers instead credit the Sassanian dynasty with raising Zoroastrianism from the humiliation caused by the Greek invasion, reviving national spirit, and making Mazdeism a cornerstone of the new political order. The author finds it strange that the initial step toward making Mazdeism a state religion could have been taken by Philhellenic Parthian princes steeped in Greek culture. Finally, the passage notes that a Brahmanical account of the origin of the castes in a related text was certainly borrowed from India, although it is uncertain whether this occurred in late Sassanian times or after the Parsis settled in India. XXXV / C   2 / XXXVI  VENDIDAD.; lines 1843-1888","start":"1843","end":"1888","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The author argues that the language of the Avesta (Zend) shows that its groundwork predates the Sassanian period. Zend is closely related to ancient Persian but is an independent dialect and was never the national language of Persia. After Alexander’s death, Pahlavi, derived from ancient Persian, became the language of Persia under the Arsacide and Sassanian dynasties. Because Sassanian kings were bound to represent genuine old Persian tradition, they would not have chosen an old foreign dialect for newly composed religious books, so their adoption of Zend as the language of religion implies that Zend sacred texts already existed and were used by the editors of the Avesta. Zend is described as a dead foreign language but still understood by the learned class (priests), as shown by their Pahlavi translation, and the author notes that editors may also have composed new Zend texts.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The groundwork of the Avesta is presented as anterior to the age of the Sassanians based on linguistic evidence.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Avesta is written in the language called Parsi tradition holds that it is the only one of twenty-one Nosks preserved in full, though its fragmentary character suggests otherwise. The work is often called the book of Parsi laws but more precisely a code of purification, since rules of purification occupy much of it. Parsis are described as strict monotheists whose supreme deity is Ahura Mazda; Angra Mainyu is viewed much like the orthodox Christian devil. The word Vendidad derives from Vidaevo-datem, ‘anti-demonic law,’ and can refer to the whole legal corpus. The first two chapters are mythic remnants: one about the creations and counter-creations of Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu, the other about Yima, founder of civilisation. Additional mythical chapters treat the origin of medicine, and Fargard XIX describes Ahura’s revelation of the law to Zarathustra. Seventeen other chapters focus on religious observances but include mythic fragments and moral digressions. Cycles of time (months of Tir and Di) are said to overturn powerful rulers like Djem and Kai. Venus and the moon are invoked to frame the claim that nothing on earth surpasses ruby wine, and wine-merchants are paradoxically said to buy something superior to what they sell. XXXI X; lines 3884-3984","start":"3884","end":"3984","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage compares the Vedic Yama, son of Vivasvat, with his Avesta twin-brother Yima, son of Vivanghat. Yama is described as the first man and first of the dead, king of the dead and center of gathering for departed souls in the heavenly Yamasadanam near Varuṇa. Yima, though no longer the first man (a role transferred to Gayo Maratan), retains related attributes as first king and founder of civilisation; the "best mortals" gather around him in a marvellous palace in Airyanem Vaejo, identified with Yamasadanam, where he meets Ahura and the gods and his people live a blessed life. The text explains that Yima’s people were originally the dead going to their ancestor and king of heaven, but later were reinterpreted as a supernatural race distinct from humans who still go day by day from earth to heaven to join Ahura Mazda.

It then outlines eschatological myths: the world’s life is limited to a long year of twelve millennia; an old myth had the world end in a frightful winter followed by an eternal spring, when the blessed will come down from Yima’s Vara to repeople the earth. A more dramatic version, which became definitive, has the world end in a storm. At the end, the serpent Azi Dahaka is let loose and seizes the world; the temporary disappearance and reappearance of light are mythically described as the sleeping or death of the god and the awakening, return, or birth of his son. This yields tales of Keresaspa awakening from sleep to kill the serpent, of Peshotanu, Aghraeratha, Khumbya and others living in remote lands until the day of the last fight, and of Saoshyant, the son to be born to Zarathustra at the end of time, who will bring eternal light and life to mankind as his father brought law and truth, and who is expected to destroy Ahriman.

Finally, the author discusses whether any historical reality underlies the legend of Zoroaster. Mazdeism is often called Zoroaster’s religion, as Islam is Muhammad’s, suggesting a single human founder, and this view is encouraged by Parsi and Greek accounts and by the system’s unity. The moral and abstract spirit of Mazdeism differs from the Vedic spirit, and the word "deva" shifts from meaning "god" in Sanskrit to "demon" in the Avesta, inspiring the idea that Zoroaster’s work was a reaction against Indian polytheism. Yet Zoroaster’s historical dates are unknown and traditional accounts are deemed mere legend. The author concludes, based on the Avesta, that Zoroaster is an essential mythological figure within Mazdeism, comparable to the son expected to be born to him at the end of time to destroy XXXI X; lines 3781-3882","start":"3781","end":"3882","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Man, according to his deeds, belongs to Ormazd or to Ahriman.\"","summary":"The passage explains how animals, humans, and celestial bodies are classified as belonging to Ormazd or Ahriman, often through storm imagery and zoomorphic incarnations of gods and fiends. A storm fiend is described as serpent-like because cloud coils encircle a goddess of light or heavenly milch cows. Killing Ahrimanian creatures (Khrafstras) is treated as killing Ahriman himself and can atone for sin, while killing Ormazdean animals is equated with killing God and condemned. Birds of prey are linked to the lightning god and Ormazd, prompting Parsi theologians to narrate Ormazd’s conflicted creation of a hunting hawk and to cite a Bundahis passage about Ahriman’s potential hawk. Ahriman is also said to create a lovely peacock to display wilful wickedness, and Satan is noted as being invoked by Yezidis as Melek Taus, the “angel peacock.” The storm deity Tistrya, conqueror of the demon Apaosha, appears as boar, horse, or youth and is compared to a shining star; stars fight on Ahura’s side with Tistrya, while planets join Ahriman’s army, influenced by Chaldaean ideas. Humans are divided morally: a man of Asha belongs to Ormazd by sacrifice, good thoughts, words, and deeds, and by spreading life and destroying Ahriman’s creatures; such a man may be a priest (Athravan), warrior (Rathaejta), or husbandman (Vastryo). The nature of the Yatu (wizard) is said to show itself in the look (evil eye) and in howled spells, which send forth deadly witchcraft to kill and strike. A gloss adds that wizards produce snow and hail and increase the plague of locusts and compares this to material in Hippocrates' De Morbo Sacro and Pausanias. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l1891-l1984","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXV / C   2 / XXXVI  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXVU; lines 1891-1984","start":"1891","end":"1984","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Darmesteter discusses the dating and redaction of the Avesta and related Zend texts. He notes that the bulk of the Avesta is pre-Sassanian, though some passages may be late. Drawing on the Dinkard and the Kissah-i San‘ah, he describes how Mazdeism was shaken by Mani’s religion and how Adarbad Mahraspand under Shapur II is said to have restored the faith, given the Avesta its definitive form, and closed the Holy Writ. A prophecy attributed to Zoroaster foretells that the holy religion will be overthrown three times and restored three times, with a final restoration at the end of time by Soshyos. Parsi tradition recognizes three ‘founders’ of the Avesta—Zoroaster (receiving it from Ormazd), Gamasp (receiving it from Zoroaster), and Adarbad (teaching and purifying it). Darmesteter infers that the last revision occurred early in Shapur II’s reign in response to Mani’s heresy and notes a chronological parallel with the Christian Council of Nicaea. He also allows that some Zend texts may have been composed as late as the fourth century CE.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The earliest date for a particular translation of the Avesta, in its present form, is placed in the last century of the Sassanian dynasty because it alludes to the death of the heresiarch Mazdak, son of Bamdad, executed at the beginning of Khosrav Anosharvan’s reign.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Darmesteter argues that the ability to translate a dead language implies the ability to write in it, so some Zend texts may have been newly composed by editors when the book took its definitive form, though he believes the proportion of new texts is small and that the bulk of the Avesta is pre-Sassanian.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Dinkard assigns a date to the final edition of the Avesta and its promulgation as the sacred law of Iran that fits the religious situation in Shapur II’s time, when Mazdeism had been threatened by Mani’s religion.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Mani’s religion is described as having sprung from Mazdeism and as having counted Shapur I among its followers for a time; although Mani was put to death, his work continued.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the Kissah-i San‘ah, Zoroaster is portrayed as prophesying that the holy religion will be overthrown three times and restored three times.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"According to the prophecy, the religion is first overthrown by Iskander and restored by Ardeshir.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The prophecy further states that the religion will be overthrown again and restored by Shapur II and Adarbad Mahraspand.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Lastly, the prophecy says the religion will be overthrown by the Arabs and restored at the end of time by Soshyos.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Parsi traditions describe Adarbad as a holy man under Shapur II who lived when many religions and heresies flourished in Iran and the true religion was falling into oblivion.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"These traditions state that Adarbad restored the true religion through a miracle, allowing melted brass to be poured on his breast without being harmed, as a sign of the religion’s truth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Darmesteter suggests that Adarbad’s miracle is probably borrowed from the legend of Zoroaster.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Kissah-i San‘ah and the Dinkard imply that Adarbad restored Mazdeism, which had been shaken by the Manichean heresy, and that he gave a definitive form to Iran’s religious book, closing the Holy Writ.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"During recitation of the Patet, Parsi worshippers acknowledge Adarbad as the third founder of the Avesta.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The same tradition identifies Zoroaster as the first founder, who received the Avesta from Ormazd, and Gamasp as the second, who received it from Zoroaster; Adarbad is the third, who taught the Avesta and restored it to purity.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Darmesteter infers that the Avesta likely took its definitive form from Adarbad Mahraspand under King Shapur II, as a response to the danger posed by Mani’s heresy to the national religion.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"He notes that Mani’s death and the first persecution of his followers occurred about thirty years before Shapur II’s accession to the throne.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Darmesteter presumes that the last revision of the Avesta was carried out in the first years of Shapur II’s reign, when agitation over Mani’s doctrines and incomplete persecutions had not subsided and the old religion was still unstable.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"From this he concludes that Zend texts could theoretically have been composed as late as the fourth century A.D., although this is presented as a possibility rather than a firm claim.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"He mentions the liturgical parts of the Yasna, Visperad, and Sirozah in connection with the discussion of possible later composition.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"A footnote reports that Shapur II ascended the throne around 309, “before being born” according to tradition, and that he seems from the Dinkard to have taken a personal part in Adarbad’s work.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The footnote argues that the promulgation of the Avesta as sacred law could hardly have taken place before 325–330.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The note compares Adarbad and the Fathers at Nicaea as contemporaries and suggests that Zoroastrian threats by the king of Iran and Catholic anathemas by the Kaisar of Rum may have been issued on the same day.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Zoroaster","description":"Prophetic founder of the holy religion, depicted prophesying three overthrows content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-vendidad-darmesteter-archive-l2295-l2398","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-1-vendidad.md","passage_locator":{"label":"C   2 / XXXVI  VENDIDAD. / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXVU / INTRODUCTION,    III.  XXXI X; lines 2295-2398","start":"2295","end":"2398","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendidad","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains that Avesta law treats burial of corpses in the earth as a heinous sin and instead prescribes laying bodies on mountain summits to be devoured by birds and dogs; this exposure of corpses became a distinctive mark of Mazdean adherence and was strictly enforced under the Sassanians. Under the Achaemenian kings, however, general Persian practice was to bury corpses in the earth, while the Magi alone followed the exposure custom. From this the author concludes that Avesta ideas and customs originally belonged to a sacerdotal caste, so that there were practically two religions in Iran: one for laypeople and one for priests, with the Avesta initially the sacred book of the Magi and later extended to laymen. The passage then argues that the Avesta’s non-Persian dialect reflects the non-Persian origin of the Magi, locating them in Media according to Greek historians and Parsi traditions. Ammianus Marcellinus is cited as describing the Magi as a hereditary priestly tribe in Media, taught magical science by King Hystaspes, living in unwalled towns under their own laws, and providing priests for Iran; Strabo and Herodotus likewise treat the Magi as a sacerdotal tribe among the Medes, and Parsi traditions are said to agree with these testimonies.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"According to the Avesta, burying corpses in the earth is described as one of the most heinous sins that can be committed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Avesta prescribes that corpses are to be laid down on the summits of mountains to be devoured by birds and dogs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The exposure of corpses is presented as the most striking practice of Mazdean profession, and adopting this practice is called the sign of conversion.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Under the Sassanians, a prime minister named Seoses was put to death for infringing the Avesta law on the treatment of corpses.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Under Achaemenian rule, burial of the dead in the earth was not forbidden and was the general Persian practice.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Herodotus reports that Persians bury their dead in the earth after coating the corpses with wax.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Herodotus adds that the Magi do not follow the general Persian practice but lay corpses on the ground to be devoured by birds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The author concludes that Avesta ideas and customs already existed under the Achaemenian kings but were originally those of The Parsis and their sacred books are described as \"ruins\" of a once-great religion, yet the Avesta and Parsi belief are valued as the last reflex of ideas in Iran from several centuries around the time of Christ, influencing movements connected with the Gospels, Talmud, and Qur'an and marking a blending of Aryan and Semitic thought. The passage then traces Greek and later inquiries into Persian religion—from Aristotle and other historians to late antique religious and philosophical sects, Neo-Platonists, and Gnostics—who produced oracles and secret books under the name of Zoroaster, whose name had become an emblem of wisdom. Ahura is entirely light, truth, goodness, and knowledge, dwelling in infinite light, while Angra Mainyu is darkness, falsehood, wickedness, and ignorance, dwelling in infinite night. Whatever the good Spirit creates, the evil Spirit corrupts: Angra Mainyu invades the created world, opposes each good creation with a plague, kills the first-born bull that was the first offspring and source of life, and mixes poison with plants, smoke with fire, sin with man, and death with life.
